We begin with the taut string met in chapter 13. There the string was at rest, and it had a wave equation, modes and frequencies. Now the string does not only move sideways, it also runs along its own length. The chapter shows what changes because of this, and it uses what we know from chapters 8 and 10, where we treated systems with finitely many degrees of freedom.

The words of the title mean something simple. A belt (jermen) is a band that runs over wheels and carries motion from one to another. Axially (aksialno) means along the axis, that is along the band through which the material runs. A moving continuum (gibajoči se zvezni sistem) is a body that we describe not by a few points but by all its points at once, and that moves as a whole. The title therefore says: we treat a belt as a continuous body through which material flows without end.

Why does this matter? A belt in a machine, a band saw between two wheels and a cable car between two towers are all such systems. For a steel strip of length 1 m, running at 40 m/s lowers the first frequency of vibration from 56.61 Hz to 49.55 Hz. At a high enough speed the frequencies fall to zero and the string loses stability, which a string at rest does not predict.

The chapter promises three things. First, from the balance of a piece of string we derive the equation for the running string and show that the waves in the two directions travel at different speeds. Next we find the modes of vibration, the speed at which the frequencies fall to zero, and a quantity that is conserved while the string runs. Last, we extend the equation to a belt with bending stiffness, turn it into finite elements and apply it to a drive with two pulleys, saying what our model leaves out.

26.1 The moving string (gibajoča struna)

A magnetic tape runs past a head, a band saw runs over two wheels, a cable car pulls its cable over two pylons, a fluid flows through a pipe, a chain and a belt run over pulleys. What they share is that matter flows along its own length and at the same time can oscillate sideways (WM1990, PDF p. 1, read). We call such a system an axially moving continuum (aksialno gibajoč se kontinuum): axially means in the direction of the axis, and a continuum is a continuous system from chapter 13. The chapter treats belts, so we take the simplest part of a belt, the span (razpon) between two pulleys, and write it as a string that runs. The question of this section is simple: does the wave equation of section 13.1 hold for such a span, or must it be changed, and how does it change?

From history

The methods for axially moving materials reach back into the nineteenth century, which WM1990 (PDF p. 1) says by naming Skutch. The text on page 1 gives the year 1987 there, which is a printing error: on the image of the page 1987 is indeed printed, but the reference list of the same paper (PDF p. 6) and the reference list of CHEN2005 (PDF p. 21) give 1897 for the same work, published in Annalen der Physik und Chemie on pages 190 to 195. The title of the work is German and in free translation reads the motion of a taut thread that is forced to run at constant speed through two fixed points and between them oscillates sideways with small amplitude (WM1990, PDF p. 6, CHEN2005, PDF p. 21). This is exactly the model of this section. According to CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2) Skutch was the first to study a moving string without excitation.

Let us return to the span between the pulleys. The story told what the model is: a taut thread that runs through two fixed points. Here we build it and derive the equation ourselves, on a steel band that we choose as the running example.

We draw the span in several steps in figure 26.1. First we take the axis \(x\) and on it two eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). An eyelet is a small ring through which the thread runs, as a thread runs through the eye of a needle, and the word means a small eye. The eyelets stand in space and the string runs through them. In this way we replace the pulleys: the span is clamped at a pulley, so the transverse displacement there is zero, and what happens to the belt on the pulley itself (wrapping, friction) the model does not ask about (idealization 6 below). We draw the string blackwhite: at rest it is a straight line along the axis \(x\), and during oscillation it is a curve \(w(x, t)\), where \(w\) is the transverse displacement of the point at \(x\) at time \(t\), as in section 13.1. The slope in the figure is strongly exaggerated so that the curve can be seen. Outside the eyelets the string runs on along the axis: the arrows \(v\) show that it enters on the left and leaves on the right, and all points of the string move along the axis \(x\) with speed \(v > 0\) in the direction of increasing \(x\). The number \(v\) in m/s we call the transport speed (hitrost transporta). In addition the string moves transversely in \(w\).

Now we can say what it is that moves. On the string we imagine a mark, like a coloured line on a thread: a material particle (točka snovi) is a piece of the string that we follow as it runs. Two dots at \(a\) and \(b\) at time \(t\) are two such particles, and the blue part of the string between them is a material piece (kos snovi): the same pieces of matter all the time, wherever they are. The lower row of the figure shows time \(t + \tau\). The material particles have moved by \(v\tau\) along the axis \(x\), since they run with speed \(v\), and the material piece now lies over the interval from \(a + v\tau\) to \(b + v\tau\). We drew the shape of the curve at \(t + \tau\) the same only to make the shift of matter visible, in real motion the shape changes too. The neighbouring parts pull the piece with force \(T\) along the tangent, each force starting at the point where it acts, as in section 13.1. The forces are drawn at both times.

The model has eight idealizations (idealizacije). We name each and give it a measure. The example is a steel band that we choose ourselves: thickness \(0{,}9\) mm, width \(50\) mm, with span length \(L = 1\) m and stress \(\sigma = 100\) MPa. Bands are found on band saws (WM1990, PDF p. 1), the dimensions, stress and speeds are our choice, we have no data on real belts (the project sources contain none). The cross-section is \(A = 4{,}5\cdot 10^{-5}\) m\(^2\), the density of steel \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m\(^3\) and the elastic modulus \(E = 196\) GPa (BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100), so the mass per unit length is \(\mu = \rho A = 0{,}3510\) kg/m and the tension is \(T = \sigma A = 4500\) N.

  1. The string is homogeneous: \(\mu\) is constant. Since all points of the string move along \(x\) with the same speed, the spacing between them along \(x\) does not change, so the mass per unit length stays \(\mu\) also in the running flow (WM1990, PDF p. 1: the axial speed is approximately \(V\)).
  2. The string has no bending stiffness, so the force in it is along the tangent. For the band \(EI = E\,b h^3/12 = 0{,}595\) N m\(^2\) and the ratio \(EI/(T L^2) = 1{,}3\cdot 10^{-4}\), which is an order-of-magnitude estimate and is small. We include bending stiffness later in this chapter, with the moving beam.
  3. The tension \(T\) is constant along the span and in time. When the string moves it stretches and the tension changes. For our band, \(EA = 8{,}82\) MN, the strain at slope \(5\cdot 10^{-3}\) is at most \(1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) and the tension changes by \(EA\cdot 1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5} = 110\) N, which is \(2{,}4\) % of \(T\), and the wave speed by \(1{,}2\) %. For the wire of section 13.1 the estimate at slope \(0{,}01\) was \(1{,}8\) %. The tension in a real belt depends also on the speed and on friction at the pulleys, about which the project sources have no data: \(T\) is here a given number (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, assumption 2).
  4. The slope is small, \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\) (stricter than \(0{,}01\) for the wire, because the band is much stiffer under tension). The tangent then makes an angle with the axis \(x\) of less than \(0{,}29^\circ\).
  5. The axial speed of every material particle is \(v\), constant and equal for all (WM1990, PDF p. 1). If a particle ran along the arc with the same speed, the component along \(x\) would be smaller by at most a relative \(1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) at slope \(0{,}005\), which we neglect.
  6. The eyelets are fixed in space, \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\). The connection of the span with the pulley (wrapping, friction, oscillation of the pulley) is neglected (CHEN2005, §2.4.2, PDF p. 4).
  7. Weight is neglected: the weight of the span \(\mu g L = 3{,}4\) N is \(7{,}6\cdot 10^{-4}\) of the tension force.
  8. The transport speed \(v\) is constant in time. We require only \(v > 0\). The ratio between \(v\) and the wave speed \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4) we shall restrict only where it is needed.

For the example \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu} = \sqrt{\sigma/\rho} = 113{,}23\) m/s. The ratio \(v/c\) at \(v = 40\) m/s is \(0{,}353\). We write this ratio simply as \(v/c\), with no new letter: WM1990 denotes it by \(\nu\), which in this book means Poisson's ratio, and CHEN2005 uses the letter \(c\) for the transport speed, which with us means the wave speed. So we keep \(v\) for the transport speed, \(c\) for the wave speed, \(T\) for the tension force (WM1990 writes \(P\)) and \(\mu\) for the mass per length (WM1990 writes \(\rho\)). In the chapter on beams (5) \(v\) meant the deflection, here the deflection is \(w\), as in section 13.1. The letter \(T\) is not the kinetic energy of chapter 9, we shall write the kinetic energy differently when we need it.

What remains from section 13.1? There the acceleration of a point of the string was simply \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), because the point stayed at the same \(x\). A material particle of the moving string does not stay at the same \(x\). How large its acceleration is, is shown by figure 26.2, which we build in three panels. In all three the same string at the same time, bulging upward, and on it one material particle, the blackwhite dot at \(x_0\).

In panel (a) we ask: what would be the acceleration of a point that stayed at the same \(x\), as in section 13.1? The string moves in time \(\tau\) and the dashed curve is its position at time \(t + \tau\). The point at constant \(x\) would rise, its acceleration is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), called the local acceleration (krajevni pospešek), because it is the acceleration at a fixed place. The arrow \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is drawn upward for the case where the curve rises ever faster. That the curve rises says only that the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is positive, the acceleration points upward when this velocity grows. In panel (b) we take the point to run. The tangent to the string at it has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), and since the shape changes, the slope changes with rate \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), the tangent turns like a rod. The point runs along the tangent with speed \(v\), like a bead on a turning rod. A bead on a rod that turns with angular velocity \(\Omega\) and runs along it with speed \(v\) relative to the rod has, besides other terms, an acceleration \(2\Omega v\) perpendicular to the rod (Coriolis acceleration, Coriolisov pospešek), as school physics knows it. At small slope the angular velocity of the tangent is \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), so the acceleration is \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), drawn upward, because the slope grows. In panel (c) the point runs along a curved curve. The circle that fits the curve best at this point has by definition 5.16 radius \(R = 1/|w_{\mathrm{xx}}|\), and whoever runs along a circle with speed \(v\) has acceleration \(v^2/R\) toward the centre of the circle (school physics, uniform circular motion). That is why this term is called the centripetal acceleration (centripetalni pospešek): Latin centrum means centre and petere to seek, so an acceleration that seeks the centre. At small slope the arrow toward the centre is almost vertical and equal to \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The curve bulges upward, \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} < 0\), so it points downward.

The above are explanations from the figure and school physics. The exact computation with the chain rule is given by the lemma that follows.

Lemma 26.1 Velocity and acceleration of a material particle of the moving string (hitrost in pospešek točke snovi gibajoče strune)

Let \(v > 0\) and let \(w\) be a function on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\) with continuous partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tx}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) (definition 1.25). Let \(s\) be a number and let the material particle that at time \(t\) is at \(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t) = s + vt\) lie in \((0, L)\) during an open interval of times. Then its transverse displacement is \(W(t) = w(s + vt, t)\), its transverse velocity is

\[\dot W = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}} \tag{26.1}\]

and its transverse acceleration is

\[\ddot W = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} , \tag{26.2}\]

both at the point \((s + vt, t)\). The terms \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are in turn the local, the Coriolis and the centripetal acceleration.

Proof

We must show the first and second derivative of the displacement along the path of the material particle \((s + vt, t)\). We get each with the chain rule, the second by applying the same rule to the velocity.

  1. The material particle is at time \(t\) at \(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t) = s + vt\) by idealization 5, so \(x_{\mathrm{p}}' = v\). Its displacement is \(W(t) = w(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t), t)\), which is \(w\) along the path \(\Phi(t) = (x_{\mathrm{p}}(t), t)\), whose derivative is \((v, 1)\).
  2. By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, point 1, where \(D\) is an interval) \(\dot W = w_{\mathrm{x}}\,v + w_{\mathrm{t}}\). This is equation (26.1).
  3. The function \(g = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) has continuous derivatives \(g_{\mathrm{x}} = w_{\mathrm{tx}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(g_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and \(\dot W(t) = g(x_{\mathrm{p}}(t), t)\). The same rule applied to \(g\) gives \(\ddot W = g_{\mathrm{x}}\,v + g_{\mathrm{t}} = v\,w_{\mathrm{tx}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{tt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\).
  4. The mixed derivatives are continuous at every point, so by the theorem on the interchange of mixed derivatives (theorem 8.30) \(w_{\mathrm{tx}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and from step 3 equation (26.2) follows.

Source: WM1990, PDF pp. 1 and 2: the transverse velocity is \(U_{\mathrm{T}} + V U_{\mathrm{X}}\) (PDF p. 1), the terms of the acceleration are in turn the local, the Coriolis and the centripetal (PDF p. 2). CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (the same description). The proof by steps is not from the source.

The acceleration therefore has three terms, not one, as in panel (a) of figure 26.2. The computation has confirmed the explanations of panels (b) and (c): the second term is the Coriolis one, the third the centripetal one.

Let us check the lemma on numbers and on figure 26.2. Let \(v = 40\) m/s, which is \(v/c = 0{,}353\), and let

\[w_*(x, t) = \varepsilon\,\sin\frac{\pi x}{L}\,\cos(\omega t + k x) , \qquad \varepsilon = 1\ \text{mm} , \quad \omega = \frac{\pi c}{L}\Big(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\Big) = 311{,}32\ \text{1/s} , \quad k = \frac{\pi v}{c L} = 1{,}110\ \text{1/m} . \tag{26.3}\]

We chose the function so that it will be a motion of the span. Why exactly these \(\omega\) and \(k\), the section on the modes of the moving string shows later in the chapter, here it is only a test function. At the point \(x = 0{,}3\) m at \(t = 0\), \(w_* = 0{,}765\) mm and \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 1{,}452\cdot 10^{-3}\). By the lemma the three terms of the acceleration are \(-74{,}10\), \(-36{,}17\) and \(-15{,}72\) m/s\(^2\), so the transverse acceleration of the material particle there is \(-126{,}0\) m/s\(^2\) (SymPy), and not only \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -74{,}10\) m/s\(^2\). The largest values over time and \(x\) of the terms are \(97{,}0\), \(78{,}2\) and \(17{,}8\) m/s\(^2\), so the Coriolis term reaches \(81\) % of the local one, and the centripetal \(18\) %. At \(v/c = 0{,}353\) we therefore must not neglect them: the Coriolis term is almost equal to the local one (panels (a) and (b) of figure 26.2).

Now we can write the equation of motion of the material piece. The law of motion of a body (definition 8.70), integrated over the points of the piece, says that the resultant of the forces on the piece equals the integral of the mass density times the acceleration. The piece of section 13.1 was over an interval that did not move. Now the material piece is over an interval that moves with speed \(v\), as the lower row of figure 26.1 shows, so in the law we use the acceleration from the lemma.

Derivation 26.2 Equation of motion of a material piece of the moving string (gibalna enačba kosa snovi gibajoče strune)

Goal: for a material piece that at time \(t\) is over the interval \([A, B] \subset (0, L)\), \(A < B\), to write the law of motion in the transverse direction. The assumptions are idealizations 1 to 8 and \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\) on \([A, B]\).

1
\[\text{material piece} = \{\text{material particles } s \in [a, b]\} , \qquad a = A - vt , \quad b = B - vt , \qquad m = \mu\,(b - a) .\]
Hint

The material particle with label \(s\) is at time \(t\) at \(x = s + vt\) (idealization 5), so the material piece with labels from \(a\) to \(b\) lies over \([a + vt, b + vt] = [A, B]\) at time \(t\), and over \([a + v t', b + v t']\) at time \(t'\) (upper and lower row of figure 26.1). All particles run with the same speed, so the length of the piece along \(x\) does not change, it stays \(b - a\), and the mass is by idealization 1 constant: \(m = \mu\,(b - a)\).

2
\[F_{\text{navp}} = T\,\big(w_{\mathrm{x}}(B, t) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(A, t)\big) .\]
Hint

The forces of the neighbouring parts are by idealization 2 along the tangent, by idealization 3 of magnitude \(T\), so the sum of the vertical components, \(T\sin\theta_{\mathrm{B}} - T\sin\theta_{\mathrm{A}}\) with \(\tan\theta = w_{\mathrm{x}}\), equals this, with a relative error at \(\sin\theta\) of at most \(1 - 1/\sqrt{1 + 0{,}005^2} = 1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\) (step 3 of derivation 13.1 with the bound \(0{,}005\)). The horizontal resultant, \(T|\cos\theta_{\mathrm{B}} - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{A}}| \le 1{,}25\cdot 10^{-5}\,T = 56\) mN, would accelerate the piece along \(x\), but by idealization 5 this speed does not change, so we neglect it. We do not count the weight (idealization 7). The forces are drawn in the upper row of figure 26.1.

3
\[\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,\ddot W_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mathrm{d}s = F_{\text{navp}} , \qquad \ddot W_{\mathrm{s}}(t) = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} \quad \text{at the point } (s + vt, t) .\]
Hint

The law of motion of a body (definition 8.70) for the material piece: the mass density per label \(s\) is \(\mu\), because the spacing between the particles does not change (step 1), the transverse acceleration of the particle with label \(s\) is by lemma 26.1 equation (26.2). On the right is the resultant from step 2.

4
\[\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B \mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big)(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(B, t) - T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(A, t) . \tag{26.4}\]
Hint

The change of variable \(x = s + vt\) at constant \(t\) (lemma 9.78, point 2, shift) turns the integral over \(s\) from \(a\) to \(b\) into an integral over \(x\) from \(a + vt = A\) to \(b + vt = B\). The function is the same, only the argument is shifted.

Equation (26.4) holds for every material piece that at time \(t\) is over the interval \([A, B]\). For the piece with labels \(a = A - vt\) and \(b = B - vt\) this is a piece that stays in \((0, L)\) for a time around \(t\) if \(A\) and \(B\) are interior points, so the equation is a condition for every interior pair \(A < B\). For the end points we extend it by continuity of both sides.

Source: WM1990 (1), PDF p. 2, and CHEN2005 (1), PDF p. 2, obtain the equation with Newton's second law (Swope and Ames, 1963) or with Hamilton's principle for travelling media (Archibald and Emslie, 1958, Benjamin, 1961, WM1990, PDF p. 2). The derivation with the material piece and with the error bounds is not from the source.

With this the model is fixed. Let us write it as a definition in which it gets its name.

Definition 26.3 Moving string (gibajoča struna)

Let \(L\), \(\mu\), \(T\) and \(v\) be positive numbers: the span length in m, the mass per unit length in kg/m, the tension force in N and the transport speed in m/s. The moving string with length \(L\), mass \(\mu\) per unit length, tension \(T\) and transport speed \(v\) is a motion described by a function \(w : [0, L] \times [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) that has continuous partial derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tx}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) (definition 1.25), satisfies \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) for every \(t \ge 0\) and for every \(A < B\) from \([0, L]\) and every \(t \ge 0\) the equation (26.4). The function \(w(x, t)\) is the transverse displacement of the point at \(x\) at time \(t\) in metres. The model holds with the error from derivation 26.2 as long as \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\) and idealizations 1 to 8 hold.

Source: WM1990, PDF p. 2 (first paragraph of section 2.1: "uniform, flexible, axially moving string of linear density, tension and transport speed that travels between two fixed eyelets"), CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (section 2.1.1, assumptions 1 and 2). The error measures are ours.

Equation (26.4) is one condition for every pair \(A < B\), as for the string of section 13.1. Does the equation at every point follow from it? Yes, and also conversely, as in theorem 13.3.

Theorem 26.4 Equation of the moving string (enačba gibajoče strune)

Let \(w\) be a function with continuous \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\). Then for every \(t \ge 0\) equation (26.4) holds for all \(A < B\) from \([0, L]\) if and only if for every \(x \in [0, L]\) and every \(t \ge 0\)

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} , \tag{26.5}\]

which with \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4) is equal to

\[w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - (c^2 - v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.6}\]
Proof

We must show that equation (26.4) for all pieces is equivalent to equation (26.5) at all points. We write the difference of the two sides as an integral of one continuous function and use that a continuous function with zero integral over every piece is zero everywhere, as in theorem 13.3.

  1. Fix \(t \ge 0\) and let \(f(x) = \mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}})(x, t) - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}(x, t)\). The function \(f\) is continuous, because the derivatives are continuous.
  2. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, point 1) \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = w_{\mathrm{x}}(B, t) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(A, t)\).
  3. By step 2 and linearity of the integral (lemma 3.39) \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B f\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the difference of the left and right side of equation (26.4). The equation holds for the piece \([A, B]\) if and only if \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\).
  4. If (26.5) holds, \(f = 0\) and every integral is zero, so by step 3 (26.4) holds.
  5. Conversely let (26.4) hold for all \(A < B\). By step 3 \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B f\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for all \(A < B\), so \(G(x) = \int_0^x f\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) for \(x \in [0, L]\). The function \(G\) is differentiable with \(G' = f\) (theorem 3.40, point 2), because \(f\) is continuous, and it is zero, so \(f = G' = 0\).
  6. From \(f = 0\) follows (26.5). Division by \(\mu\) gives \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} = c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which is (26.6).

Source: WM1990 (1), PDF p. 2, CHEN2005 (1), PDF p. 2. The proof with an arbitrary finite piece is not from the source.

At \(v = 0\) equation (26.6) simplifies to the wave equation (13.2): the string of section 13.1 is a special case of the moving string. At \(v \ne 0\) the mixed derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is added and the second derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) has a different coefficient, \(c^2 - v^2\) instead of \(c^2\).

Let us test the theorem on numbers. The function \(w_*\) of equation (26.3) at \(v = 40\) m/s satisfied equation (26.5) by SymPy: the residual of the left and right side is at five points at most \(1\cdot 10^{-14}\) N/m in magnitude, so zero up to rounding. For the material piece over \([0{,}2\ \text{m},\ 0{,}5\ \text{m}]\) at \(t = 0\) the left side of equation (26.4) is \(-13{,}142\) N, the right \(-13{,}142\) N. At \(t = 4\) ms the piece is over \([0{,}360,\ 0{,}660]\) and both sides are \(3{,}629\) N (numbers by SymPy). The equality is no accident: we chose a function that satisfies the equation, and the theorem says that then it holds for every piece.

The theorem is tied to the material piece. Would it not be simpler to take an interval that stands in space, as in section 13.1? Let us try, and on the same motion \(w_*\).

A window (okno) is an interval \([a, b]\) that stands in space: such was the piece in section 13.1. In figure 26.3 the blackwhite row is the window and the blue row is the material piece. At time \(t\) they have the same matter, as the upper row of the figure says. At time \(t + \tau\) the window is still over \([a, b]\), but the material piece is over the interval from \(a + v\tau\) to \(b + v\tau\). So the matter in the window is not the same: the left orange area, of width \(v\tau\), is matter that entered through the left edge, the right orange one, also of width \(v\tau\), is matter of the piece that left the window through the right edge. The window is therefore not an unchanging set of material particles, so the law of motion of a body for it does not mean that mass times \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) equals the force: matter enters the window and leaves it and carries momentum with it. If we write the equation of motion as in section 13.1, \(\int_{\mathrm{A}}^B \mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(B) - T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(A)\), then for the motion \(w_*\) and \([A, B] = [0{,}2\ \text{m},\ 0{,}5\ \text{m}]\) at \(t = 0\) we get on the left \(-8{,}027\) N, on the right \(-13{,}142\) N. The difference is \(5{,}115\) N, which is \(39\) % of the force. The wave equation (13.2) itself is not satisfied either: the residual \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} - c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is at the point \(x = 0{,}3\) m \(51{,}9\) m/s\(^2\), at \(x = 0{,}5\) m \(38{,}6\) m/s\(^2\), not zero. The window therefore does not give the law.

What is missing is told by the momentum of the window. Let \(P_{\text{ok}}(t) = \int_{\mathrm{A}}^B \mu\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\,\mathrm{d}x\) be the momentum in the window (by equation (26.1) \(\mu(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\) is the density of transverse momentum). At \(t = 0\) its derivative in time is \(-9{,}764\) N, and the flux of momentum through the edges of the window, \(\mu v\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})\) at \(B\) minus the same expression at \(A\), is \(-3{,}377\) N. The sum is \(-9{,}764 - 3{,}377 = -13{,}141\) N (the deviation from \(-13{,}142\) N is rounding), and this is exactly the left side of equation (26.4). The momentum of the window therefore changes because of the force, which is \(T\) at the edges, and because of matter that enters and leaves through the edges. Only the second part is missing when we use the window with \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\).

At \(v = 0\) the flux is zero, the material piece equals the window and equation (26.6) is equation (13.2). For a string at rest the window is therefore a material piece, and so in section 13.1 it was correct to take an interval that stands still.

The section has set up the model of the moving string: a span between eyelets that runs with speed \(v\), a material piece with the same matter, and the acceleration of a material particle with three terms. From this followed equation (26.6) with the mixed derivative \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), which at \(v = 0\) equals the wave equation. For our band of the example \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, the speed \(v = 40\) m/s is \(0{,}353\,c\) and \(T - \mu v^2 = 3938\) N instead of \(4500\) N at \(v = 0\). The next section introduces the material coordinate \(x - vt\), which finds solutions of the equation in the form of two waves that travel with different speeds.

26.2 Two waves in a moving string

A string at rest has, by lemma 13.5, two parts of its motion: a shape that runs to the right and a shape that runs to the left, both with speed \(c\). A band that runs through two fixed ends carries along everything that lies on it. Do both parts still run with \(c\), and are there still two of them?

From history

In 1897 Skutch published a paper on a taut thread that is forced to run with constant speed through two fixed points and between them vibrates transversally with small amplitude (CHEN2005, PDF p. 21, reference list). This is the model of section 26.1. He was the first to study the string without excitation and found the natural frequencies by adding two waves that travel in opposite directions (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2). In 1954 Sack excited the same string by a harmonic motion of one end and found the natural frequencies from the resonance condition (CHEN2005, PDF pp. 2 and 21). Both obtained the same natural frequencies (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2). The path of two waves is the path of this section. For d'Alembert's string (section 13.1) the boundary conditions linked the two shapes, and since the end is fixed, here too a wave that arrives at it must become another wave there. The calculation begins with the question of what two fixed ends do to the fact that the band runs.

Let us return to the steel band of the running example of section 26.1: the span between the ends is \(L = 1\) m, the tension \(T = 4500\) N, the mass per unit length \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m and hence \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu} = 113{,}23\) m/s. The dimensions, the tension and the speed are our choice and not data of any real drive. The transport speed is \(v = 40\) m/s, with the idealizations of definition 26.3.

Let us draw what the band does. In the left picture we measure horizontally the place \(x\) along the band from the first end and vertically the time \(t\). The ends stand at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) at every time, so they are vertical lines. A particle of the band that is at \(x = \xi\) at time \(0\) is at \(x = \xi + vt\) at time \(t\), because the band runs with speed \(v\). Its path is the dashed oblique line \(x = \xi + vt\). The particle with \(\xi = 0\) would reach \(x = L\) at \(t = L/v = 25{,}0\) ms, and a particle with negative \(\xi\) enters the span only through the first end. The number \(\xi = x - vt\) does not change along such a path, so it labels a particle and not a place in space. That is why we call it the material coordinate (snovna koordinata): the Slovenian word snov means material, and \(\xi\) is the label of the piece of material that we follow.

Let us choose the event \(P\), the place \(x = 0{,}6\) m at time \(t = 11{,}78\) ms. We draw the same event in the right picture, where we measure \(\xi\) horizontally. Every particle now has a constant \(\xi\), so its paths are vertical, and \(P\) lies at \(\xi = 0{,}6 - 40\cdot 0{,}01178 = 0{,}129\) m. The ends have turned around: \(x = 0\) means \(\xi = -vt\) and \(x = L\) means \(\xi = L - vt\), so each of them flees to the left with speed \(v\) and runs past the particles, just as the band runs past the ends when we look from outside.

Why is this view useful? By Newton's second law the force determines the acceleration of a particle, that is the change of its velocity as we follow it. We follow the particle with \(\xi\) along a vertical line of the right picture. Its transverse displacement is \(u(\xi, t) = w(\xi + vt, t)\), its velocity \(u_{\mathrm{t}}\) and its acceleration \(u_{\mathrm{tt}}\). Section 26.1 computed the same acceleration as \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (lemma 26.1). We show that the two calculations agree and that the view from the band turns into the equation of a string at rest.

We write the equation of the moving string in the form (26.6) (theorem 26.4, \(c^2 = T/\mu\)) once more:

\[w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - (c^2 - v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.7}\]
Lemma 26.5 Material coordinate (snovna koordinata)

Let \(c > 0\) and \(v \ge 0\) be numbers and \(w\) a function with continuous partial derivatives up to and including second order on \([0, L] \times [0, \infty)\). For \(t \ge 0\) and \(-vt \le \xi \le L - vt\) let \(u(\xi, t) = w(\xi + vt, t)\). Then, if the derivatives of \(w\) are taken at the point \((\xi + vt, t)\):

  1. \(u_\xi = w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\xi\xi} = w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  2. The function \(w\) satisfies equation (26.7) exactly when \(u\) satisfies \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2\,u_{\xi\xi}\), that is the wave equation of a string at rest (theorem 13.3).
  3. \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) holds for every \(t \ge 0\) exactly when \(u(-vt, t) = u(L - vt, t) = 0\) holds for every \(t \ge 0\).
Proof

We must show that the view from the band turns all three parts of the model. We obtain the derivatives of \(u\) from those of \(w\) by the chain rule and then compare the two sides of the equation.

  1. The function \(u\) is composed of \(w\) and the linear map \((\xi, t) \mapsto (\xi + vt, t)\), so by the chain rule (lemma 4.43) \(u_\xi = w_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot 1 + w_{\mathrm{t}} \cdot 0 = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{x}} \cdot v + w_{\mathrm{t}} \cdot 1 = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). These two derivatives are again continuously differentiable.
  2. The same rule for \(u_\xi = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) gives \(u_{\xi\xi} = w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). For \(u_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) it gives \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = (w_{\mathrm{tt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{tx}}) + v\,(w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}})\), and since the mixed derivatives are equal (theorem 1.125, the derivatives are continuous), \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). This is item 1.
  3. The left side of equation (26.7) is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} - c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}} = u_{\mathrm{tt}} - c^2 u_{\xi\xi}\) by step 2. It is zero exactly when \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2 u_{\xi\xi}\). This is item 2.
  4. The end point \(x = 0\) has \(\xi = -vt\) at time \(t\) and the point \(x = L\) has \(\xi = L - vt\), and \(u(-vt, t) = w(0, t)\), \(u(L - vt, t) = w(L, t)\). This is item 3.

Source: WM1990, PDF p. 2: the acceleration of a particle has three terms, which the source calls the local, the Coriolis and the centripetal acceleration. The passage to the material coordinate and the proof are not from the source.

The lemma says what we drew. In \(\xi\) the equation is the one that chapter 13 solved for a string at rest, and every acceleration is the acceleration of a particle. The only difference is the ends: instead of resting at constant \(\xi\), they flee along the oblique lines of the right picture. The reason for this is Newton's law: an observer sitting on the band moves with constant velocity and his acceleration is zero, so he sees the same forces and the same accelerations as an observer on the ground, and for him the string is at rest.

A string at rest has, by lemma 13.5, solutions \(F(\xi - ct) + G(\xi + ct)\), and in \(x\) and \(t\) we have \(\xi - ct = x - (c + v)t\) and \(\xi + ct = x + (c - v)t\). Are these all the solutions? Lemma 13.5 proved only that such shapes are solutions, not that there are no others. Where the speeds come from we see from the left side of equation (26.7): the operators \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}} + (v + c)\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}} + (v - c)\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}\) multiply to \(\partial_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + 2v\,\partial_{\mathrm{t}}\partial_{\mathrm{x}} - (c^2 - v^2)\,\partial_{\mathrm{x}}^2\). The first annihilates \(F(x - (c + v)t)\), because its derivative with respect to time is \(-(c + v)F'\) and with respect to place \(F'\). The second annihilates \(G(x + (c - v)t)\) for the same reason. That there are no other solutions is shown by the proof with the new coordinates \(p = \xi - ct\) and \(q = \xi + ct\).

Lemma 26.6 Converse of d'Alembert's solution (obrat d'Alembertove rešitve)

Let \(c > 0\) and \(v \ge 0\) be numbers and \(S = \{(x, t) : 0 < x < L,\ t > 0\}\) an open strip. Let \(w\) have continuous partial derivatives up to and including second order on \(S\) and satisfy equation (26.7). Then there exist twice continuously differentiable functions \(F\) and \(G\) of one variable, \(F\) on the interval of values that \(x - (c + v)t\) takes on \(S\), and \(G\) on the interval of values that \(x + (c - v)t\) takes on \(S\), such that

\[w(x, t) = F\big(x - (c + v)t\big) + G\big(x + (c - v)t\big) \qquad \text{for every } (x, t) \in S . \tag{26.8}\]

Conversely, for any twice continuously differentiable \(F\) and \(G\) the function (26.8) satisfies equation (26.7). For \(v = 0\) this is the converse of lemma 13.5: every solution of the equation \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the sum of a wave running to the right and a wave running to the left.

Proof

We must show that equation (26.7) turns into the equation \(\omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = 0\) for the new coordinates, and that a solution of this equation on a set whose sections are intervals is the sum of a function of one coordinate and a function of the other.

  1. By lemma 26.5 (items 1 and 2 use only derivatives at a single point, so they hold on the open strip too) the function \(u(\xi, t) = w(\xi + vt, t)\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(S' = \{(\xi, t) : t > 0,\ -vt < \xi < L - vt\}\) and satisfies \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = c^2 u_{\xi\xi}\).
  2. We introduce \(p = \xi - ct\) and \(q = \xi + ct\). This is a linear map with the inverse \(\xi = (p + q)/2\), \(t = (q - p)/(2c)\), because \(c > 0\). Since \(\xi = x - vt\), we have \(p = x - (c + v)t\) and \(q = x + (c - v)t\). The image of the set \(S'\) is the set \(D\) of points \((p, q)\) for which \(q > p\) (this is \(t > 0\)) and \(0 < (c - v)\,p + (c + v)\,q < 2cL\) (this is \(0 < x < L\), since \(x = \xi + vt = \big((c - v)p + (c + v)q\big)/(2c)\)). This set is open. Let \(\omega(p, q) = u\big((p + q)/2,\ (q - p)/(2c)\big)\), twice continuously differentiable on \(D\) by the chain rule (lemma 4.43).
  3. By the chain rule \(\omega_{\mathrm{p}} = \tfrac12 u_\xi - \tfrac{1}{2c}\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}} = \tfrac12 u_\xi + \tfrac{1}{2c}\,u_{\mathrm{t}}\). Next, \(\omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = \tfrac14 u_{\xi\xi} + \tfrac{1}{4c}\,u_{\xi \mathrm{t}} - \tfrac{1}{4c}\,u_{\mathrm{t}\xi} - \tfrac{1}{4c^2}\,u_{\mathrm{tt}}\). The mixed derivatives are equal (theorem 1.125), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = \tfrac{1}{4c^2}\,(c^2 u_{\xi\xi} - u_{\mathrm{tt}}) = 0\) by step 1.
  4. For a given \(q\) the set of values \(p\) with \((p, q) \in D\) is determined by inequalities that are linear in \(p\) (and \(p < q\)), so it is an interval. The function \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}}(\cdot, q)\) has on it the derivative \(\omega_{\mathrm{qp}} = \omega_{\mathrm{pq}} = 0\) (theorem 1.125), so by corollary 1.85 it is constant. Its value is a number \(g(q)\). At every point \((p_0, q_0)\) of \(D\) we have \(g(q) = \omega_{\mathrm{q}}(p_0, q)\) for \(q\) near \(q_0\), because \(D\) is open, so \(g\) is continuously differentiable.
  5. Let \(G\) be a primitive function of \(g\) on the interval of values of \(q\) (theorem 3.40), so \(G' = g\) and \(G\) is twice continuously differentiable. The function \(\omega - G(q)\) has derivative with respect to \(q\) equal to \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}} - g = 0\). For a given \(p\) the set of values \(q\) is an interval for the same reason as in step 4, so by corollary 1.85 \(\omega(p, q) - G(q)\) is independent of \(q\). We denote it \(F(p)\). Since \(F(p) = \omega(p, q_0) - G(q_0)\) for \(p\) near \(p_0\) and fixed \(q_0\), \(F\) is twice continuously differentiable.
  6. Hence \(\omega(p, q) = F(p) + G(q)\), which is equation (26.8).
  7. Conversely let \(w = F(x - (c + v)t)\). Then \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = F'\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = -(c + v)F'\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F''\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -(c + v)F''\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = (c + v)^2 F''\). The left side of equation (26.7) is \(\big((c + v)^2 - 2v(c + v) - (c^2 - v^2)\big)F'' = (c + v)\big((c + v) - 2v - (c - v)\big)F'' = 0\). For \(w = G(x + (c - v)t)\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = G'\), \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = (c - v)G'\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = G''\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = (c - v)G''\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = (c - v)^2 G''\) and the left side is \((c - v)\big((c - v) + 2v - (c + v)\big)G'' = 0\). The equation is linear, so the same holds for the sum.

Source: CHEN2005, PDF p. 2: Skutch obtained the natural frequencies by adding two waves in opposite directions. WM1990, PDF p. 5: for the motion considered, a forward wave with speed \(1 + v\) and a reflected one with speed \(1 - v\) (in dimensionless units). The proof is not from the source.

The proof did not need the ends, only the interior of the strip. It matters that the sections of the set \(D\) are intervals: for a set with a gap in a section, \(\omega_{\mathrm{q}}\) in step 4 could be a different constant on the two sides of the gap, the number \(g(q)\) would not exist, and the solution would not have the form (26.8).

The lemma also fulfils a promise of chapter 13. There we knew only that the waves \(F(x - ct) + G(x + ct)\) are solutions of the string at rest, here we know that there are no others, and the string at rest is the case \(v = 0\). But where do the shapes run? This is told by the shift of the values of a shape.

Corollary 26.7 Wave speeds (hitrosti valov)

Let \(0 \le v < c\) and \(w(x, t) = F\big(x - (c + v)t\big) + G\big(x + (c - v)t\big)\) as in lemma 26.6. Then:

  1. The shape \(x \mapsto F(x - (c + v)t)\) at time \(t + \tau\) is the shape at time \(t\), shifted by \((c + v)\tau\) towards larger \(x\), that is in the direction of motion of the band. We call it the forward wave (val naprej).
  2. The shape \(x \mapsto G(x + (c - v)t)\) at time \(t + \tau\) is the shape at time \(t\), shifted by \((c - v)\tau\) towards smaller \(x\), that is against the direction of motion of the band. We call it the backward wave (val nazaj).
  3. In the material coordinate \(\xi\) both waves go with speed \(c\): \(F(\xi - ct)\) travels towards larger \(\xi\), \(G(\xi + ct)\) towards smaller.
Proof

We must show that the value of each shape at time \(t + \tau\) appears shifted. For this we insert the shifted place.

  1. \(F\big((x + (c + v)\tau) - (c + v)(t + \tau)\big) = F\big(x - (c + v)t\big)\). The value of the forward wave at the point \(x\) at time \(t\) is therefore the value at time \(t + \tau\) at the point \(x + (c + v)\tau\).
  2. \(G\big((x - (c - v)\tau) + (c - v)(t + \tau)\big) = G\big(x + (c - v)t\big)\). The value of the backward wave at the point \(x\) at time \(t\) is the value at time \(t + \tau\) at the point \(x - (c - v)\tau\), because \(c - v > 0\) is a shift towards smaller \(x\).
  3. By lemma 26.5, \(x - (c + v)t = \xi - ct\) and \(x + (c - v)t = \xi + ct\), which is lemma 13.5 in \(\xi\).

Source: CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (superposition of two waves), WM1990, PDF p. 5 (forward wave with speed \(1 + v\), reflected with \(1 - v\)). The proof is not from the source.

The names have a reason: the forward wave goes forward, in the direction of the band, the backward wave goes backward, against it. The speeds \(c \pm v\) are a sum of speeds as in every motion on a moving base. The waves run with speed \(c\) relative to the band (item 3, where the band is at rest), and the band itself with speed \(v\) relative to the ends. Someone who walks on a moving walkway with speed \(c\) in the direction of the walkway is seen from the ground with speed \(c + v\), and someone who walks against it with speed \(c - v\), if \(v < c\). The first is the forward wave, the second the backward wave.

Example 26.8 Two shapes that are not a wave of the string

For the steel band of the example, \(v = 40\) m/s, take the shape \(F(s) = \varepsilon\sin(\pi s/L)\) with \(\varepsilon = 1\) mm and move it with speed \(V\) through space: \(w = F(x - Vt)\). The slope is at most \(\varepsilon\pi/L = 3{,}14\cdot 10^{-3}\), below the limit \(0{,}005\) of definition 26.3.

  1. For every speed \(V\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = V^2 F''\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -V F''\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = F''\), so the left side of equation (26.7) equals \(\big(V^2 - 2vV - c^2 + v^2\big)F'' = \big((V - v)^2 - c^2\big)F''\).
  2. The factor is zero exactly when \(V - v = \pm c\), that is \(V = v + c = 153{,}23\) m/s or \(V = v - c = -73{,}23\) m/s. These are the speeds of the forward and the backward wave of corollary 26.7.
  3. The speed \(V = c = 113{,}23\) m/s was the speed of the waves on a string at rest. Now the factor is \((c - v)^2 - c^2 = v(v - 2c) = -7458\) m\(^2\)/s\(^2\). At the crest \(F'' = -(\pi/L)^2\varepsilon = -9{,}87\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/m, so the left side is \(+73{,}6\) m/s\(^2\) and not zero.
  4. The speed \(V = v = 40\) m/s is the speed with which the band carries its shape. The factor is \(-c^2 = -12\,820\) m\(^2\)/s\(^2\) and the left side at the crest \(+126{,}5\) m/s\(^2\). The cause: the particles of such a shape have transverse acceleration zero, since each keeps its displacement, but the tension still acts on a curved piece with a force \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) per unit length, which is not balanced. A shape that the band merely carries is therefore not a motion of the string.

The speed \(c\) from the chapter on the string at rest therefore holds only for \(v = 0\). For \(v \ne 0\) the speed of the waves relative to the band is \(c\) and relative to the ends \(c \pm v\).

What happens when \(v\) approaches \(c\)? The speed of the backward wave \(c - v\) falls towards zero, and at \(v = c\) the backward wave is a shape at rest \(G(x + 0\cdot t) = G(x)\). At \(v = c = 113{,}23\) m/s the factor \(c^2 - v^2\) in equation (26.7) is zero, the equation reduces to \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2c\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\), and every shape at rest \(w(x)\) with \(w(0) = w(L) = 0\) satisfies it, because \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\). The reason is that the particles run along the curved path at rest with speed \(v\) and have transverse acceleration \(u_{\mathrm{tt}} = v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (item 1 of lemma 26.5 with \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\)). By Newton's second law they need for it a force per unit length \(\mu v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and the tension supplies \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \mu c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The two are equal exactly at \(v = c\). At \(v = c\) every shape at rest is therefore possible, at \(v = 40\) m/s it is not, since \(\mu v^2 = 561{,}6\) N against \(T = 4500\) N: the tension is too large for the shape to stay at rest. For \(v > c\) we have \(c - v < 0\) and the backward wave too goes in the direction of the band, no wave goes against the band any more. The algebra of lemma 26.6 still holds, but the string model (definition 26.3) is set up for \(v < c\) and for \(v \ge c\) we claim nothing. Section 26.4 shows what happens to the energy at \(v = c\).

Now we can compute what happens to a shape that we release. For a string at rest (section 13.1) d'Alembert's formula (13.11) split a pulse with initial velocity zero into two equal halves. Let us release a pulse on the band.

Example 26.9 A pulse released at rest

Into the band of the example (\(v = 40\) m/s, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, \(L = 1\) m) we release a pulse between the ends: at time \(0\) the displacement is \(w_0(x) = h\,(1 - r^2)^3\) for \(|r| < 1\) and \(0\) elsewhere, \(r = (x - x_0)/s\), \(x_0 = 0{,}4\) m, \(s = 0{,}1\) m, \(h = 0{,}25\) mm, the initial transverse velocity is \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, 0) = 0\) (as in the top picture). The function \(w_0\) is twice continuously differentiable, because the factor \((1 - r^2)^3\) has zero first and second derivative at \(r = \pm 1\). Its largest slope, at \(r = \pm 1/\sqrt5\), is \(h\cdot 1{,}717/s = 4{,}3\cdot 10^{-3}\), below the limit \(0{,}005\) of definition 26.3.

  1. By lemma 26.6, \(w = F(x - (c + v)t) + G(x + (c - v)t)\). Since \(w\) and its derivatives are continuous up to \(t = 0\), as \(t \to 0\) and for \(0 < x < L\) we have \(F(x) + G(x) = w_0(x)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, 0) = -(c + v)F'(x) + (c - v)G'(x) = 0\) for \(0 < x < L\).
  2. The derivative of the first condition is \(F' + G' = w_0'\). From the second, \(G' = \frac{c + v}{c - v}\,F'\). Inserting: \(F'\big(1 + \frac{c + v}{c - v}\big) = w_0'\), that is \(F' = \frac{c - v}{2c}\,w_0'\) and \(G' = \frac{c + v}{2c}\,w_0'\).
  3. Integration gives \(F = \frac{c - v}{2c}\,w_0 + k\) and \(G = \frac{c + v}{2c}\,w_0 - k\) with a constant \(k\). Since in the sum \(F(p) + G(q)\) the constant \(k\) cancels, we take \(k = 0\).
  4. Numbers: \(\frac{c - v}{2c} = 0{,}3234\), \(\frac{c + v}{2c} = 0{,}6766\), the sum is \(1\). At \(t = 2\) ms the forward wave has its centre at \(x_0 + (c + v)t = 0{,}7065\) m and height \(0{,}081\) mm, the backward wave has its centre at \(x_0 - (c - v)t = 0{,}2535\) m and height \(0{,}169\) mm. The point of the band that was at \(x_0\) at time \(0\) is at \(x_0 + vt = 0{,}480\) m.
  5. The ends need not be taken into account yet at \(t = 2\) ms. For \(x < (c + v)t\) the argument \(x - (c + v)t\) is negative. There \(F\) is not determined by step 3 but by the boundary condition \(w(0, t') = 0\), that is \(F(-(c + v)t') = -G((c - v)t')\) for \(0 < t' \le t\). Since \((c - v)t' \le 0{,}147\) m and \(G = 0{,}6766\,w_0\) is zero below \(0{,}3\) m, \(F\) is zero there too. In the same way \(G\) is zero at arguments between \(L\) and \(L + (c - v)t\), because \(w_0\) is zero above \(0{,}5\) m.

The speeds \(c + v\) and \(c - v\) of corollary 26.7 are seen in the shifts \(0{,}3065\) m and \(0{,}1465\) m. For \(v = 0\) the shares would be \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12\) (formula (13.11)), as for a string at rest. Now the backward wave is higher. The reason is the initial condition \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) at time \(0\): the transverse velocities of the two waves, \(-(c + v)F'\) and \((c - v)G'\), must cancel at every point. The slower wave has at equal slope a smaller transverse velocity, so it must have a larger slope, in the ratio \((c + v)/(c - v) = 2{,}09\). For \(v \to c\) the share of the forward wave goes to zero and the pulse stays entirely in the backward wave, which stands still, as we saw above.

In its splitting the pulse changed not only in height. At the ends each part turns around and becomes another wave. For this we need the boundary conditions.

Lemma 26.10 Reflection at an end (odboj na krajišču)

Let \(0 \le v < c\) and \(w\) a motion of the moving string with fixed ends (definition 26.3), written as \(F(x - (c + v)t) + G(x + (c - v)t)\) (lemma 26.6). Then for every \(t > 0\)

\[F\big(-(c + v)t\big) = -G\big((c - v)t\big) , \qquad F\big(L - (c + v)t\big) = -G\big(L + (c - v)t\big) . \tag{26.9}\]

So a backward wave that arrives at the end \(x = 0\) leaves as a forward wave with the opposite sign, its width multiplied by \((c + v)/(c - v) > 1\). A forward wave that arrives at the end \(x = L\) leaves as a backward wave with the opposite sign, its width multiplied by \((c - v)/(c + v) < 1\). The height does not change at a reflection.

Proof

We must show that \(w(0, t) = 0\) and \(w(L, t) = 0\) link the values of \(F\) and \(G\) at the points that the end requires, and that the width follows from the time that the wave spends at the end.

  1. The arguments \(-(c + v)t\) and \(L - (c + v)t\) lie in the interval of values of \(x - (c + v)t\) on \(S\), which is \((-\infty, L)\). The arguments \((c - v)t\) and \(L + (c - v)t\) lie in the interval of values of \(x + (c - v)t\), which is \((0, \infty)\), because \(c - v > 0\). The functions \(F\) and \(G\) are continuous, \(w\) is continuous on the closed strip, so \(w(0, t) = F(-(c + v)t) + G((c - v)t)\) and \(w(L, t) = F(L - (c + v)t) + G(L + (c - v)t)\).
  2. Both values are zero. This is equation (26.9).
  3. Let the backward wave occupy on the \(q\) axis an interval of length \(\ell\). At the end \(x = 0\) we have \(q = (c - v)t\), so the end sees it for the whole time \(\ell/(c - v)\). The forward wave that leaves must fill the same time, and on the axis \(p = -(c + v)t\) this occupies an interval of length \((c + v)\,\ell/(c - v)\). The same for \(x = L\) with the roles exchanged.

Source: The proof is not from the source. WM1990, PDF p. 5: a forward wave with speed \(1 + v\) is reflected from the right support as a wave with speed \(1 - v\).

The last figure puts everything in one place.

Let us draw everything that we computed in the \((x, t)\) plane next to the last picture. The point \(x_0\) is where the pulse starts. From it go two lines: the blue one with slope \(c + v\) to the right and the orange one with slope \(c - v\) to the left, slower and higher. The dashed line of the band has slope \(v\) and lies between. The blue line reaches the end \(x = L\) at \(t_1 = (L - x_0)/(c + v) = 3{,}916\) ms (marked \(t_1\)) and by lemma 26.10 is reflected as a backward wave with the opposite sign, unchanged height \(0{,}081\) mm and width multiplied by \((c - v)/(c + v) = 0{,}478\), that is with half-width \(0{,}048\) m instead of \(0{,}1\) m. The orange line reaches the end \(x = 0\) at \(t_2 = x_0/(c - v) = 5{,}462\) ms and becomes a forward wave with height \(0{,}169\) mm and half-width \(0{,}1\cdot 2{,}09 = 0{,}209\) m. The end sees the pulse for equally long before and after the reflection, \(2s/(c - v) = 2{,}73\) ms, because the condition \(w = 0\) there is a condition in time. Then the orange line reaches \(x = L\) at \(t_3 = t_2 + L/(c + v) = 11{,}99\) ms and the blue one reaches \(x = 0\) at \(t_4 = t_1 + L/(c - v) = 17{,}57\) ms. Every reflection turns the sign, so the displacement after one reflection is negative and after two positive again.

The next section will compute from these paths the round-trip time and the natural frequencies. Here we have shown that the band has two waves instead of one, that the speeds \(c + v\) and \(c - v\) each belong to their own direction, and that after a reflection the width of a wave changes and the height does not. We have also shown where this model stops being valid: at \(v = c\) the backward wave stands still.

26.3 Modes of the moving string

A steel band for a band saw, 50 mm wide and 0,9 mm thick, runs at 40 m/s through two fixed eyelets (očesci) 1 m apart and is pulled with a stress of 100 MPa. These dimensions are our choice, not data from a source. We pluck the band. What frequency do we hear, and how does it change when the band runs faster? Do all points of the band oscillate together, as on a string at rest? In section 13.2 (chapter 13) we found for the string at rest the standing wave \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), and the chapter promised that for belts this shape is no longer a solution. Here we prove it and find what replaces it.

The model is the moving string of section 26.1: the deflection \(w(x, t)\) of the point of the string that lies at \(x \in [0, L]\) at time \(t\) is transverse, \(x\) is measured from the first eyelet in the direction of motion, and the transport speed \(v\) is constant and positive. The letter \(v\) here is the transport speed in m/s, and the deflection is \(w\) as in chapter 13 (in the chapters on beams \(v\) is a deflection). The string has tension \(T\) and mass per length \(\mu\) as in definition 13.2, \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) is the wave speed of definition 13.4, and everything below holds for subcritical speed \(0 \le v < c\). The equation of motion of theorem 26.4 and the two ends are

\[w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (v^2 - c^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 , \qquad w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0 . \tag{26.10}\]

The first term is the local acceleration at the place \(x\), the second is the Coriolis term, the third is the centripetal term. The second is named after Coriolis because it is the acceleration of a body that moves along a path that itself moves: a particle of the string runs at speed \(v\) along a curve whose slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) changes in time, and the transverse velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) of the particle therefore changes also through \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The third is centripetal because it is the acceleration of a particle that runs at speed \(v\) along a curve of curvature \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and points to the centre of curvature, as in a car in a bend. Section 26.1 derived both from the chain rule. For \(v = 0\) the wave equation of theorem 13.3 remains.

Where is the difficulty? As for the string at rest, we try a motion in which every point oscillates with the same frequency \(\omega\): \(w = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) with a real function \(\varphi\). The terms \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are then proportional to \(\cos\omega t\), but the mixed derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -\omega\varphi'\sin\omega t\) is proportional to \(\sin\omega t\). The functions \(\cos\omega t\) and \(\sin\omega t\) are not proportional: at \(t = 0\) the first is \(1\) and the second \(0\), at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the other way round. So the part of the equation with each of them must vanish separately. The following lemma shows this, and it is also the proof that was promised.

Lemma 26.11 A standing wave is not a solution (stoječe valovanje ni rešitev)

Let \(L > 0\), \(c > 0\), \(0 < v < c\) and \(\omega > 0\), and let \(\varphi : [0, L] \to \mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. If \(w(x, t) = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\) solves equation (26.10) for every \(t \ge 0\), then \(\varphi = 0\). In particular \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega t)\) is not a solution for any \(\omega\).

Proof

We must show that the equation forces two different conditions on \(\varphi\) at two times.

  1. For \(w = \varphi\cos\omega t\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2\varphi\cos\omega t\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -\omega\varphi'\sin\omega t\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi''\cos\omega t\) (theorem on derivatives of sine and cosine, 8.12).
  2. At \(t = 0\) we have \(\cos 0 = 1\) and \(\sin 0 = 0\), so equation (26.10) gives \(-\omega^2\varphi + (v^2 - c^2)\varphi'' = 0\).
  3. At \(t = \pi/(2\omega)\) we have \(\cos = 0\) and \(\sin = 1\), so the equation gives \(-2v\omega\varphi'(x) = 0\) for every \(x\). Since \(v\) and \(\omega\) are positive, \(\varphi' = 0\).
  4. A function with zero derivative is constant (corollary 1.85), and \(\varphi(0) = 0\) by the boundary condition, so \(\varphi = 0\). The function \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) is not zero everywhere, so by this it is not a solution.

Source: The proof is not from the sources. WM1990 (PDF p. 4) and CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2) state only the result that the eigenfunctions of the moving string change.

What do we use instead of \(\cos\omega t\)? Every point still oscillates with \(\omega\), but not all at once: the point \(x\) reaches its crest with a delay that depends on \(x\). We say the point \(x\) has amplitude \(|\varphi(x)|\) and phase shift \(\arg\varphi(x)\), and we write this with one complex function, as for systems with one degree of freedom in chapter 9: \(w(x, t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\big)\) (definition 9.28). If \(\varphi = |\varphi|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\), then \(w = |\varphi|\cos(\omega t + \theta)\). The word phase means the stage a point has reached in its oscillation: two points with different \(\theta\) are not at the same stage and do not reach their crests at the same time.

Definition 26.12 Mode of the moving string (način nihanja gibajoče se strune)

Let \(L > 0\), \(c > 0\) and \(0 \le v < c\). Let \(\omega > 0\) be a number and \(\varphi : [0, L] \to \mathbb{C}\) a complex function that is not zero everywhere and whose real and imaginary parts are twice continuously differentiable. The pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode (način nihanja) of the string with equation (26.10) if the real function

\[w(x, t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\big) = \mathrm{Re}\,\varphi(x)\cos\omega t - \mathrm{Im}\,\varphi(x)\sin\omega t\]

solves equation (26.10) for all \(t \ge 0\), boundary conditions included. The number \(\omega\) is the natural circular frequency (lastna krožna frekvenca), \(\varphi\) is the complex mode shape (kompleksna oblika načina). A point \(x\) with \(\varphi(x) = 0\) is a node (vozel).

Source: WM1990 section 3 (PDF pp. 2-3) and CHEN2005 section 2.2 (PDF pp. 2-3) treat complex eigenfunctions of the moving string. The notation with \(\mathrm{Re}(\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) is not from the sources. For \(v = 0\) and real \(\varphi\) this is the mode of definition 13.6.

Which pairs \((\omega, \varphi)\) exist? We look for them in three moves. First we insert \(\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}\) into the equation and get an ordinary equation with complex coefficients. Then we remove the term with the first derivative by writing \(\varphi\) as the product \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\psi\) with a phase \(kx\) that grows with position. The equation of section 13.2 remains.

Theorem 26.13 Modes of the moving string (načini nihanja gibajoče se strune)

Let \(L > 0\), \(c > 0\) and \(0 \le v < c\). The pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of the string with equation (26.10) if and only if there are a natural number \(n\) and a complex number \(C \ne 0\) with

\[\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\Big) , \qquad \varphi(x) = C\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}} x}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L} , \qquad k_{\mathrm{n}} = \frac{n\pi v}{cL} . \tag{26.11}\]

For \(C = |C|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\) the real form of the mode is

\[w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t) = |C|\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\cos\big(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t + k_{\mathrm{n}} x + \theta\big) . \tag{26.12}\]

For \(v = 0\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi c/L\) and \(\varphi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\), which is theorem 13.7.

Proof

We must show that the condition for a mode is equivalent to an ordinary equation with end conditions, and solve it. We write \(\varphi' = \mathrm{d}\varphi/\mathrm{d}x\), and derivatives of complex functions are taken by components (lemma 9.30).

  1. For \(w = \mathrm{Re}(\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) theorem 9.29, item 3, gives \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\omega\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = \mathrm{Re}(-\omega^2\varphi\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = \mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}\omega\varphi'\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \mathrm{Re}(\varphi''\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\). Equation (26.10) is then \(\mathrm{Re}(P\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}) = 0\) with the complex function \(P = -\omega^2\varphi + 2\mathrm{i}v\omega\varphi' + (v^2 - c^2)\varphi''\).
  2. If \(\mathrm{Re}(P(x)\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}) = 0\) for every \(t \ge 0\), then \(t = 0\) gives \(\mathrm{Re}\,P = 0\) and \(t = \pi/(2\omega)\) gives \(\mathrm{Re}(\mathrm{i}P) = -\mathrm{Im}\,P = 0\). So \(P = 0\), that is
    \[(c^2 - v^2)\,\varphi'' - 2\mathrm{i}v\omega\,\varphi' + \omega^2\varphi = 0 . \tag{26.13}\]
    Conversely \(P = 0\) gives the equation for every \(t\). The same argument (at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\)) shows that the boundary conditions hold if and only if \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\).
  3. Let \(k = v\omega/(c^2 - v^2)\) (a defined number, since \(v < c\)) and \(\psi(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}kx}\varphi(x)\). By the rules for complex functions (lemma 9.30, item 1) and the derivative \((\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx})' = \mathrm{i}k\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\) we get \(\varphi' = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}(\psi' + \mathrm{i}k\psi)\) and \(\varphi'' = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}(\psi'' + 2\mathrm{i}k\psi' - k^2\psi)\).
  4. We insert into (26.13) and divide by \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx} \ne 0\) (theorem 9.29, item 2). The coefficient of \(\psi'\) is \(2\mathrm{i}k(c^2 - v^2) - 2\mathrm{i}v\omega = 0\) by the choice of \(k\). The coefficient of \(\psi\) is
    \[-(c^2 - v^2)k^2 + 2v\omega k + \omega^2 = \frac{-v^2\omega^2 + 2v^2\omega^2}{c^2 - v^2} + \omega^2 = \frac{\omega^2 c^2}{c^2 - v^2} .\]
    What remains is \((c^2 - v^2)\psi'' + \dfrac{\omega^2c^2}{c^2 - v^2}\psi = 0\), that is \(\psi'' = -\kappa^2\psi\) with \(\kappa = \omega c/(c^2 - v^2) > 0\). The boundary conditions are \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx} \ne 0\).
  5. The real and imaginary parts of \(\psi\) are real, twice continuously differentiable, and each solves \(\psi'' = -\kappa^2\psi\) with zeros at \(0\) and \(L\) (the coefficient \(-\kappa^2\) is real). Since \(\psi\) is not zero everywhere, at least one of them is not. For that part steps 3 to 5 of the proof of theorem 13.7 hold, with \(\kappa\) in place of the number \(k = \omega/c\) used there: \(\sin\kappa L = 0\), so \(\kappa L = n\pi\) with a natural number \(n\), and the part is a multiple of \(\sin\kappa x\). The same holds for the other part if it is not zero, so \(\psi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with a complex \(C \ne 0\).
  6. From \(\kappa = n\pi/L\) we get \(\omega = \kappa(c^2 - v^2)/c = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(k = v\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(c^2 - v^2) = n\pi v/(cL) = k_{\mathrm{n}}\). So \(\varphi = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}} x}\psi = C\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}\sin(n\pi x/L)\). This is the direction "only if".
  7. Conversely, let \(\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\varphi\) from (26.11). Then \(\kappa = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} c/(c^2 - v^2) = n\pi/L\) and \(\psi = C\sin(n\pi x/L)\) solves \(\psi'' = -\kappa^2\psi\) with zeros at \(0\) and \(L\). Steps 4 and 3 in reverse give (26.13), and step 2 shows that \(w\) is a solution with the boundary conditions.
  8. The real part: \(\mathrm{Re}\big(|C|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}\sin(n\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t}\big) = |C|\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x + \theta)\), because \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\alpha} = \cos\alpha + \mathrm{i}\sin\alpha\) (definition 9.28) and \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) is real.

Source: WM1990 (27a) and (27b) (PDF p. 4): \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi(1 - \nu^2)\) and the eigenfunction with components \(\sin(n\pi x)\cos(n\pi\nu x)\) and \(\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi\nu x)\) in dimensionless quantities, where \(\nu = v/c\) and not Poisson's ratio. CHEN2005 (5) (PDF p. 2): \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = (n\pi/l)(1 - \rho c^2/P)\sqrt{P/\rho}\), where \(c\) means the transport speed. The proof by removing the first derivative with the phase \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\) is not from the sources, it is checked with SymPy (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 1 and 2).

The theorem is short, its meaning is in the shape, and figure 26.7 builds it. We draw first the two eyelets in each row, with the string of length \(L\) between them, and the horizontal position of the string at rest. Each row is one time in the oscillation, from top to bottom \(\omega t = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\). Into it we put the shape of the string at time \(\omega t = 0\) and the grey dashed envelope \(\pm\sin(\pi x/L)\), which is the largest deflection a point reaches. The left column is the string at rest, \(v = 0\): at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the string is straight, at \(\omega t = \pi\) it is inverted, and at every time the shape is symmetric about the middle. In the right column \(v/c = \tfrac12\) and \(k_1 = \pi/(2L)\): at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the string is not straight, because the factor \(\cos(\omega t + k_1x)\) differs from point to point, and at none of the four times is the shape symmetric. The place of largest deflection, the orange dot, is at \(0{,}39\,L\) at \(\omega t = 0\), at \(0{,}61\,L\) at \(\pi/2\), at \(0{,}39\,L\) again at \(\pi\) and at \(0{,}61\,L\) at \(3\pi/2\) (computed in outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 5). The envelope and the eyelets stay as they were.

Corollary 26.14 Nodes and amplitudes of the mode (vozli in amplitude načina)

Let \((\omega_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) be a mode from theorem 26.13. The amplitude of the point \(x\) is \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x)| = |C|\,|\sin(n\pi x/L)|\), as for the string at rest. Mode \(n\) has \(n - 1\) nodes in the interior, at the points \(x = jL/n\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n - 1\). For \(v > 0\) there is no time at which the string is straight everywhere.

Proof

We must show three claims. The theorem gives the amplitude and the nodes, straightness needs one more argument.

  1. By theorem 9.29, item 2, \(|\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}| = 1\), so \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}| = |C|\,|\sin(n\pi x/L)|\).
  2. A node is a point with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = 0\), that is \(\sin(n\pi x/L) = 0\), since \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x} \ne 0\) and \(C \ne 0\). The zeros of the sine are the multiples of \(\pi\) (step 5 of the proof of theorem 13.7), so \(x = jL/n\), and the condition \(0 < x < L\) gives \(j = 1, \dots, n - 1\).
  3. At time \(t\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t) = |C|\sin(n\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x + \theta)\). For \(x \in (0, L)\) the first factor is nonzero except at the nodes, and the second is zero only where \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x + \theta\) is an odd multiple of \(\pi/2\). For \(v > 0\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\) and the argument grows with \(x\) by \(k_{\mathrm{n}}L > 0\), so the cosine has at most finitely many zeros on \((0, L)\). Hence \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(\cdot, t)\) is not zero everywhere.

Source: WM1990 (PDF p. 4): the nodes are the same as for the string at rest, but the axial motion distorts the shapes strongly (figure 2, PDF p. 4). The proof is not from the sources.

Figure 26.7 shows this in numbers and the theorem says why. The nodes stay in the same places because their condition is \(\sin(n\pi x/L) = 0\) and the phase \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}}x}\) does not change the amplitude. A string that is straight at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) for \(v = 0\) is not straight at this time for \(v > 0\), because every point has its own phase. The description of this phase by travelling waves shows a second picture.

By the addition formulas (corollary 8.15) the product \(\sin A\cos B\) is half the sum \(\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B)\). With \(A = n\pi x/L\) and \(B = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x\) from mode \(n\) we get the sum of two waves of the kind that lemma 26.6 of section 26.2 knows.

Corollary 26.15 A mode as a sum of two travelling waves (način kot vsota dveh potujočih valov)

Let \(w_{\mathrm{n}}\) be from equation (26.12) with \(\theta = 0\) and \(|C| = 1\). Then

\[w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t) = \tfrac12\sin\!\Big(\frac{n\pi(c - v)}{cL}\,x - \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\Big) + \tfrac12\sin\!\Big(\frac{n\pi(c + v)}{cL}\,x + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\Big) . \tag{26.14}\]

The first wave has the form \(F(x - (c + v)t)\) and moves in the direction of motion with speed \(c + v\). The second has the form \(G(x + (c - v)t)\) and moves against the direction of motion with speed \(c - v\). Both speeds are measured relative to the fixed eyelets. The waves have the same frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and wavelengths \(2Lc/(n(c - v))\) and \(2Lc/(n(c + v))\).

Proof

We must show the equality and, for each wave, its speed and wavelength.

  1. By the addition formulas (corollary 8.15), \(\sin(A + B) + \sin(A - B) = 2\sin A\cos B\). With \(A = n\pi x/L\) and \(B = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + k_{\mathrm{n}}x\) we have \(\sin A\cos B = \tfrac12\sin(A + B) + \tfrac12\sin(A - B)\), where \(A + B = (n\pi/L + k_{\mathrm{n}})x + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\) and \(A - B = (n\pi/L - k_{\mathrm{n}})x - \omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\). Since \(n\pi/L \pm k_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi(c \pm v)/(cL)\), this is (26.14).
  2. The first term is \(\tfrac12\sin(q(x - st))\) with \(q = n\pi(c - v)/(cL)\) and \(s = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/q = (c^2 - v^2)/(c - v) = c + v\). This is the form \(F(x - (c + v)t)\). The wavelength is \(2\pi/q = 2Lc/(n(c - v))\).
  3. The second term is \(\tfrac12\sin(q'(x + s't))\) with \(q' = n\pi(c + v)/(cL)\) and \(s' = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/q' = c - v\), wavelength \(2\pi/q' = 2Lc/(n(c + v))\).

Source: CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2): Skutch determined the natural frequencies by superposing two waves in opposite directions. The derivation from the mode is not from the sources, it is checked in outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 2.

Figure 26.8 builds this for the first mode at \(v/c = \tfrac12\) at \(\omega t = \pi/3\). In each row there are the two eyelets a distance \(L\) apart and between them the horizontal position of the string at rest. Then we draw the first row, the wave \(\tfrac12\sin(\pi x/(2L) - \omega_1t)\), which the arrow \(c + v\) moves in the direction of motion. Its wavelength is \(4L\), four times the length of the string, so we see only a good part of one half-wave. The second row is the wave \(\tfrac12\sin(3\pi x/(2L) + \omega_1t)\) with speed \(c - v\) against the motion, wavelength \(\tfrac43 L\). In the third row is the sum, which is the shape of figure 26.7. For \(v = 0\) the waves have the same wavelength and are mirror images, so the sum is a standing wave. For \(v > 0\) the string carries both waves along at speed \(v\), so the first runs at \(c + v\) and the second at \(c - v\). At the same frequency they therefore have different wavelengths, they are no longer mirror images, and the sum is not a standing wave.

The two waves traverse the length of the string and are reflected at the eyelet. How long does it take for the motion to repeat? The wave in the direction of motion needs the time \(L/(c + v)\) to the second eyelet, and the reflected wave against the motion needs \(L/(c - v)\) back to the first. At a fixed end the two waves are equal and opposite there (boundary condition \(w = 0\)), so after the passage in both directions the shapes fit again. The theorem gives the same number without this picture.

Corollary 26.16 Period and round-trip time (perioda in čas obhoda)

The period of the first mode equals the round-trip time,

\[\tau = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_1} = \frac{L}{c + v} + \frac{L}{c - v} = \frac{2Lc}{c^2 - v^2} , \tag{26.15}\]

and \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\tau = 2\pi n\), so every mode is periodic with period \(\tau\).

Proof

We must show the equality of the three expressions and the multiple.

  1. \(\omega_1 = (\pi c/L)(1 - v^2/c^2) = \pi(c^2 - v^2)/(cL)\) by equation (26.11), so \(2\pi/\omega_1 = 2cL/(c^2 - v^2)\).
  2. With the same denominator, \(L/(c + v) + L/(c - v) = L\big((c - v) + (c + v)\big)/(c^2 - v^2) = 2Lc/(c^2 - v^2)\).
  3. \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\omega_1\), so \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\tau = 2\pi n\), and \(k_{\mathrm{n}}\) does not depend on time, so \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t + \tau) = w_{\mathrm{n}}(x, t)\).

Source: CHEN2005 (PDF p. 2): Skutch's route by two waves. The calculation is not from the sources. The reflection at a fixed end is treated in more detail in section 26.2.

Example 26.17 Frequencies of the band at different speeds (frekvence traku pri različnih hitrostih)

The band from the start of the section has \(c = \sqrt{\sigma/\rho} = 113{,}23\) m/s with \(\sigma = 100\) MPa and \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³ (steel from BOWER, table 3.1, PDF p. 100, as in section 26.1). By theorem 26.13 we have \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(2\pi) = n\,\dfrac{c}{2L}\,(1 - v^2/c^2)\), so:

\(v\) (m/s) \(v/c\) \(f_1\) (Hz) \(f_2\) (Hz) \(f_3\) (Hz) \(k_1\) (1/m)
0 0 56,61 113,23 169,84 0
20 0,177 54,85 109,69 164,54 0,555
40 0,353 49,55 99,10 148,65 1,110
80 0,707 28,35 56,70 85,06 2,220

At \(v = 40\) m/s the two wavelengths of the first mode by corollary 26.15 are \(2Lc/(c - v) = 3{,}092\) m and \(2Lc/(c + v) = 1{,}478\) m. The round-trip time by corollary 26.16 is \(6{,}526 + 13{,}656 = 20{,}182\) ms, equal to \(1/f_1 = 1/49{,}55\) s. For the string at rest \(2L/c = 17{,}664\) ms.

Source: The numbers are our calculation (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, lines 4). The choice of band and speed is not from a source, WM1990 (PDF p. 1) names band saws only as an example of an axially moving material.

Figure 26.9 shows these numbers on curves. We draw the axes: speed \(v\) horizontally, frequency \(f\) vertically, and on them the ticks every 20 m/s, with the speed \(c\) marked separately. The curve of the first mode is \(f_1\), which falls from 56,61 Hz to zero at \(v = c\). The orange dots are the values of the table. The curves \(f_2\) and \(f_3\) have the same shape, twice and three times as high, since \(f_{\mathrm{n}} = n f_1\) at every speed: the ratio \(1 : 2 : 3\) of section 13.2 stays. At \(v = 40\) m/s the frequency \(f_1\) is \(1 - 0{,}8752 = 12{,}5\,\%\) lower than at \(v = 0\), because \(v^2/c^2 = 0{,}125\). At \(v/c = 0{,}1\), which is 11,3 m/s, the decrease would be only \(1\,\%\).

One more step: we show in numbers that the standing wave of section 13.2 is indeed not a solution, and why. Lemma 26.11 says that there is no real standing mode, but not how large the imbalance is. We take \(\sin(\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_1t)\) with the correct frequency \(\omega_1\) of the band and look at the eyelet.

Example 26.18 The standing wave at the first eyelet (stoječe valovanje na prvem očescu)

At \(x = 0\) we have \(w = 0\) at every time, so \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = 0\) there. For \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\cos\omega_1t\) also \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(\pi/L)^2 w = 0\) at \(x = 0\). The mixed derivative, however, is \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -(\pi/L)\omega_1\sin\omega_1t\), equal to \(-\pi\omega_1/L\) at \(\omega_1t = \pi/2\). The left side of equation (26.10), which should be zero, is then \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} = -2\pi v\omega_1/L\). At \(v = 40\) m/s and \(\omega_1 = 311{,}32\) 1/s this is \(-78\,244\) m/s² per unit amplitude. As a scale we take the tension term \(c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in the middle of the string at \(\omega_1 t = 0\), where it is largest: \(c^2(\pi/L)^2 = 126\,533\) m/s² per unit amplitude. The imbalance is thus \(2g(1 - g^2) = 62\,\%\) of this size, with \(g = v/c = 0{,}353\). For small \(v\) it is about \(2g\), that is linear in the speed.

Source: The calculation is ours (outlines/ch-jermeni/num-03.out, line 3). WM1990 (PDF p. 4) says only that the axial motion distorts the shapes.

Why is it so? Figure 26.10 shows what happens to a particle that runs through the eyelet. We draw the eyelet and the taut string on the left. The shape of the string at \(\omega t = 0\) has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = \pi A/L\) at the eyelet (\(A\) is the drawn deflection in the middle), at \(\omega t = \pi\) the opposite one, and at \(\omega t = \pi/2\) the string is straight. The particle running through the eyelet has a velocity along the tangent, that is the horizontal component \(v\) and the transverse component \(v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The velocity vectors differ at the three times: the transverse component goes from \(v\pi A/L\) through zero to \(-v\pi A/L\). The transverse velocity of the particles running through the eyelet thus changes in time. The transverse acceleration of a particle is \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by equation (26.2), and since \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) are zero at the eyelet, the Coriolis term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) remains.
