By Newton's law something must act on it. The transverse force per unit mass is by equation (26.10) equal to \(c^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and for the standing wave it is zero at the eyelet. An acceleration without a force is a contradiction, so the standing wave cannot be a motion of the string at the eyelet.

Having found the modes, we ask whether they are enough: can every free motion of the string be written as a sum of modes? Section 26.6 treats this with the orthogonality of complex modes. First, however, the real limit demands attention, the critical speed \(v = c\), at which all \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) vanish: section 26.4.

26.4 Critical speed and a conserved quantity

In section 26.3 we found the frequencies of the modes of the moving string, \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \dfrac{n\pi c}{L}\Big(1 - \dfrac{v^2}{c^2}\Big)\) (theorem 26.13). With a higher transport speed \(v\) they all fall, and at \(v = c\) they are all zero. For our band of example A (steel, \(L = 1\) m, \(\sigma = 100\) MPa, \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, \(T = 4500\) N, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s) the first frequency is \(56{,}61\) Hz at \(v = 0\), \(49{,}55\) Hz at \(v = 40\) m/s and \(0\) at \(v = c\). Why exactly at \(c\), and what does it mean for a band that runs so fast? This is the first question of the section. The second is about energy. For the strings of section 13.1 the sum of kinetic and elastic energy stays constant during the motion. Does this hold here too, where the material runs through the eyelets? And if not, does any quantity exist that is conserved and that tells us in the end that the motion stays small?

From history

Archibald and Emslie modelled a belt running from an eccentric pulley to a smooth pulley as a string running through eyelets and excited by the harmonic motion of an eyelet. They found that the natural frequencies decrease with the transport speed and that the moving string, at a sufficiently high speed, becomes unstable by divergence (divergence instability, divergenčna nestabilnost) (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, a work of 1958 by the reference list on PDF p. 21). Why their belt matters to us: the span between two pulleys is our moving string, and their finding is exactly what this section shows, the frequencies of section 26.3 and the speed at which they fail. Swope and Ames investigated with the method of characteristics how a disturbance spreads along such a string when it is excited at an end. They predicted irregular behaviour of the string near the critical speed, that is the speed of waves in the material (CHEN2005, PDF p. 2, a work of 1963 by the reference list on PDF p. 21), which for us is \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4).

The story tells two things: at the speed \(c\) something jumps, and this speed is the same number as the wave speed in a string at rest. Let us see why. We stay with the model of section 26.1: the moving string (definition 26.3) of length \(L\), mass \(\mu\) per unit length, tension \(T\) and transport speed \(v > 0\) in the eyelets, which stand at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), with the equation

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} \tag{26.16}\]

from theorem 26.4. By idealization 4 the slope is small, \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}005\). In this section the letter \(T\) is always the tension force, not the kinetic energy of chapters 8 and 9, and \(v\) is the transport speed, not the deflection.

26.4.1 When the tension is just enough

Let us look first at the simplest possible motion: a string whose shape does not change. Like water in a steady channel: the shape of the channel rests and the material flows along it. Can this be a motion of the moving string? The answer is given by the force on a piece of material, so we build figure 26.11.

In the left panel we take the axis \(x\) and on it the string, held in the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\). We have given it a resting shape \(w(x) = h\sin(\pi x/L)\), where \(h\) is the largest deflection. The string runs through the eyelets with speed \(v\), which in the left panel is half of \(c\), so the arrow is half of the one in the right panel. Take the piece of material that is at this moment over the interval from \(a\) to \(b\), that is the same material points that we follow as they run (section 26.1). What acts on it? The neighbouring parts of the string pull the piece with the force \(T\) along the tangent, each force starting at the point where it acts. The horizontal components of these two forces are opposite and cancel, the vertical ones add up to one force \(T\sigma\) with \(\sigma = w_{\mathrm{x}}(b) - w_{\mathrm{x}}(a)\). The number \(\sigma\) is negative, because the slope decreases along the piece (the string bulges upwards), so this force points down. What is it equal to? By Newton's second law the sum of forces on a body is mass times acceleration, which for a piece of material is written by equation (26.4) of section 26.1. Since the shape does not change, \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), and by lemma 26.1 the acceleration of each material point is only the centripetal one, \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\): the point runs along a curved curve with speed \(v\) and something must pull it towards the centre of curvature. The sum of these accelerations along the piece, multiplied by the mass, is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \mu v^2\sigma\) by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40). This is the orange arrow, also pointing down. We draw the two arrows from two different points of the piece, so that they do not overlap.

Each arrow has its role. The blue one is what the piece gets from the neighbouring parts, the orange one what the piece needs to stay on the steady curve. In the left panel the blue is four times the orange. So the piece would get more than it needs: the surplus \(T\sigma - \mu v^2\sigma = (T - \mu v^2)\sigma\) would pull it towards the straight line and the shape would not stay. On the band of example A and a piece from \(0{,}3\) to \(0{,}7\) m with \(h = 1{,}5\) mm, at \(v = 40\) m/s the force is \(T\sigma = -24{,}93\) N, the needed force \(\mu v^2\sigma = -3{,}11\) N, the surplus \(-21{,}82\) N. At \(v = 0{,}9c = 101{,}90\) m/s the needed force is \(-20{,}19\) N, the surplus \(-4{,}74\) N, and as \(v\) grows towards \(c\) the surplus falls to zero. In the right panel the string runs with speed \(v = c\) (the longer arrow \(v\)), the same piece feels the same tension forces and their sum \(T\sigma\), and the needed force is \(\mu c^2\sigma = T\sigma\), because \(\mu c^2 = T\) (definition 13.4). The two arrows are equal: the tension is exactly enough for the material points to run along the curve, and there is no surplus that would straighten the shape. Is this shape special? It is not: the other shapes below the right panel have the same property. The lemma below states this exactly.

Lemma 26.19 Arbitrary steady shape at the speed \(c\) (poljubna stalna oblika pri hitrosti \(c\))

Let \(v = c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) and let \(f : [0, L] \to \mathbb{R}\) be a twice continuously differentiable function with \(f(0) = f(L) = 0\). Then \(w(x, t) = f(x)\) is a moving string (definition 26.3). For \(v \ne c\) the only steady shape \(w(x, t) = f(x)\) that is a moving string is \(f = 0\).

Proof

We must show that the function satisfies equation (26.16) exactly when \((T - \mu v^2) f'' = 0\), and that the claim follows from this.

  1. For \(w = f(x)\) we have \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), hence also \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{tx}} = 0\). The derivatives \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = f'\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = f''\) are continuous, as definition 26.3 requires, and the boundary conditions \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) are satisfied.
  2. For \(w = f(x)\) equation (26.16) is rewritten as \(\mu v^2 f'' = T f''\), so \((T - \mu v^2)\,f'' = 0\).
  3. If \(v = c\), then \(T - \mu v^2 = T - \mu c^2 = 0\) by definition 13.4. The equation holds for every \(f\), because the connection with the equation of the piece (26.4) is an equivalence by theorem 26.4.
  4. If \(v \ne c\), then \(T - \mu v^2 \ne 0\), so \(f'' = 0\) everywhere, hence \(f'\) is constant and \(f\) is a straight line (corollary 1.85 twice). From \(f(0) = f(L) = 0\) it follows that \(f = 0\).

Source: WM1990, appendix, section 1 (PDF p. 6): every natural frequency of the travelling string is zero at \(v = 1\) (dimensionless, that is \(v = c\)), the critical speed is \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 1\). The claim about an arbitrary steady shape and its proof are ours.

What does the claim say? At \(v = c\) we have infinitely many resting equilibria, each with its own shape. At \(v \neq c\) a string at rest is only straight. So the moving string at \(v = c\) loses a property that the string without flow has: the string of section 13.1 always has, after we displace it, a force that returns it towards the straight line. This restoring is measured by \(T - \mu v^2\), as we saw in the surplus. Let us test it on the band. At \(v = 40\) m/s and \(w(x) = 1{,}5\text{ mm}\cdot\sin(\pi x/L)\) the residual of the equation \((\mu v^2 - T)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) has the largest value \(58{,}31\) N/m, at \(v = 0{,}9c\) only \(12{,}66\) N/m, at \(v = c\) it is zero (recomputed in num-04.out).

Definition 26.20 Critical speed of the moving string (kritična hitrost gibajoče se strune)

The critical speed (kritična hitrost) of a moving string with mass \(\mu\) per unit length and tension \(T\) is the number

\[v_{\mathrm{c}} = \sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = c , \tag{26.17}\]

in m/s, that is the wave speed of definition 13.4. The transport speed \(v > 0\) is subcritical (podkritična) for \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\), critical for \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\) and supercritical (nadkritična) for \(v > v_{\mathrm{c}}\).

Source: WM1990, PDF p. 2 and appendix, section 1, PDF p. 6 (string: \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 1\) in dimensionless form), CHEN2005, PDF p. 2 (Swope and Ames: the critical speed is the characteristic wave speed in the material). The form as a definition is ours.

The word critical comes from the Greek krisis, which means decision or break. The name fits, because at this speed the behaviour of the string jumps: below it every resting shape except the straight line has a surplus of force, at it none, above it \(T - \mu v^2\) is negative. What follows at a supercritical speed we do not claim here. The model with two fixed eyelets is outside its validity for \(v > c\): WM1990 (PDF p. 2) requires the speed to be subcritical, as will we in the theorems that require \(v < c\). The critical speed of the band of example A is \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c = 113{,}23\) m/s. Above it this model does not describe the band.

From history

Archibald and Emslie found the divergence instability at a sufficiently high speed in the story above, and WM1990 (PDF p. 6, appendix) shows that at \(v = c\) every natural frequency of the string vanishes. At a zero frequency the difference between oscillation and static deformation is lost, and this is the lemma above: the string stays in every shape. Hence divergence (divergence): the deflection does not oscillate but stays.

The story showed where the name divergence comes from. Let us return to the model and to the second question: energy.

26.4.2 The conserved quantity

For the strings of section 13.1 the sum \(\tfrac12\mu\int w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + \tfrac12 T\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) is constant during the motion: the first half is the kinetic, the second the elastic energy. Let us try the same here. The kinetic energy of the material is no longer only \(\tfrac12\mu\int w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\), because the material runs: each material point has the transverse velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (lemma 26.1), so the kinetic energy per unit length is \(\tfrac12\mu\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v w_{\mathrm{x}})^2\). When we expand the square we get three parts. Summed over the span, they are called by chapter 8 (theorem 8.86) \(T_2\), \(T_1\) and \(T_0\):

\[T_2 = \tfrac12\mu\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad T_1 = \mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad T_0 = \tfrac12\mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{26.18}\]

where \(T_2\) is the part quadratic in \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(T_1\) the mixed part, linear in \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), and \(T_0\) the part without the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\). The elastic energy is \(V = \tfrac12 T\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). Why this expansion at all? Because the energy integral \(\mathcal{E}^* = T_2 - T_0 + V\) of chapter 8 (theorem 8.109) warns us that with time-dependent constraints it is this combination that is conserved, not \(T + V\). Does this hold here too? Theorem 8.109 is proved for a system with finitely many coordinates, and strings have infinitely many, so we do not use it but check the same idea directly. The test is simple: \(\mathcal{E}^*\) should be a conserved quantity (definition 8.104).

From history

Chubachi was the first to discuss the periodicity of energy transfer in a moving string (CHEN2005, PDF p. 6, a work of 1958 by PDF p. 21). Miranker discussed the energy of the moving string and from the equation without excitation derived an expression for the rate of change of energy, which is usually not zero (CHEN2005, PDF p. 6, year 1960 by PDF p. 21). Wickert and Mote pointed out that this expression describes only the local rate of change, since it does not account for the flow of energy through the supports (CHEN2005, PDF p. 6, a work of 1989 by PDF p. 22). Miranker also showed that there is another functional that is constant for the moving string (CHEN2005, PDF p. 7). We shall check all this: first the constant functional, then the expression for the energy.

The story showed two things: the energy of the span is not constant, something else is. Now we prove it.

Theorem 26.21 Conserved quantity of the moving string (ohranjena količina gibajoče strune)

Let \(w\) be a moving string (definition 26.3) and

\[\mathcal{E}^*(t) = \tfrac12\int_0^L\Big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, t)^2 + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(x, t)^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = T_2 - T_0 + V . \tag{26.19}\]

Then \(\mathcal{E}^*(t)\) is constant for every \(t \ge 0\).

Proof

We must show that the derivative \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime}(t)\) is zero. We differentiate under the integral. The term with \(w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is transformed by integration by parts so that it can be compared with the equation of motion. What then remains of the Coriolis term is a derivative in \(x\) and vanishes at the eyelets.

  1. The integrand has a \(t\)-derivative \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) that is continuous, because \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) are continuous. By lemma 4.19 therefore \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime}(t) = \int_0^L\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big)\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. Since \(w(0, t) = 0\) for every \(t\), we have \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(0, t) = 0\), and likewise \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t) = 0\).
  3. By theorem 1.125 \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = w_{\mathrm{tx}}\), and integration by parts (corollary 3.41) with \(f = w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(g = w_{\mathrm{t}}\) gives \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\big]_0^L - \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{xx}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{xx}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), because the square bracket is zero by step 2.
  4. Steps 1 and 3 give \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big)\mathrm{d}x\).
  5. Equation (26.16) is equivalent to \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). Insert into step 4: \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = -2\mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\mu v\int_0^L \big(w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big)_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \((w_{\mathrm{t}}^2)_{\mathrm{x}} = 2 w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\).
  6. By the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40) the last integral is \(\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L = 0\) by step 2. So \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = 0\), and by corollary 1.85 \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is constant.

Source: CHEN2005 (33), PDF p. 7 (Miranker): \(S_{\mathrm{E}}[V] = \int_0^L \tfrac12\big[\rho V_{\mathrm{T}}^2 + (P - \rho c^2)V_{\mathrm{X}}^2\big]\mathrm{d}X\) is constant for the moving string. The proof by steps and the connection with theorem 8.109 are not from the source.

What does the theorem say? The mixed term \(2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) in the equation of motion (the Coriolis one, section 26.1) turns out in step 5 to be the \(x\)-derivative of the square of \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), which is zero at the eyelets. The velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero at the eyelets because they stand still (idealization 6). The power of the Coriolis force on the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), \(-2\mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), is therefore zero, and a force without power does not change \(\mathcal{E}^*\). The connection with \(T_2 - T_0 + V\) tells what happened to \(T_0\): the kinetic energy of the flow, \(\tfrac12\mu v^2\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\), reduces the stiffness by \(\mu v^2\). Since \(T_0\) has no velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\), it acts as a negative elastic energy. This is the surplus of figure 26.11: the tension must spend a part of its force on making the material points run along a curved path, and only \(T - \mu v^2 = \mu(c^2 - v^2)\) is left for the return towards the straight line.

Let us test the conserved quantity on the band. For the first mode, \(w = a\sin(\pi x/L)\cos(\omega_1 t + k_1 x)\) with amplitude \(a = 1{,}5\) mm, \(\omega_1 = 311{,}32\) 1/s and \(k_1 = \pi v/(cL)\), at \(v = 40\) m/s (theorem 26.13) the largest slope \(a\pi/L = 4{,}71\cdot 10^{-3}\) matches the limit of idealization 4. A computation with NumPy gives \(\mathcal{E}^* = 21{,}86\) mJ at each of \(200001\) times spread evenly over one period (period \(\tau = 2\pi/\omega_1 = 20{,}18\) ms), the difference between the largest and the smallest value is below \(10^{-12}\) mJ. The residual of the equation of motion for this mode is below \(3\cdot 10^{-14}\) N/m.

Corollary 26.22 Boundedness of the motion below the critical speed (omejenost gibanja pod kritično hitrostjo)

Let \(w\) be a moving string (definition 26.3) with \(0 < v < c\), initial displacement \(w_0(x) = w(x, 0)\) and initial velocity \(w_1(x) = w_{\mathrm{t}}(x, 0)\). Then for every \(t \ge 0\)

\[\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le \int_0^L w_0'^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \frac{\mu}{T - \mu v^2}\int_0^L w_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \qquad \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le \frac{T - \mu v^2}{\mu}\int_0^L w_0'^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L w_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{26.20}\]

and for every \(x \in [0, L]\) we have \(|w(x, t)| \le \sqrt{L}\,\Big(\int_0^L w_0'^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \dfrac{\mu}{T - \mu v^2}\int_0^L w_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x\Big)^{1/2}\).

Proof

We must show that from the constancy of \(\mathcal{E}^*\) and from both of its terms being nonnegative each of the three inequalities follows. The displacement is obtained from the slope by the fundamental theorem and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

  1. By theorem 26.21 \(\mathcal{E}^*(t) = \mathcal{E}^*(0) = \tfrac12\mu\int w_1^2 + \tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int w_0'^2\).
  2. Since \(v < c\), we have \(T - \mu v^2 > 0\), so both terms in (26.19) are nonnegative. Hence each of them is at most \(\mathcal{E}^*(0)\): \(\tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 \le \mathcal{E}^*(0)\) and \(\tfrac12\mu\int w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 \le \mathcal{E}^*(0)\).
  3. Division by \(\tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\) or \(\tfrac12\mu\) and insertion of \(\mathcal{E}^*(0)\) from step 1 give the first two inequalities.
  4. Since \(w(0, t) = 0\), by the fundamental theorem \(w(x, t) = \int_0^x w_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t)\,\mathrm{d}s\). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (lemma 6.19) for the product of the functions \(1\) and \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}|\) we have \(|w(x, t)| \le \sqrt{x}\,\big(\int_0^x w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)^{1/2} \le \sqrt{L}\,\big(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)^{1/2}\), and the first inequality gives the third.

Source: The claim is ours, the idea is the same Dirichlet criterion as in chapter 8 (theorem 8.115): a conserved quantity that is positive definite bounds the motion. WM1990 (PDF p. 2) requires a subcritical speed, because then the stiffness operator is positive definite.

What do the inequalities say? The motion stays bounded in energy: the initial data determine a bound that it never exceeds. On the band with \(a = 1{,}5\) mm and \(v = 40\) m/s (\(T - \mu v^2 = 3938{,}4\) N) we have \(\int w_0'^2 = 8{,}24\cdot 10^{-6}\) m, the second term of the bound \(\mu\int w_1^2/(T - \mu v^2) = 2{,}87\cdot 10^{-6}\) m, together \(1{,}110\cdot 10^{-5}\) m, and the real value of \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) is at most \(1{,}072\cdot 10^{-5}\) m over one period: the bound is \(3{,}5\) % too high. The bound for the displacement is \(3{,}33\) mm at an amplitude of \(1{,}5\) mm. At \(v = 0{,}9c\) we have \(T - \mu v^2 = 855{,}0\) N, so the coefficient of the second term is \(5{,}26\) times larger than at \(v = 0\) (\(1/(1 - 0{,}81)\)), and the sum of the bound is \(1{,}110\cdot 10^{-5}\) m (for the first mode with amplitude \(a\) the bound is \(a^2\pi^2/(2L)\) at every speed \(v < c\), that is \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) of the resting shape \(a\sin(\pi x/L)\), recomputed with SymPy), the real maximum \(1{,}066\cdot 10^{-5}\) m. The bound does not say that the slope is small everywhere, because \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) bounds the average and not the largest values, so idealization 4 still has to be checked on the solution.

Where does the bound fail? Look back at lemma 26.19. At \(v = c\) we have \(T - \mu v^2 = 0\), and \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is zero for every resting shape \(w = f(x)\), even if \(f \neq 0\): the case \(f = 1{,}5\text{ mm}\cdot\sin(\pi x/L)\) has \(\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 1{,}110\cdot 10^{-5}\) m and \(\mathcal{E}^* = 0\). The conserved quantity then tells nothing about the slope, and the bound (26.20) has a zero in the denominator. For \(v > c\) it is worse. The same shape gives \(\mathcal{E}^* = \tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 < 0\), at \(v = 1{,}2c\) it is \(-10{,}99\) mJ (the model is here outside the limit of the subcritical speed, the number only shows that \(\mathcal{E}^*\) is no longer nonnegative). The theorem still holds, since its proof does not require \(v < c\), but the corollary does not.

26.4.3 The energy of the span is not conserved

What remains is the second question: what about the sum of kinetic and elastic energy of the span, that is what everyone would expect? Let us call it

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \tfrac12\int_0^L\Big(\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\big)^2 + T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = T_2 + T_1 + T_0 + V . \tag{26.21}\]

Here we have left out the constant part \(\tfrac12\mu v^2 L\) of the kinetic energy of the flow along the axis, which does not show in the derivative. Comparison with (26.19) tells that \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathcal{E}^* = T_1 + 2T_0\), which is the difference between \(T + V\) and \(T_2 - T_0 + V\) of theorem 8.109. If \(T_1 + 2T_0\) changes during the motion, \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) cannot be constant. On the band of example A at \(v = 40\) m/s and \(a = 1{,}5\) mm we draw figure 26.12 as follows: the axis \(t\) runs to the period of the first mode \(\tau\) \(= 20{,}18\) ms and the vertical axis shows energy in mJ. The blue line is \(\mathcal{E}^* = 21{,}9\) mJ, which is constant, and the orange curve is \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\), which oscillates between \(25{,}6\) and \(30{,}6\) mJ, the ratio of the largest and the smallest value is \(1{,}197\). Two cycles per period \(\tau\) arise because \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) contains squares of \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), which repeat after half an oscillation.

Why does \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) change? The answer is given by the work of forces. The span is not closed: material runs through it and the neighbouring parts of the string pull it at the eyelets. Let us look first at the piece of material that is at this moment over \([0, L]\). At its ends the neighbours pull it with the force \(T\) along the tangent, and the power of a force is force times the velocity of the point in its direction. At an eyelet \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) and the material point has the transverse velocity \(v w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (lemma 26.1), the transverse component of the force is \(T w_{\mathrm{x}}\). At \(x = L\) the power is \(T v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)^2\), at \(x = 0\) the force is reversed, \(-T v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t)^2\). The energy of the piece of material changes by the theorem on work and energy with the sum \(T v\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L\). But the span is not this piece: in a short time \(h\) the piece moves by \(v h\) along \(x\), at the left end of the span material enters with energy per unit length \(\hat e(0, t)\), at the right end it leaves with \(\hat e(L, t)\). At an eyelet \(\hat e = \tfrac12(\mu v^2 + T)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \tfrac12\mu v^2\), since \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\). The energy of the span therefore changes by the work of forces minus the energy that the material carries away: \(v\,\hat e\) at the right end and brings in at the left. The constant \(\tfrac12\mu v^2\) cancels. What remains is stated by the next lemma.

Lemma 26.23 Rate of change of the energy of the span (sprememba energije razpona)

Let \(w\) be a moving string (definition 26.3). Then \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}\) of (26.21) is differentiable and

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}'(t) = \frac{v}{2}\,\big(T - \mu v^2\big)\,\Big(w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)^2 - w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t)^2\Big) . \tag{26.22}\]
Proof

We must show that the difference \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathcal{E}^*\) differentiates into the right-hand side, because \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = 0\) by theorem 26.21.

  1. By expanding the square in (26.21), \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathcal{E}^* = \mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x + \mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. By lemma 4.19, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{tt}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. The last integral is \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L = 0\) by the fundamental theorem and by step 2 of the proof of theorem 26.21.
  4. From equation (26.16), \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Hence \(\mu\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{tt}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -2\mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x + (T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the last integral is \(\tfrac12\big[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big]_0^L\) by the fundamental theorem, because \((w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)_{\mathrm{x}} = 2 w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  5. The derivative of step 1 is by steps 2 to 4 equal to \(v\Big(-2\mu v\int w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} + \tfrac12(T - \mu v^2)\big[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big]_0^L\Big) + 2\mu v^2\int w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). The terms with the integral cancel (\(-2\mu v^2 + 2\mu v^2 = 0\)), what remains is \(\tfrac{v}{2}(T - \mu v^2)\big[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big]_0^L\). Since \(\mathcal{E}^{*\prime} = 0\), this is \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}'\).

Source: CHEN2005 (32), PDF p. 7 (Renshaw and others, a work of 1998 by the reference list on PDF p. 22): \(\mathrm{d}E_{\mathrm{E}}/\mathrm{d}T = \tfrac12 c(P - \rho c^2)\,(V_{\mathrm{X}})^2\big|_0^L\), and (28), PDF p. 6 (Lagrangian piece of material): \(\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}T = P c\,(V_{\mathrm{X}})^2\big|_0^L\). The proof by steps is ours, a similar explanation with the flow of energy through the eyelets is in CHEN2005, PDF p. 6.

Let us check on numbers. If we add the work of forces and the flow of energy, as described before the lemma, we get the same as the right-hand side of (26.22). On the band with \(a = 1{,}5\) mm and \(v = 40\) m/s at time \(t = 0\) the slopes are \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(0) = 4{,}712\cdot 10^{-3}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(L) = -2{,}096\cdot 10^{-3}\). The power of the tension forces is \(T v\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L = -3{,}206\) W, the energy carried out minus carried in \(v\,\tfrac12(T + \mu v^2)\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L = -1{,}803\) W, the difference \(-1{,}403\) W, and \(\tfrac{v}{2}(T - \mu v^2)\,[w_{\mathrm{x}}^2]_0^L = -1{,}403\) W, and the numerical derivative \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{r}}'\) from a central difference \(-1{,}403\) W. At \(t = 2{,}523\) ms we have \(-1{,}592 - (-0{,}896) = -0{,}697\) W and the right-hand side \(-0{,}697\) W. At \(v = 0{,}9c\) at \(t = 0\) we have \(-0{,}972 - (-0{,}880) = -0{,}092\) W, and the right-hand side and the derivative are equal to it. So the energy of the span changes although there is no damping: material runs through the eyelets and the flow of energy is not zero, because the squares of the slopes at the ends differ: the flow would vanish only for \(w_{\mathrm{x}}(0)^2 = w_{\mathrm{x}}(L)^2\), which does not hold for the band in general. CHEN2005 (PDF p. 6) says the same: the moving string is nonconservative in this sense, although the equation has no dissipative term, and Hamilton's principle holds because the forces are potential.

What does this section show and what returns? The critical speed \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c\) is not an ansatz but the point where we have infinitely many resting shapes, where the conserved quantity loses positive definiteness and where all frequencies vanish (lemma 26.19, theorem 26.21, corollary 26.22, theorem 26.13). Below it the motion is bounded in energy. The energy of the span is not conserved (lemma 26.23), because material carries energy at the eyelets and because the tension force does work on the moving material. The mixed part \(T_1\) of (26.18) is not zero, yet it is absent from the constant functional: the force \(-2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) it brings does no work over the span, as the Coriolis force in a rotating frame. Its name, the matrix that writes it and the eigenvalues of the discrete system we shall meet in section 26.5. Above \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) we claim nothing, nor whether the motion dies out in time, because the model has no damping (chapter 20).

26.5 Gyroscopic systems

We found the exact modes of the moving string in section 26.3 with an ansatz containing a phase factor. For a belt with bending stiffness (section 26.7), with finite elements (section 26.8) and in rotating machines (chapter 24) there is no such closed formula, but we do have finitely many coordinates. So in this section we look at what system of ordinary equations we get from the moving string if we describe it with finitely many sines, and at what we can prove about such a system. First we put the sines into the equation and obtain three matrices. One of them is skew-symmetric and is called gyroscopic (žiroskopska). Then we show that gyroscopic forces do no work, that for a positive definite stiffness matrix every eigenvalue is purely imaginary, and, on an example, where this condition fails. We finish with numbers for the band of example A and with the question of why the sines converge poorly at high speed (figures 26.13 to 26.16).

26.5.1 Sines in the equation of the moving string

Take the string of section 26.1: length between the eyelets \(L\), mass per length \(\mu\), tension \(T\), axial speed \(v\), transverse displacement \(w(x, t)\), and the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\) fixed in space (the ends of the rest lines in figure 26.13 below). By theorem 26.4, \(\mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). We move the term \(\mu v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) to the right-hand side and obtain

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - S\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 , \qquad S = T - \mu v^2 . \tag{26.23}\]

The letter \(S\) is in this section only an abbreviation for a force in newtons. Since \(S/\mu = c^2 - v^2\) with \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4), it is positive for \(v < c\). We take only \(v < c\).

We look for the solution in a family we already know. The sines \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}(x) = \sin(j\pi x/L)\) are zero at both eyelets, and by corollary 13.13 there are enough of them to approximate uniformly any smooth shape that is zero at the eyelets, and we take the first \(N\) of them (figure 26.13). We try

\[w(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{N} q_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}(x) , \tag{26.24}\]

where \(q_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\) are unknown functions of time in metres. Since such a sum does not satisfy equation (26.23) exactly, we use the same requirement as the Galerkin method (definition 6.42): the residual of the equation, that is the left-hand side \(r\) of equation (26.23), must at every instant be orthogonal to every function \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(i = 1, \dots, N\), which means \(\int_0^L r\,\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). In the static problem the definition applied this requirement to a bilinear form, here we apply it to the residual of the dynamic equation. By lemma 6.43 it suffices to write it for the \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) alone, because the residual is linear in \(w\).

What will be in the equation we get? Figure 26.13 shows what we shall need. We draw the first four shapes \(\varphi_1\) to \(\varphi_4\), each with its own rest line between the eyelets. In between we draw a dashed midpoint \(L/2\). The shapes with odd \(j\) (blue) are mirror images of themselves about the midpoint, the shapes with even \(j\) (orange) are mirrored about the midpoint and change sign. For our computation what matters is what happens to the derivative: the slope of a mirror-symmetric curve has opposite signs on the two sides of the midpoint, so the derivative of an even function is an odd function and conversely.

Lemma 26.24 Galerkin system of the moving string (Galerkinov sistem gibajoče strune)

Let the string be that of theorem 26.4 with the eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and let \(v < c\). Let \(w\) be as in equation (26.24) with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \sin(j\pi x/L)\). The residual of equation (26.23) is orthogonal to \(\varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_{\mathrm{N}}\) at every instant exactly when

\[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0 , \tag{26.25}\]

where \(\vek q = (q_1, \dots, q_{\mathrm{N}})^\T\) and

\[M_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{\mu L}{2}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad K_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac{S\,j^2\pi^2}{2L}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu v\int_0^L \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \begin{cases} \dfrac{4\mu v\,i\,j}{i^2 - j^2} & i + j \text{ odd} , \\[1ex] 0 & i + j \text{ even} . \end{cases} \tag{26.26}\]
Proof

We must show what each term of the residual becomes after integration with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\).

  1. The residual is \(r = \mu w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} - S\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (equation (26.23)). From equation (26.24), \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \ddot q_{\mathrm{j}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} q_{\mathrm{j}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}''\), since the \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) are differentiable and the sum is finite.
  2. The product of sines is \(\sin a\,\sin b = \tfrac12\big(\cos(a - b) - \cos(a + b)\big)\). For \(a = i\pi x/L\) and \(b = j\pi x/L\) the integral \(\int_0^L\cos(m\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x\) is zero for integer \(m \ne 0\) (the integral of a cosine over whole half-periods). Hence \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{L}{2}\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'' = -(j\pi/L)^2\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) also \(-\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}''\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = (j\pi/L)^2\,\tfrac L2\,\delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\).
  3. For the term with the mixed derivative, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}' = (j\pi/L)\cos(j\pi x/L)\). We use \(\sin a\,\cos b = \tfrac12\big(\sin(a + b) + \sin(a - b)\big)\) and \(\int_0^L\sin(m\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{L}{m\pi}\big(1 - (-1)^m\big)\) for an integer \(m \ne 0\), which is \(2L/(m\pi)\) for odd and zero for even \(m\).
  4. For \(i + j\) even, \(i + j\) and \(i - j\) are both even (or \(i - j = 0\), where \(\sin 0 = 0\)), so \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). For \(i + j\) odd both are odd and \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{j\pi}{L}\cdot\tfrac12\Big(\tfrac{2L}{(i + j)\pi} + \tfrac{2L}{(i - j)\pi}\Big) = j\Big(\tfrac{1}{i + j} + \tfrac{1}{i - j}\Big) = \dfrac{2ij}{i^2 - j^2}\).
  5. Row \(i\) of the condition \(\int_0^L r\,\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) is, by steps 2 to 4, equal to \(\mu\tfrac L2\,\ddot q_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} G_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\dot q_{\mathrm{j}} + S\,i^2\pi^2/(2L)\,q_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\). This is equation (26.25). The converse holds because the steps are equalities.

Source: The procedure is ours: the sines after section 13.2, the residual requirement after definition 6.42. WM1990 (PDF p. 6) mentions the choice of the eigenfunctions of the string at rest as expansion functions for moving systems. The numbers in equation (26.26) are checked by quadrature in num-05.py.

The reason \(\mat G\) has entries only for \(i + j\) odd is seen in figure 26.13. The integrand \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\,\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\) is the product of the shape \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and the slope \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\). The slope has the opposite symmetry to the shape \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\). If \(i\) and \(j\) have the same parity, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\) therefore have opposite symmetries, the product is odd about the midpoint, and the integral over a region symmetric about the midpoint is zero, since the area left of the midpoint is subtracted from the area on the right. If they have different parities, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\) have the same symmetry, the product is even and the areas do not subtract, which step 4 of the proof confirms. So the first shape does not couple to itself but couples to the second. Physically: motion in the first shape produces, through the term \(2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\), a force in the second shape, because the slope of the first shape (the derivative of an even shape is odd) has the same symmetry as the second shape.

Figure 26.14 shows all the values for \(N = 4\). We draw the frame of the matrix with row \(i\) and column \(j\) and write in the values \(4ij/(i^2 - j^2)\) from equation (26.26). The cells with zeros are where \(i + j\) is even, so a checkerboard. On the diagonal are only zeros, because \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,[\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^2]_0^L = 0\) (the eyelet is fixed). Every element below the diagonal is the negative of its mirror element above it: \(G_{21} = +2{,}67\,\mu v\) and \(G_{12} = -2{,}67\,\mu v\). This is no accident, since integration by parts with \(\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}(0) = \varphi_{\mathrm{i}}(L) = 0\) gives \(\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = -\int_0^L\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}'\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and swapping \(i\) and \(j\) changes the sign. It is exactly this property of the matrix that carries the rest of the section.

26.5.2 The gyroscopic matrix and the gyroscopic system

System (26.25) has the same structure as the system of GR (example 1.8, PDF p. 54 to 56), where a mass on springs in a wheel turning with constant angular velocity is described in the coordinates of the wheel. GR writes there that the equation of motion acquires a term \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\), that this term belongs to the Coriolis or gyroscopic forces, and that these are apparent forces, because they arise only from the description in a moving frame (GR PDF p. 47 and 56, remark 1.1). The name gyroscopic comes from the gyroscope, a device with a spinning wheel (Greek gyros, circle), since such forces show up precisely in spinning bodies. Why GR uses it is not written, so this is the name in use and not our conclusion. In our string nothing spins. The term \(2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is the one that section 26.1 calls Coriolis, because in the acceleration of a particle it arises from the simultaneous motion along the string with speed \(v\) and the changing slope. In the coordinates \(q_{\mathrm{j}}\) it has the same property as for the wheel: it is linear in the velocities \(\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}\) and has skew-symmetric coefficients. So we keep the same name for the matrix that is skew-symmetric, as figure 26.14 shows.

Definition 26.25 Gyroscopic matrix and gyroscopic system (žiroskopska matrika in žiroskopski sistem)

Let \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) be real symmetric \(n \times n\) matrices with \(\mat M\) positive definite (definition 6.27). A real \(n \times n\) matrix \(\mat G\) is gyroscopic (skew-symmetric, poševno simetrična) if \(\mat G^\T = -\mat G\), that is \(G_{\mathrm{ji}} = -G_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\). The system of ordinary differential equations for \(\vek q : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^n\),

\[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0 , \tag{26.27}\]

is a (linear conservative) gyroscopic system. The matrix \(\mat G\) is called the gyroscopic matrix and the vector \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) the gyroscopic forces.

Source: GR (2.242), PDF p. 137, and (1.39), (1.40), PDF p. 47, where the coefficients of the gyroscopic forces are skew-symmetric. The matrix \(\mat G\) has nothing to do with the shear modulus \(G\) (a scalar), which it does not meet.

By lemma 26.24 the Galerkin system of the moving string is a gyroscopic system: \(\mat M\) is a positive definite matrix with the number \(\mu L/2\) on the diagonal, \(\mat K\) is positive definite because \(S > 0\) for \(v < c\), and \(\mat G\) is skew-symmetric by figure 26.14.

Lemma 26.26 Gyroscopic forces do no work (žiroskopske sile ne opravijo dela)

Let \(\vek q(t)\) be a twice continuously differentiable solution of the gyroscopic system (26.27). Then the power of the gyroscopic forces \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) is zero at every instant and the quantity

\[E = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\,\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q \tag{26.28}\]

is constant.

Proof

We must show that the scalar \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x\) is zero and that the derivative of \(E\) is zero.

  1. For every column \(\vek x\), \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x\) is a number, hence equal to its transpose: \(\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x = (\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x)^\T = \vek x^\T\mat G^\T\vek x = -\,\vek x^\T\mat G\,\vek x\). A number equal to its own negative is zero. For \(\vek x = \dot{\vek q}\) the first claim follows.
  2. Because \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric, \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat K\,\vek q = \dot{\vek q}^\T(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q)\).
  3. By equation (26.27), \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = -\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\), so \(\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}t = -\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek q} = 0\) by step 1.

Source: GR (2.243), PDF p. 137: gyroscopic forces neither add nor remove energy, they only transfer it between coordinates. The proof follows GR.

What is \(E\) for our string? From step 2 of the proof of lemma 26.24, \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac L2\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\dot q_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) and \(\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac L2\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (j\pi/L)^2 q_{\mathrm{j}}^2\), so \(E = \tfrac12\int_0^L\big(\mu w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + S\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\). This is the functional of theorem 26.21, and lemma 26.26 says that it is conserved already in the Galerkin system (checked on a random state with five sines and the band of example A, both sides equal to six places). It is also the energy integral \(\mathcal{E}^* = T_2 - T_0 + V\) of theorem 8.109. The kinetic energy of the transverse motion of the string is \(\tfrac12\mu\int_0^L (w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) (the velocity of a particle from lemma 26.1, the axial part \(\tfrac12\mu v^2 L\) is constant and does not enter the equations), so by theorem 8.86 it splits into \(T_2 = \tfrac12\mu\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), \(T_1 = \mu v\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(T_0 = \tfrac12\mu v^2\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), the potential energy is \(V = \tfrac12 T\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(T_2 - T_0 + V = E\). The term \(T_1\) is linear in the velocities. From the definition of \(G_{\mathrm{ij}}\), \(T_1 = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat G\,\vek q\), and in Lagrange's equations \(\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\tfrac{\partial T_1}{\partial\dot{\vek q}} - \tfrac{\partial T_1}{\partial\vek q} = \tfrac12\mat G\,\dot{\vek q} - \tfrac12\mat G^\T\dot{\vek q} = \mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\). The gyroscopic force is thus the part of the equations that \(T_1\) brings (GR (1.39), (1.40), PDF p. 47), and it does not change the energy by itself, as the skew-symmetry of the matrix in figure 26.14 shows.

26.5.3 Eigenvalues of a gyroscopic system

The trial \(\vek q = \vek x\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\) solves equation (26.27), because the derivative of a complex exponential is a product with \(\lambda\) (theorem 9.29), if \((\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\,\vek x = \vek 0\) with \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) from \(\mathbb{C}^n\). For \(\mat G = \mat 0\), \(\mat K\,\vek x = -\lambda^2\mat M\,\vek x\), so by lemma 10.18 \(-\lambda^2\) is real and, for positive definite \(\mat K\), positive, and \(\lambda\) is purely imaginary. Does it stay so when \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\)? The answer depends on the stiffness matrix, as figure 26.15 shows.

Theorem 26.27 Eigenvalues of a gyroscopic system (lastne vrednosti žiroskopskega sistema)

Let \((\mat M, \mat G, \mat K)\) be a gyroscopic system (definition 26.25) and let \(\lambda \in \mathbb{C}\) with \(\vek x \in \mathbb{C}^n \setminus \{\vek 0\}\) solve \((\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\,\vek x = \vek 0\). Denote \(m = \bar{\vek x}^\T\mat M\,\vek x\), \(k = \bar{\vek x}^\T\mat K\,\vek x\) and \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x = \mathrm{i}g\). Then \(m > 0\), \(k\) and \(g\) are real numbers, and

  1. \(\lambda\) is purely imaginary exactly when \(g^2 + 4mk \ge 0\). Then \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) with \(\omega = \big(-g \pm \sqrt{g^2 + 4mk}\big)/(2m)\).
  2. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, \(k > 0\), and so every eigenvalue is purely imaginary and different from zero. The system then has no solution that grows exponentially.
  3. If \(g^2 + 4mk < 0\), \(\lambda\) has a nonzero real part and the system is not stable (it has a solution that grows exponentially).
Proof

We must show that the equation with the eigenvector reduces to a quadratic equation for \(\lambda\) with real coefficients.

  1. Write \(\vek x = \vek a + \mathrm{i}\vek b\) with real columns. For a real symmetric matrix \(\mat A\), \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat A\,\vek x = \vek a^\T\mat A\,\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat A\,\vek b + \mathrm{i}\,(\vek a^\T\mat A\,\vek b - \vek b^\T\mat A\,\vek a)\) and the remainder is zero, because \(\vek b^\T\mat A\,\vek a = \vek a^\T\mat A\,\vek b\) (as in the proof of lemma 10.18). Hence \(m\) and \(k\) are real, and \(m > 0\), because \(\mat M\) is positive definite and \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\).
  2. For \(\mat G\), \(\overline{(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x)} = \vek x^\T\mat G\,\bar{\vek x}\), which is a number equal to its transpose \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G^\T\vek x = -\,\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x\). A number equal to the negative of its conjugate is purely imaginary: \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x = \mathrm{i}g\) with real \(g\).
  3. We multiply the equation \((\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\,\vek x = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\): \(m\lambda^2 + \mathrm{i}g\,\lambda + k = 0\). The solutions are \(\lambda = \big(-\mathrm{i}g \pm \sqrt{-(g^2 + 4mk)}\big)/(2m)\).
  4. For \(g^2 + 4mk \ge 0\) the root is \(\mathrm{i}\sqrt{g^2 + 4mk}\), so \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\,\big(-g \pm \sqrt{g^2 + 4mk}\big)/(2m)\) is purely imaginary. For \(g^2 + 4mk < 0\) the root is real and nonzero, so \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = \pm\sqrt{|g^2 + 4mk|}/(2m) \ne 0\). This is point 1.
  5. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, \(k = \vek a^\T\mat K\,\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat K\,\vek b > 0\) by step 1, so \(g^2 + 4mk > 0\) and by step 4 \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\). The product of the solutions \(\omega\) is \(-k/m < 0\), so \(\omega\) and the other root have different signs and \(\omega \ne 0\). No solution grows either: by lemma 26.26, \(\tfrac12\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q \le E(0)\) for every \(t\), and since \(\vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u \ge \kappa\,\vek u^\T\vek u\) with \(\kappa > 0\), the smallest value of \(\vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u\) at \(\vek u^\T\vek u = 1\) (it exists by the extreme value theorem), we get \(\vek q^\T\vek q \le 2E(0)/\kappa\). This is point 2.
  6. The determinant \(\Delta(\lambda) = \det(\lambda^2\mat M + \lambda\mat G + \mat K)\) equals the determinant of the transposed matrix, \(\det(\lambda^2\mat M - \lambda\mat G + \mat K) = \Delta(-\lambda)\), because \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric and \(\mat G^\T = -\mat G\) (GR (2.246), PDF p. 138). If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue, so is \(-\lambda\). For \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \ne 0\) one of the values \(\lambda\), \(-\lambda\) therefore has \(a = \mathrm{Re} > 0\) and an eigenvector \(\vek y \ne \vek 0\). The real part \(\vek q(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\vek y\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\big)\) is a solution, because the system is real. It is not zero: for \(\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda = 0\), \(\vek q = \mathrm{e}^{at}\,\mathrm{Re}\,\vek y\) and we may take \(\vek y\) real (the kernel of a real matrix is closed under real and imaginary parts), and for \(\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda = \beta \ne 0\), at \(\beta t = 0\) and \(\beta t = \pi/2\) the values of \(\mathrm{e}^{-at}\vek q\) are \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek y\) and \(-\mathrm{Im}\,\vek y\), at least one of which is nonzero. The solution grows as \(\mathrm{e}^{at}\). This is point 3.

Source: GR (2.244) to (2.247), PDF p. 137 to 138: the eigenvalues are real pairs or purely imaginary pairs, and a real eigenvalue is possible only if the effective stiffness matrix is not positive definite. The notation with \(m\), \(g\), \(k\) and the condition \(g^2 + 4mk \ge 0\) is ours.

How many eigenvalues does the system have for positive definite \(\mat K\)? The polynomial \(\Delta(\lambda)\) has degree \(2n\), because \(\mat M\) is positive definite, so there are \(2n\) eigenvalues (with multiplicity), all \(\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\). The eigenvalues \(\pm\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) lie on the imaginary axis of figure 26.15. The eigenvector for \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the conjugate of the eigenvector for \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), because the system is real. For \(\mat G = \mat 0\) the eigenvector can be real. For \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\) it is in general complex, as in the stabilization example below with \(\vek x = (1, \pm\mathrm{i})^\T\). This is the mathematical form of what we saw in the moving string as the phase factor \(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}kx}\) in theorem 26.13: the shapes are no longer standing, the waves travel. We prove the orthogonality of these modes in section 26.6.

As a special case take \(N = 1\). Then \(\mat G = (0)\), because \(G_{11} = 0\), and \(\omega_1^2 = K_{11}/M_{11} = S\,\pi^2/(\mu L^2)\), so \(\omega_1 = (\pi/L)\sqrt{c^2 - v^2}\). For the band of example A (0,9 × 50 mm, \(L = 1\) m, tension 100 MPa, steel \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³, \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, the dimensions and speed are our choice) at \(v = 40\) m/s this is \(f_1 = 52{,}963\) Hz, while the exact value from theorem 26.13 is \(49{,}548\) Hz: the approximation is \(6{,}89\,\%\) too high. What is missing? A single shape cannot represent the coupling between the shapes \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) that \(G_{12} \ne 0\) brings. Take \(N = 2, 4, 8\): \(f_1 = 49{,}783\) (\(+0{,}47\,\%\)), \(49{,}584\) (\(+0{,}07\,\%\)) and \(49{,}554\) Hz (\(+0{,}01\,\%\)). For \(N = 2\), \(f_2 = 112{,}695\) Hz against the exact \(99{,}097\) Hz. The error decreases at our \(v/c = 0{,}353\), but not uniformly over the frequencies: the second frequency needs more shapes than the first (figure 26.16).

26.5.4 Gyroscopic stabilization

Theorem 26.27 requires a positive definite \(\mat K\). What if it is not? For \(\mat G = \mat 0\), theorem 8.119 says that the equilibrium is unstable if there is a \(\vek u\) with \(\vek u^\T\mat K\,\vek u < 0\). Does the same hold when \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\)? Let us look first at the example from GR, then at an example that we can compute to the end by hand and that is drawn in figure 26.15.

Example 26.28 Inertia wheel: stability when positive definiteness is lost (kolo z maso: stabilnost ob izgubi pozitivne definitnosti)

GR (example 2.9, PDF p. 139 to 141) takes a mass \(m = 1\) on springs of stiffness \(k_1 = 50\) and \(k_2 = 98\) in a wheel turning with constant angular velocity \(\Omega\) (the numbers are GR's). The matrices are \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat G = 2m\Omega\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mat K^* = \mathrm{diag}(k_1 - \Omega^2 m,\ k_2 - \Omega^2 m)\) (GR PDF p. 140). The matrix \(\mat K^*\) is positive definite for \(\Omega < \omega_1 = \sqrt{50} = 7{,}0711\). The eigenvalues for three speeds (computed in num-05.py):

\(\Omega\) \(\mat K^*\) \(\det\mat K^*\) eigenvalues \(\lambda\)
\(5\) \(\mathrm{diag}(25, 73)\) \(1825\) \(\pm 3{,}1131\,\mathrm{i}\), \(\pm 13{,}7226\,\mathrm{i}\)
\(8\) \(\mathrm{diag}(-14, 34)\) \(-476\) \(\pm 1{,}3092\), \(\pm 16{,}6648\,\mathrm{i}\)
\(12\) \(\mathrm{diag}(-94, -46)\) \(4324\) \(\pm 3{,}1865\,\mathrm{i}\), \(\pm 20{,}636\,\mathrm{i}\)

For \(\Omega = 5\) theorem 26.27 applies, everything is purely imaginary. For \(\Omega = 8\), \(\mat K^*\) has one negative eigenvalue, \(\det\mat K^* < 0\), and we get the real pair \(\pm 1{,}3092\), so instability, as theorem 26.27 (point 3) allows. For \(\Omega = 12\) both eigenvalues of \(\mat K^*\) are negative, \(\mat K^*\) is negative definite and \(\det\mat K^* > 0\), yet all eigenvalues are again purely imaginary: the system is stable although \(\mat K^*\) is not positive definite. GR PDF p. 141 ascribes this precisely to the gyroscopic forces.

Theorem 8.119 assumes \(\mat G = \mat 0\), and the example shows that the conclusion fails for \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\). The next example shows the mechanism in its simplest form, with one number \(g\) (figure 26.15).

We take a dimensionless system with two coordinates, unit mass \(\mat M = \mat I\), negative definite stiffness matrix \(\mat K = -\mat I\) and \(\mat G = g\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) with a number \(g > 0\). Without the gyroscopic term (\(g = 0\)), \(\lambda^2 = 1\) and \(\lambda = \pm 1\) twice: the system is unstable, as theorem 8.119 says. In the figure the axes show the real and imaginary parts of \(\lambda\). At \(g = 0\) the eigenvalues are on the real axis at \(\pm 1\). The characteristic equation is

\[\det\begin{pmatrix}\lambda^2 - 1 & g\lambda\\ -g\lambda & \lambda^2 - 1\end{pmatrix} = (\lambda^2 - 1)^2 + g^2\lambda^2 = \lambda^4 + (g^2 - 2)\,\lambda^2 + 1 = 0 . \tag{26.29}\]

For \(\nu = \lambda^2\), \(\nu^2 + (g^2 - 2)\nu + 1 = 0\) with discriminant \((g^2 - 2)^2 - 4 = g^2(g^2 - 4)\).

  • For \(g < 2\) the discriminant is negative, \(\nu\) is not real and so \(\lambda\) is neither real nor purely imaginary. Since the product of the roots \(\nu\) is \(1\), \(|\nu| = 1\) and \(|\lambda| = 1\): the eigenvalues lie on a circle of radius \(1\). At \(g = 1\), \(\lambda = \pm 0{,}866 \pm 0{,}5\,\mathrm{i}\) (num-05.py), so \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = 0{,}866 > 0\) and the solution grows as \(\mathrm{e}^{0{,}866\,t}\) (theorem 26.27, point 3).
  • At \(g = 2\) the discriminant is zero, \(\nu = -1\) doubly and \(\lambda = \pm\mathrm{i}\) doubly: the eigenvalues arrive at the imaginary axis.
  • For \(g > 2\) the discriminant is positive, the sum of the roots is \(-(g^2 - 2) < 0\) and the product \(1 > 0\), so both \(\nu\) are real and negative, hence all four eigenvalues are purely imaginary. At \(g = 3\), \(\nu^2 + 7\nu + 1 = 0\), \(\nu = (-7 \pm \sqrt{45})/2 = -0{,}1459\) and \(-6{,}854\), \(\lambda = \pm 0{,}382\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(\pm 2{,}618\,\mathrm{i}\). Computing the eigenvalues of the state matrix gives the same.

The matrix \(\mat K = -\mat I\) is negative definite, yet at \(g \ge 2\) the system stays bounded: this is gyroscopic stabilization (žiroskopska stabilizacija). The reason is in the condition of theorem 26.27: for the eigenvector \(\vek x = (1, \pm\mathrm{i})^\T/\sqrt2\), \(m = 1\), \(k = -1\) and \(\bar{\vek x}^\T\mat G\,\vek x = \pm\mathrm{i}g\), so \(g^2 + 4mk = g^2 - 4\), which is nonnegative exactly for \(g \ge 2\) (the labels \(m\), \(k\), \(g\) are those of the theorem). The gyroscopic term must be large enough that the discriminant of the quadratic equation from step 3 of the proof is not negative. Positive definiteness is therefore a sufficient, but not a necessary condition for purely imaginary eigenvalues. We shall meet the same structure in the moving beam: in section 26.7, for \(T L^2/EI = 100\) the system is stable between \(v = 11{,}811\) and \(v = 12{,}177\) (dimensionless), although \(\mat K\) is not positive definite there.

26.5.5 Convergence of the Galerkin frequencies

How well does the Galerkin system predict the frequencies of the moving string, where we know the exact value? Take \(L = c = \mu = 1\) (dimensionless) and the ratios \(v/c = 0{,}5\) and \(0{,}9\). The exact frequencies are \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = n\pi\,(1 - v^2/c^2)\) (theorem 26.13): \(\omega_1 = 2{,}35619\) and \(\omega_2 = 4{,}71239\) at \(0{,}5\), \(\omega_1 = 0{,}59690\) and \(\omega_2 = 1{,}19381\) at \(0{,}9\). We write system (26.25) as a first-order system of dimension \(2N\) with the state vector \((\vek q, \dot{\vek q})\) (GR §2.11.3, PDF p. 139) and the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}\mat 0 & \mat I\\ -\mat M^{-1}\mat K & -\mat M^{-1}\mat G\end{pmatrix}\), whose eigenvalues are \(\lambda\), and solve it with \(N = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\) sines. The largest absolute real part of the eigenvalues is everywhere below \(4 \cdot 10^{-15}\), as theorem 26.27 demands. The relative errors \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) of the first and second frequency are shown in figure 26.16.

We draw the axes: the number of sines \(N\) from \(2\) to \(32\) and the error \(\varepsilon\) from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{1}\), both logarithmic, so that the powers have the same length. First the blue curve: at \(v/c = 0{,}5\), \(\varepsilon_1 = 1{,}37 \cdot 10^{-2}\) at \(N = 2\) and \(3{,}95 \cdot 10^{-6}\) at \(N = 32\), \(\varepsilon_2 = 0{,}315\) at \(N = 2\) and \(1{,}51 \cdot 10^{-5}\) at \(N = 32\). Then the orange curve at \(v/c = 0{,}9\): \(\varepsilon_1 = 0{,}111\) and \(1{,}34 \cdot 10^{-5}\), \(\varepsilon_2 = 3{,}74\) (frequency \(5{,}65\) against the exact \(1{,}19\)) and \(5{,}38 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The labels say which colour is which speed. At both speeds the error decreases about eightfold with every doubling of \(N\) (for example \(\varepsilon_1\) at \(0{,}5\): \(1{,}73 \cdot 10^{-3} \to 2{,}31 \cdot 10^{-4} \to 3{,}06 \cdot 10^{-5} \to 3{,}95 \cdot 10^{-6}\)), but at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) more shapes are needed to get onto this path: \(\varepsilon_2\) at \(N = 4\) is \(0{,}120\) at \(0{,}9\) and \(6 \cdot 10^{-3}\) at \(0{,}5\). All computed errors are positive, so the approximations are above the exact values. This is an observation on the computed cases, not a proof: Ritz's upper-bound theorem (theorem 10.42) requires \(\mat G = \mat 0\), and for gyroscopic systems we do not prove an upper bound.

Why so poor at \(v/c = 0{,}9\)? Take the shape of mode \(n = 1\) from theorem 26.13, that is \(\psi_1(x) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_1x}\sin(\pi x/L)\) with \(k_1 = \pi v/(cL)\) (the theorem calls it \(\varphi\), here it is \(\psi_1\), since \(\varphi_1\) is the first sine in this section). Its real and imaginary parts are the shapes of the string at two instants, a quarter of a period apart, figure 26.17. The string moves as \(w = \mathrm{Re}(\psi_1\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega_1 t})\), so at \(t = 0\) the shape is \(\mathrm{Re}\,\psi_1\), and a quarter of a period earlier, at \(\omega_1 t = -\pi/2\), it is \(\mathrm{Re}(-\mathrm{i}\,\psi_1) = \mathrm{Im}\,\psi_1\).

We draw the rest line between the eyelets, a distance \(L\) apart, and above it the shape at rest \(\sin(\pi x/L)\), which is the first sine. Over it we lay the real part of the mode: the factor \(\cos(0{,}9\,\pi x/L)\) falls at \(x = 0{,}5\,L\) to \(0{,}156\) (at \(v/c = 0{,}5\) it would be \(0{,}707\)), so at this instant the middle of the string is nearly on the rest line and the crest moves towards the left eyelet. Next we draw the imaginary part, which is the shape of the string a quarter of a period earlier and has its crest towards the right eyelet. Since neither of these shapes resembles a single sine, the first sine \(\sin(\pi x/L)\) captures only the fraction \(0{,}083\) of the squared norm of the real part and \(0{,}968\) of the imaginary part (the squared norm over \(x \in [0, L]\)), and at \(v/c = 0{,}5\) it captures \(0{,}922\) of both. The first two sines together capture at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) \(0{,}998\) of the real and \(0{,}975\) of the imaginary part (recomputed in num-05.py), so the real part lies almost wholly in the second sine. So the first mode at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) needs at least two sines, and the higher modes more. WM1990 (PDF p. 6) writes the same: at high transport speed the eigenfunctions of the string at rest, which it calls solutions with constant phase, are a poor approximation of the motion and many of them are needed for a sufficiently accurate computation. For the string we avoid this because the complex modes are known (section 26.3). For systems that have no closed formula, for example finite elements (section 26.8), we must take enough shapes, and we use the eigenfunctions of the moving string for orthogonality in section 26.6.

Let us summarize what we showed and how. With the sines and the residual requirement (lemma 26.24) we reduced the moving string to the system \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) with a matrix \(\mat G\) that is skew-symmetric because of the fixed eyelets, and, because of the parity of the shapes (figure 26.13), nonzero only for \(i + j\) odd. From the skew-symmetry we derived that gyroscopic forces do no work (lemma 26.26) and that for positive definite \(\mat K\) all eigenvalues are purely imaginary (theorem 26.27). Positive definiteness is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one: example 26.28 has a negative definite \(\mat K\) and a stable system. For our string \(\mat K\) is positive definite exactly when \(S = T - \mu v^2 > 0\), that is for \(v < c\) (section 26.4). In the computed cases the frequencies lie above the exact ones and converge, more slowly at high speed, because the sines are not adapted to the travelling waves.

26.6 Orthogonality and expansion in modes

In section 26.3 we found the exact modes (načini) of the moving string, the complex functions \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}k_{\mathrm{n}} x}\sin(n\pi x/L)\) with frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (theorem 26.13). For the string at rest we expanded the initial shape and the initial velocity in modes (theorem 13.11), and the coefficients came from the orthogonality of the modes (theorem 13.43). The question is whether the same holds for a string that runs through its two eyelets with speed \(v\). The answer has two parts. Ordinary orthogonality in the mass fails, but orthogonality survives in another product, which has to be found first. This section finds it, proves the orthogonality and derives the coefficients of the expansion from it.

From history

Methods for axially moving materials date to the nineteenth century, and the eigenfunctions of the moving string and beam had been calculated before. Wickert and Mote (1990) state that orthogonality relations among the eigenfunctions had not been derived until then (WM1990, PDF p. 1). The generalized coordinates in an expansion in eigenfunctions therefore remained coupled, and the classical modal analysis and the Green's function method, which had been applied to the stationary string and beam, were not applicable to axially moving materials. The response was known only for special excitations, for example a constant transverse point force (Chonan, 1986) or harmonic motion of a support (Miranker, 1960) (WM1990, PDF p. 1). For discrete systems Meirovitch (1974, 1975) had studied the matrix eigenvalue problem of gyroscopic systems and derived a corresponding modal analysis, in which a transformation of the generalized coordinates and momenta decouples the equations (WM1990, PDF p. 2). Wickert and Mote wrote the equations of the moving string and beam in first-order form with one symmetric and one skew-symmetric differential operator and showed that the eigenfunctions are orthogonal with respect to both (WM1990, PDF p. 1 and 2).

The moving string that we last looked at in section 26.3 therefore has exact modes, but we have not been able to compute the coefficients of an expansion in them. The story showed two things: the difficulty is not in the eigenfunctions but in the product with respect to which they are orthogonal, and the way to that product is to write the equation in first-order form. We do it here on the string we already know, and prove everything with lemma 6.13.

26.6.1 State and first-order form

The string equation of theorem 26.4 is of second order in time, so the shape \(w(\cdot, t)\) alone does not suffice to continue the motion from time \(t\). Newton's second law connects the force with the acceleration, that is with the second derivative in time, so the motion is determined only when the displacement and the velocity of all particles at one time are known, as for the pendulum with one degree of freedom (chapter 9). Whoever sees only the shape of the string does not know whether a particle is on its way up or down. The displacement and the velocity together we call the state (stanje), because all later motion follows from them, as for the damped systems of section 20.8. We draw it on the string of mode 1 from the example of section 26.3. We choose units so that \(L = \mu = T = 1\), hence \(c = 1\), and take \(v = 1/2\) (the ratio \(v/c\) as in section 26.3). Then \(\omega_1 = \pi\,(1 - v^2/c^2) = 2{,}356\).

We build figure 26.18 as one draws it on the board. First we draw the axis \(x\) along which the string is stretched, and on it the two eyelets at \(0\) and \(L\), which are fixed in space (the idealization of section 26.1). Then we draw the shape \(w\) that the string has in mode 1 at time \(t = 0\), that is \(w(x, 0) = \mathrm{Re}\,\varphi_1(x) = \sin(\pi x)\cos(\pi x/2)\). Last, at four particles we add the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\): the particle at \(x\) has at this time the velocity \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = \mathrm{Re}\,(\mathrm{i}\omega_1\varphi_1) = -\omega_1\,\mathrm{Im}\,\varphi_1(x)\). At \(x = 0{,}6\) this gives \(w = 0{,}559\) and \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = -2{,}356\cdot 0{,}769 = -1{,}813\). The velocity is not in the outline of the string, so we write the state as a pair of functions.

We use the pair \((w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\) for a second purpose: we write the string equation as a pair of first-order equations, because this separates a symmetric part from a skew-symmetric one, which we did not need for the string at rest. The equation is (section 26.1)

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + \mathcal G\,w_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal K\,w = 0 , \qquad \mathcal G f = 2\mu v\,f' , \qquad \mathcal K f = -\kappa\,f'' , \qquad \kappa = T - \mu v^2 = \mu\,(c^2 - v^2) , \tag{26.30}\]

since \(\mu(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The operator \(\mathcal G\) comes from the Coriolis term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) (named in section 26.1), the operator \(\mathcal K\) from the tension reduced by the centripetal term \(\mu v^2\). For \(v < c\) we have \(\kappa > 0\). We need this condition in lemma 26.30. In this section the letters \(\mathcal G\) and \(\mathcal K\) mean operators, not the matrices of section 26.5 (the matrices \(\mat G\) and \(\mat K\) arise from them by the Galerkin method).

Definition 26.29 State and first-order form (stanje in oblika prvega reda)

Let a moving string with \(v < c\) and eyelets fixed in space (section 26.1) have mass per length \(\mu\) and tension \(T\) on \([0, L]\). The state space \(S\) is the set of pairs \(\vek z = (p, w)\) of complex functions \(p, w\colon [0, L] \to \mathbb C\) that are twice continuously differentiable and have \(p(0) = p(L) = w(0) = w(L) = 0\). The state product (produkt stanj) of two states is the complex number

\[\langle \vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = \int_0^L \big(p_1\,\bar p_2 + w_1\,\bar w_2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{26.31}\]

where the bar means the complex conjugate. The operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) act on a state \(\vek z = (p, w)\) as

\[\mathcal A\,\vek z = \begin{pmatrix} \mu\,p \\ \mathcal K\,w \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mathcal B\,\vek z = \begin{pmatrix} \mathcal G\,p + \mathcal K\,w \\ -\mathcal K\,p \end{pmatrix} , \tag{26.32}\]

with \(\mathcal G\) and \(\mathcal K\) from equation (26.30). The state of the moving string at time \(t\) is \(\vek z(t) = (w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\).

Source: WM1990 (8a), (8c), (11) (PDF p. 2). The notation with \(\mu\), \(\kappa\) and dimensions is ours, in WM1990 the quantities are dimensionless (\(\mathcal M = I\)).

The conjugation in the product is needed so that \(\langle \vek z, \vek z\rangle = \int (|p|^2 + |w|^2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) is real and nonnegative also for the complex states that we shall obtain as eigenstates. The function \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) is zero at both eyelets at every time, because \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\) for all \(t\), so \((w_{\mathrm{t}}, w) \in S\) if \(w\) is smooth enough. That equation (26.30) is equivalent to the first-order form is shown by the following computation: for \(\vek z = (w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\) we have \(\mathcal A\,\vek z_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal B\,\vek z = (\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + \mathcal G\,w_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal K\,w,\ \mathcal K\,w_{\mathrm{t}} - \mathcal K\,w_{\mathrm{t}})\). The second component is zero without any assumption, the first is the left side of equation (26.30). The string therefore moves by equation (26.30) exactly when

\[\mathcal A\,\vek z_{\mathrm{t}} + \mathcal B\,\vek z = \vek 0 . \tag{26.33}\]

The second row is there so that the operators get the properties that follow: without it the first row would be equation (26.30), but the operators would be neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric.

What should symmetry and skew symmetry mean for an operator? For a matrix, \(\mat A^{\mathsf T} = \mat A\) means \(\vek u^{\mathsf T}\mat A\,\vek v = \vek v^{\mathsf T}\mat A\,\vek u\), that is the product does not depend on the order (chapter 10). We ask the same of an operator with respect to the state product (26.31), and for skew symmetry the swap of order changes the sign, as for the matrix \(\mat B^{\mathsf T} = -\mat B\).

Lemma 26.30 Symmetry of \(\mathcal A\) and skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\) (simetrija operatorja \(\mathcal A\) in poševna simetrija operatorja \(\mathcal B\))

Let \(\vek z_1, \vek z_2 \in S\) be states of definition 26.29. Then

\[\langle \mathcal A\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = \langle \vek z_1, \mathcal A\vek z_2\rangle , \qquad \langle \mathcal B\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = -\,\langle \vek z_1, \mathcal B\vek z_2\rangle . \tag{26.34}\]

For every nonzero state \(\vek z = (p, w) \in S\)

\[\langle \mathcal A\vek z, \vek z\rangle = \int_0^L \big(\mu\,|p|^2 + \kappa\,|w'|^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x > 0 , \tag{26.35}\]

and the number \(\langle \mathcal B\vek z, \vek z\rangle\) is purely imaginary.

Idea

The operator \(\mathcal K\) is symmetric by lemma 6.13, like the second derivative in lemma 13.42, and the operator \(\mathcal G\), a first derivative, is skew-symmetric for the same reason: in integration by parts a derivative moves from one function to the other and changes sign. This is also the real reason why the Coriolis force does no work: its power \(\int p\,\mathcal G p\,\mathrm{d}x\) equals \(\mu v\,[p^2]_0^L = 0\) for real \(p\).

Proof

We must show three equalities, each with one transfer of a derivative. We start with \(\mathcal K\) and \(\mathcal G\).

  1. For functions \(f, g\) of \(S\) (twice continuously differentiable, zero at the eyelets) we have \(\int_0^L (\mathcal K f)\,\bar g\,\mathrm{d}x = \kappa\int_0^L f'\,\bar g'\,\mathrm{d}x\). By lemma 6.13, \(-\kappa\int f''\,\bar g = -\kappa\,[f'\,\bar g]_0^L + \kappa\int f'\,\bar g'\), and the boundary term is zero because \(\bar g(0) = \bar g(L) = 0\). The right side is symmetric in \(f\) and \(g\) up to conjugation, because \(\kappa\) is real: \(\int (\mathcal K f)\,\bar g = \int f\,\overline{\mathcal K g}\).
  2. For \(\mathcal G\) the same: \(\int (\mathcal G f)\,\bar g = 2\mu v\int f'\,\bar g = 2\mu v\,[f\,\bar g]_0^L - 2\mu v\int f\,\bar g' = -\int f\,\overline{\mathcal G g}\), the boundary term is zero.
  3. Symmetry of \(\mathcal A\). By definition \(\langle\mathcal A\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle = \int \mu\,p_1\,\bar p_2 + \int (\mathcal K w_1)\,\bar w_2\). By step 1 the second term equals \(\int w_1\,\overline{\mathcal K w_2}\), and the first equals \(\int p_1\,\overline{\mu p_2}\). Together this is \(\langle\vek z_1, \mathcal A\vek z_2\rangle\).
  4. Skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\). The sum \(\langle\mathcal B\vek z_1, \vek z_2\rangle + \langle\vek z_1, \mathcal B\vek z_2\rangle\) has four terms with \(\mathcal K\) and two with \(\mathcal G\). By step 2 the two terms with \(\mathcal G\) cancel: \(\int (\mathcal G p_1)\,\bar p_2 + \int p_1\,\overline{\mathcal G p_2} = 0\). The four terms with \(\mathcal K\) are \(\int (\mathcal K w_1)\,\bar p_2 - \int w_1\,\overline{\mathcal K p_2} + \int p_1\,\overline{\mathcal K w_2} - \int (\mathcal K p_1)\,\bar w_2\), and by step 1 the first cancels the second and the third the fourth. The sum is zero.
  5. Positivity. For \(\vek z_1 = \vek z_2 = \vek z\) step 1 gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek z, \vek z\rangle = \mu\int |p|^2 + \kappa\int |w'|^2\), which is equation (26.35). For \(\mu > 0\) and \(\kappa > 0\) (that is \(v < c\)) the sum is nonnegative. If it is zero, then \(p = 0\) and \(w' = 0\), so \(w\) is constant, and because \(w(0) = 0\) we get \(w = 0\), hence \(\vek z = \vek 0\).
  6. By step 4 for \(\vek z_1 = \vek z_2 = \vek z\) we have \(\langle\mathcal B\vek z, \vek z\rangle = -\langle\vek z, \mathcal B\vek z\rangle = -\overline{\langle\mathcal B\vek z, \vek z\rangle}\), since \(\langle\vek a, \vek b\rangle = \overline{\langle\vek b, \vek a\rangle}\). A number equal to minus its own conjugate is purely imaginary.

Source: WM1990 (12) (PDF p. 2): symmetry of \(\mathcal A\) and skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\), positive definiteness of \(\mathcal A\) for \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\) in the Appendix (PDF p. 2 and 7). The proof by integration by parts is ours.

Lemma 26.30 shows what happens at \(v = c\): then \(\kappa = 0\), the product \(\langle\mathcal A\vek z, \vek z\rangle\) is zero for \(\vek z = (0, w)\) with \(w \neq 0\), and \(\mathcal A\) is no longer positive. This is exactly the critical speed of section 26.4 in another dress: with the positivity of \(\mathcal A\) the theorem that follows disappears, and with it everything that follows from it.

Eigenstates are states that change only in size and phase when we write the time part as \(\vek z = \mathrm{Re}\,(\vek\zeta\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t})\). We insert this ansatz in equation (26.33) and obtain (since \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) do not differentiate in time) the eigenvalue problem

\[\lambda\,\mathcal A\,\vek\zeta + \mathcal B\,\vek\zeta = \vek 0 , \qquad \vek\zeta \in S , \ \vek\zeta \neq \vek 0 , \tag{26.36}\]

with eigenvalue \(\lambda \in \mathbb C\). The pair \((\lambda, \vek\zeta)\) we call an eigenpair (lasten par) of the operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\). The connection with the modes of section 26.3 is simple.

Lemma 26.31 Eigenstates and modes of the moving string (lastna stanja in načini gibajoče se strune)

A pair \((\lambda, \vek\zeta)\) with \(\vek\zeta = (q, \varphi)\) is an eigenpair of (26.36) exactly when \(q = \lambda\varphi\) and \(\varphi \neq 0\) solves

\[\lambda^2\mu\,\varphi + \lambda\,\mathcal G\varphi + \mathcal K\varphi = 0 , \qquad \varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0 . \tag{26.37}\]

For \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) this is the equation \(\mu\,(-\omega^2\varphi + 2\mathrm{i}\omega v\,\varphi' + v^2\varphi'') = T\varphi''\), so the pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of the moving string (definition 26.12) and \(\vek\zeta = (\mathrm{i}\omega\varphi, \varphi)\).

Proof

We must show that the second row of equation (26.36) gives \(q = \lambda\varphi\) and the first row equation (26.37).

  1. The second row is \(\lambda\,\mathcal K\varphi - \mathcal K q = 0\), so \(\mathcal K(\lambda\varphi - q) = -\kappa\,(\lambda\varphi - q)'' = 0\). The function \(y = \lambda\varphi - q\) therefore has \(y'' = 0\), that is \(y = a + bx\), and \(y(0) = y(L) = 0\) gives \(y = 0\), which is \(q = \lambda\varphi\).
  2. The first row is \(\lambda\mu\,q + \mathcal G q + \mathcal K\varphi = 0\). With \(q = \lambda\varphi\) this is equation (26.37). Conversely, if \(\varphi\) solves (26.37), both rows are satisfied.
  3. For \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) we insert \(\mathcal G\varphi = 2\mu v\,\varphi'\) and \(\mathcal K\varphi = -(T - \mu v^2)\,\varphi''\): \(-\omega^2\mu\varphi + 2\mathrm{i}\omega\mu v\,\varphi' - (T - \mu v^2)\,\varphi'' = 0\), which is the equation in the statement.

The equation in the statement is the one that the ansatz \(w = \mathrm{Re}\,(\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t})\) solved in theorem 26.13. The eigenpairs with \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) are therefore exactly the states \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = (\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) with the modes \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) of that theorem.

26.6.2 Orthogonality of the complex modes

For the matrices of section 26.5 we did the same computation with \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\) and \(\mat K\) (theorem 26.27): the eigenvalues are purely imaginary because \(\mat G\) is skew and \(\mat K\) is positive definite. Here the same proof runs on operators. Its idea: with the eigenvalue equation (26.36) we rewrite \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\) twice, once from the left argument and once from the right, and the skew symmetry says that the two forms differ by the factor \(\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\).

Theorem 26.32 Orthogonality of the complex modes of the moving string (ortogonalnost kompleksnih načinov gibajoče se strune)

Let a moving string with \(v < c\) and fixed eyelets be given (definition 26.29). Then:

  1. Every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of (26.36) is purely imaginary, \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) with real \(\omega\), and for an eigenpair \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle > 0\) and \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle = -\lambda\,\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\).
