  2. If \((\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}})\) and \((\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}})\) are eigenpairs with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\), then
    \[\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0 . \tag{26.38}\]
Idea

For the string at rest the proof of theorem 13.43 subtracts two equations. Here we subtract in the same way, but in the state space, where the eigenvalue equation connects \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\). The purely imaginary eigenvalues come from the positivity of \(\mathcal A\) and the skew symmetry of \(\mathcal B\) (lemma 26.30).

Proof

We show first item 1 and then the difference \((\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{m}})\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\).

  1. We multiply the eigenvalue equation (26.36) in the state product (26.31) by \(\vek\zeta\), which is linear in the first argument: \(\lambda\,\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle + \langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle = 0\).
  2. By lemma 26.30, \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) is real and greater than zero, and \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) is purely imaginary. From step 1, \(\lambda = -\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle/\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) is therefore a purely imaginary number. This is item 1.
  3. For two eigenpairs we write \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = -\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\) (the eigenvalue equation for \(n\), multiplied by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\)). By skew symmetry (lemma 26.30), \(-\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\).
  4. The eigenvalue equation for \(m\) is \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\), so \(\langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, -\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = -\bar\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\,\langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\), because the product is conjugate-linear in the second argument.
  5. By item 1, \(\bar\lambda_{\mathrm{m}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\), and by the symmetry of \(\mathcal A\), \(\langle\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\). Steps 3 and 4 together give \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle\).
  6. For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) this gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\), and by step 3 also \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = -\lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\cdot 0 = 0\).

Source: WM1990 (14b), (16) (PDF p. 3): the eigenvalues are imaginary, \(\langle\mathcal A\phi_{\mathrm{n}}, \phi_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = \delta_{\mathrm{nm}}\) and \(\langle\mathcal B\phi_{\mathrm{n}}, \phi_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\) for \(n \neq m\) (Meirovitch, 1974). Proved here by integration by parts from lemma 26.30, WM1990 does not give the proof.

The theorem gives orthogonality in two products at once, as for matrices (theorem 10.13, definition 10.10) in mass and stiffness. The difference is that the products are no longer the mass and the stiffness but \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\), in which mass and stiffness are mixed, as equation (26.32) shows.

We test the theorem on modes 1 and 2 with \(v/c = 1/2\) and compare it with the ordinary mass product \(\int\mu\,\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\,\mathrm{d}x\) of the string at rest. The real and imaginary part of the mode are \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = \sin(n\pi x)\cos(n\pi x/2)\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = \sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi x/2)\), therefore

\[\int_0^1\varphi_1^{\mathrm R}\varphi_2^{\mathrm R}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}16168 , \qquad \int_0^1\varphi_1^{\mathrm I}\varphi_2^{\mathrm I}\,\mathrm{d}x = -0{,}06467 , \qquad \mathrm{Re}\int_0^1\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\,\mathrm{d}x = 0{,}09701 \neq 0 . \tag{26.39}\]

The mass product of the modes is not zero. For the string at rest theorem 13.43 gave zero because the eigenvalue \(\omega^2\) is only a factor of the mass in the equation \(-T\varphi'' = \omega^2\mu\,\varphi\) (at \(v = 0\) we have \(\kappa = T\)). For the moving string equation (26.37) has the further term \(\lambda\mathcal G\varphi\) and the eigenvalue enters in two powers, so the same computation does not give zero. Zero is, by theorem 26.32, the state product (26.31), in which the mass part is accompanied by a stiffness part:

\[\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_2\rangle = \underbrace{\mu\,\omega_1\omega_2\!\int_0^1\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\,\mathrm{d}x}_{= \,1{,}0771 + 1{,}0771\,\mathrm{i}} + \underbrace{\kappa\!\int_0^1\varphi_1'\,\bar\varphi_2'\,\mathrm{d}x}_{= \,-1{,}0771 - 1{,}0771\,\mathrm{i}} = 0 . \tag{26.40}\]

The mass part is \(\omega_1\omega_2\) times the mass product, because \(p_{\mathrm{n}} = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) (lemma 26.31) and \(\mu\,p_1\bar p_2 = \mu\,\omega_1\omega_2\varphi_1\bar\varphi_2\), with \(\omega_1\omega_2 = 1{,}125\,\pi^2\). The computation is numerical (trapezoidal rule on 20001 points), the remainder is \(10^{-8}\).

In figure 26.19 we first draw the axis \(x\) between the eyelets. Then the mass part, which has area \(0{,}09701\cdot 1{,}125\,\pi^2 = 1{,}0771\): if we judged orthogonality by it alone, we would reject it. So we add the stiffness part with the opposite area. Last we add the two, the blackwhite curve is their sum: its area is zero, although the sum is not zero at any point except at the ends and at its crossings. This is the orthogonality the theorem claims, and it is not orthogonality point by point.

For the expansion we need real states. Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{n}} = \mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) is purely imaginary and \(\mathcal A\), \(\mathcal B\) map real states to real states, \(\bar{\vek\zeta}_{\mathrm{n}}\) is an eigenstate together with \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\), with eigenvalue \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\). We write \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\). By lemma 26.31, \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = (-\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})\) and \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = (\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\), since \(\mathrm{i}\omega(\varphi^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\varphi^{\mathrm I}) = -\omega\varphi^{\mathrm I} + \mathrm{i}\omega\varphi^{\mathrm R}\). The real part of the mode in time is then (with \(\omega t\) as the phase) \(w = \mathrm{Re}\,(\varphi\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\omega t}) = \varphi^{\mathrm R}\cos\omega t - \varphi^{\mathrm I}\sin\omega t\). Let us see what this means for the particles of the string.

We build figure 26.20 over the times. First we draw the first panel with \(\omega t = 0\): the shape is \(\varphi_1^{\mathrm R}\) and it is nowhere zero in the interior. On it we mark three particles at \(0{,}25\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}75\). For the second panel with \(\omega t = \pi/8\) we use \(w = \varphi^{\mathrm R}\cos\omega t - \varphi^{\mathrm I}\sin\omega t\): the particle at \(0{,}75\) is now on the axis, because there \(\varphi^{\mathrm R}\cos\omega t = \varphi^{\mathrm I}\sin\omega t\). The particle at \(x\) passes its rest position at \(\omega t = \pi/2 - k_1 x\), which with \(k_1 = \pi/2\) for \(x = 0{,}75\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}25\) is exactly \(\pi/8\), \(\pi/4\) and \(3\pi/8\), as the third panel and the fourth panel show. The particles of the string therefore do not pass through their rest positions together. For the string at rest \(\varphi^{\mathrm I} = 0\) and they all pass together at \(\omega t = \pi/2\). Wickert and Mote point out that the complex eigenfunctions give a response with varying phase, so the particles do not pass their rest positions simultaneously (WM1990, PDF p. 3). They pass at \(0{,}0625\), \(0{,}125\) and \(0{,}1875\) of the period \(\tau_1 = 2\pi/\omega_1 = 2{,}667\).

Corollary 26.33 Real pairs of modes (realni pari načinov)

Let \((\mathrm{i}\omega, \vek\zeta)\) be an eigenpair with \(\omega > 0\) and \(\vek\zeta = \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\,\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}\), where \(\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}\) are real states. With the real product \((\vek a, \vek b) = \int (a_1b_1 + a_2b_2)\,\mathrm{d}x\) we have:

  1. \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R} = \omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}\) and \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I} = -\omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}\),
  2. \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}) = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) = \tfrac12\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle\) and \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) = 0\),
  3. for two eigenpairs with \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) (both positive) all four products \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{a}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{b})\) and \((\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{a}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{b})\), \(a, b \in \{\mathrm R, \mathrm I\}\), are zero.
Proof

We must show that the real and imaginary part of theorem 26.32 separate.

  1. The eigenvalue equation with \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) is \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta = -\mathrm{i}\omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta\). Since \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) do not mix real and imaginary parts (they have real coefficients), \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R} + \mathrm{i}\,\mathcal B\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I} = \omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I} - \mathrm{i}\omega\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}\). Comparing real and imaginary parts gives item 1.
  2. The conjugate state \(\bar{\vek\zeta}\) is an eigenstate with \(-\mathrm{i}\omega \neq \mathrm{i}\omega\) (for \(\omega > 0\)). Theorem 26.32 gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \bar{\vek\zeta}\rangle = \int(\mathcal A\vek\zeta)^{\mathsf T}\vek\zeta\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\). Written out in real and imaginary part this is \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}) - (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) + 2\mathrm{i}\,(\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}) = 0\), because \(\mathcal A\) is symmetric also for the real product. The real and imaginary part give the first two equalities, and the sum \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta, \vek\zeta\rangle = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm R}) + (\mathcal A\vek\zeta^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta^{\mathrm I})\) gives the half.
  3. For \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} \neq \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) the numbers \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) and \(-\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{m}}\) are different. Theorem 26.32 for the pairs \((\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}})\) and \((\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \bar{\vek\zeta}_{\mathrm{m}})\) gives \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\) and \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}, \bar{\vek\zeta}_{\mathrm{m}}\rangle = 0\). The real and imaginary parts of both give four equations: \((R, R) + (I, I) = 0\), \((I, R) - (R, I) = 0\), \((R, R) - (I, I) = 0\) and \((I, R) + (R, I) = 0\), where \((a, b)\) means \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{a}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{b})\). All four are zero. The same for \(\mathcal B\).

Source: WM1990 (15), (16) (PDF p. 3): the structure \(\phi_{\mathrm{n}} = \phi_{\mathrm{n}}^R + \mathrm{i}\phi_{\mathrm{n}}^I\) and the orthogonality. Items 1 to 3 are our proof.

For mode 1 the same numerical computation gives \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm R}) = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm I}) = 3{,}70110\) and \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_1^{\mathrm I}) = -10^{-8}\), which is zero up to the error of the rule and is item 2 of the corollary. Together \(\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = 7{,}40220\), \(\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = -17{,}44103\,\mathrm{i}\) and so \(-\langle\mathcal B\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle/\langle\mathcal A\vek\zeta_1, \vek\zeta_1\rangle = 2{,}35619\,\mathrm{i} = \mathrm{i}\omega_1\), which is item 1 of the theorem for this mode.

26.6.3 Expansion in modes

The goal is to solve the initial value problem: at \(t = 0\) the string has shape \(w_0\) and velocity \(w_1\), so the state \(\vek z_0 = (w_1, w_0)\). Which motion follows? For the string at rest (theorem 13.11) we wrote the motion as a sum of modes with coefficients from orthogonality. Here there are two coordinates per mode, \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\), because each mode has two real parts. We write

\[\vek z(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{n}=1}^\infty\Big(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(t)\,\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(t)\,\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\Big) . \tag{26.41}\]

The theorem that follows says which coefficients this must have. We do not prove the completeness of the expansion, that is that every state of \(S\) is such a sum: Wickert and Mote assume it (WM1990, PDF p. 3, "it is assumed that the expansion is complete"). For the string at rest theorem 13.11 proves it from Fourier series, for the moving string the proof remains open and we mark it as cited, not proved.

Theorem 26.34 Modal coordinates of the moving string (modalne koordinate gibajoče se strune)

Let a moving string with \(v < c\) and fixed eyelets be given, \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}} = (\mathrm{i}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\) its modes with distinct \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\) (theorem 26.13) and \(N_{\mathrm{n}} = (\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})\). Let \(\vek z(t) = (w_{\mathrm{t}}, w)\) be a motion that the sum (26.41) represents at every time \(t\) so that the operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\), the derivative in time and the integral may be applied term by term. Then

\[\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} , \qquad \dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} , \tag{26.42}\]

so \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(t) = \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(t) = \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t - \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t\), with the initial values

\[\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0) = \frac{(\mathcal A\vek z_0, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})}{N_{\mathrm{n}}} , \qquad \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0) = \frac{(\mathcal A\vek z_0, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})}{N_{\mathrm{n}}} . \tag{26.43}\]
Idea

We insert the sum in equation (26.33) and multiply it by one of the real states. Because of theorem 26.32 and corollary 26.33 one term remains, and the equation for the coefficient is the equation of an oscillator.

Proof

We must show that multiplication by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}\) and \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}\) gives (26.42) and that the initial condition gives (26.43).

  1. Equation (26.33) for the sum (26.41) gives \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}}\big(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\,\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\,\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\big) = \vek 0\). By corollary 26.33 (item 1) \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\) and \(\mathcal B\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}\), so the sum reads \(\sum_{\mathrm{n}}\big((\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} - \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} + (\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} + \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R})\,\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\big) = \vek 0\).
  2. We multiply this by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}\). By corollary 26.33 (items 2 and 3) only the term with \(n = m\) and with \(\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}\) remains of the sum, and gives \(N_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R} - \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}) = 0\). Multiplying by \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}\) leaves \(N_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I} + \omega_{\mathrm{m}}\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}) = 0\), because \((\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}) = N_{\mathrm{m}} > 0\). This gives (26.42).
  3. From (26.42), \(\ddot\xi^{\mathrm R}_{\mathrm{n}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\,\xi^{\mathrm R}_{\mathrm{n}}\), so \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = a\cos\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t + b\sin\omega_{\mathrm{n}}t\) (theorem 9.36), and \(\dot\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0) = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\) gives \(b = \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\). The same for \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}\).
  4. Initial condition: \(\vek z(0) = \vek z_0\), so \((\mathcal A\vek z_0, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}) = \sum_{\mathrm{n}}\big(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\,(\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}) + \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0)\,(\mathcal A\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}, \vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R})\big) = N_{\mathrm{m}}\,\xi_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm R}(0)\) by items 2 and 3 of corollary 26.33. The same for \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{m}}^{\mathrm I}\). This is (26.43).

Source: WM1990 (19), (20), (21b) (PDF p. 3): modal coordinates and their initial values (Meirovitch, 1975). The proof and the choice of \(N_{\mathrm{n}}\) are ours, the completeness of the expansion is assumed (WM1990, PDF p. 3) and not proved.

Let us see whether this works on an example. We take the string with \(L = \mu = T = 1\) and \(v/c = 1/2\) from the previous examples and give it \(w_0 = \sin\pi x\), \(w_1 = 0\), so the state \(\vek z_0 = (0, \sin\pi x)\) (the initial shape is the first sine of chapter 13, not a mode of the moving string, since \(\varphi_1^{\mathrm R} = \sin\pi x\cos(\pi x/2)\)). By equation (26.43) the coefficients are

\[\xi_1^{\mathrm R}(0) = \xi_1^{\mathrm I}(0) = 0{,}67906 , \quad \xi_2^{\mathrm R}(0) = 0{,}125 , \ \xi_2^{\mathrm I}(0) = 0 , \quad \xi_3^{\mathrm R}(0) = -\xi_3^{\mathrm I}(0) = 0{,}02646 , \ \ldots \tag{26.44}\]

and the sum of the first \(N\) terms at \(t = 0\) gives the displacement \(w_0\) and velocity zero with the following errors (largest deviation over \(x\)):

\(N\) 1 2 4 8 12
\(\max\lvert w - w_0\rvert\) \(0{,}0850\) \(0{,}0397\) \(0{,}0036\) \(0{,}00042\) \(0{,}00012\)
\(\max\lvert w_{\mathrm{t}}\rvert\) \(0{,}616\) \(0{,}323\) \(0{,}036\) \(0{,}010\) \(0{,}005\)

The error falls with \(N\), which is observed, not proved: the convergence of the expansion is not proved, as said above. The motion at later times is obtained by rotating the pair \((\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}, \xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I})\) with angular velocity \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) by equation (26.42). For the steel band of section 26.1 (dimensions, tension and speeds are our choice) the frequency of the first mode at \(v = c/2 = 56{,}6\) m/s is \(f_1 = (1 - v^2/c^2)\cdot 56{,}61 = 0{,}75\cdot 56{,}61 = 42{,}5\) Hz, where \(56{,}61\) Hz is the frequency of the first mode at \(v = 0\) (section 26.3), and this expansion would write any initial displacement of the band as a sum of sines of these frequencies with shifted phases.

Let us also look at the way back to the string at rest (section 26.1 has \(v = 0\) as a special case). For \(v = 0\) we have \(\mathcal G = 0\), \(k_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\), \(\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = 0\) and \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R} = (0, \varphi_{\mathrm{n}})\), \(\vek\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I} = (\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}, 0)\). Equation (26.43) gives \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm R}(0) \propto \int\kappa\,w_0'\,\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \kappa\,(\pi n/L)^2\int w_0\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) (by lemma 6.13) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{n}}^{\mathrm I}(0) \propto \mu\,\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\int w_1\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). These are the coefficients from the initial displacement and the initial velocity, as the expansion in modes of the string at rest gives them (theorem 13.11).

What has this section given us? The orthogonality of the moving string does not go by the mass product but by the state product (26.31) with the operators \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) (theorem 26.32), which we showed by integration by parts and the eigenvalue equation. The expansion in modes (theorem 26.34) writes the response to an initial condition with the same steps as for the string at rest. We already met a first-order form for damping (section 20.8), there with two symmetric matrices, here with one symmetric and one skew-symmetric operator. Later we shall need the two operators and the state product for the beam in section 26.7, where the second order is replaced by the fourth. The completeness of the expansion and the convergence in the example remain unproved. We do not yet treat the Green's function, which WM1990 derives from the same orthogonality (PDF p. 3 and 4), nor the response to a moving force, which WM1990 computes for a monocable aerial tramway with a payload (enovrvna žičnica, PDF p. 4 and 5).

26.7 The moving beam

The string of sections 26.1 to 26.5 has no bending stiffness. A real band or saw blade has a thickness and bends only if we bend it, like a ruler. This section asks three questions. How does the equation of the moving string change if the band has bending stiffness? How large is the change for the steel band of example A, that is, is the string a good model of the band? And what happens to the critical speed of section 26.4? The last question leads to a kinship: the critical speed of the beam is the critical force of the column of chapter 8, converted into a speed.

26.7.1 Model and equation

We draw the band as before (figure 26.21, top). It is held in two supports, fixed in space at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), and slides through them with speed \(v\) towards increasing \(x\), drawn as the velocity arrow. The shape of the band is the graph of the deflection \(w(x, t)\) over the \(x\) axis, with the deflection \(w\) upwards, strongly enlarged for clarity. The particles of the band that lie between \(a + vt\) and \(b + vt\) at time \(t\) we call the piece: it is the same material all the time, moving together along \(x\) with speed \(v\) (section 26.1, lemma 26.1). Below we draw the piece in a separate picture and enter the forces that act on it.

We draw the forces on the piece in the bottom picture one by one. The piece is curved along the band like the band. At each end its neighbour pulls it with the tension force \(T\) along the tangent: the right part in the direction of increasing \(x\), the left part in the opposite direction. Each pull starts at the end of the piece on which it acts. The tension along the tangent gives the vertical component \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). Because the band has bending stiffness, the neighbour does not act only along the tangent: the part to the right of \(b + vt\) also acts on the piece with the vertical shear force \(V(b + vt, t)\) upwards and the part to the left of \(a + vt\) with \(-V(a + vt, t)\), drawn as the force \(V(a + vt, t)\) downwards, by the law of action and reaction, as for the beam in chapter 13 (lemma 13.29). Finally the right part also acts with a bending moment \(M(b + vt, t)\) counterclockwise and the left part with \(-M(a + vt, t)\), drawn as \(M(a + vt, t)\) clockwise.

A band with bending stiffness is thus a moving string with one more force. We write the model with all idealizations named.

Definition 26.35 Axially moving beam (gibajoči nosilec)

An axially moving beam is a band of length \(L\) between two supports fixed in space at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), which moves through them with constant transport speed \(v > 0\) in the direction of increasing \(x\). Its deflection \(w(x, t)\) is a real function of two variables with continuous partial derivatives up to the fourth order. The idealizations of the moving string of definition 26.3 hold (constant mass \(\mu\) per unit length, constant tension \(T\), \(|w_{\mathrm{x}}| \le 0{,}01\), the transport speed \(v\) the same for all particles), except the idealization of zero bending stiffness, which is replaced by two new ones, (i) and (ii):

(i) The band has constant bending stiffness \(EI\) and in every cross-section the moment \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), as the beam in chapter 13 (theorem 13.28). (ii) The rotary inertia of the cross-sections, that is the kinetic energy of the rotation of the cross-sections owing to the turn \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\), is neglected, as for that beam.

The supports are either simple (členkasta), where \(w = 0\) and \(M = EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), or fixed (vpeta), where \(w = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), at both ends and at every time.

Source: Model: WM1990 §2.2 (PDF p. 2), which extends the moving string by bending stiffness, and Mote 1965 (cited there, not in the books). The naming of the idealizations and the bounds are ours.

The idealization (ii) has a measure. We estimate it for the steel band of example A (band \(0{,}9 \times 50\) mm, \(L = 1\) m, stress \(100\) MPa, \(T = 4500\) N, \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, the dimensions and speeds are our choice, we have no data of real belts). A cross-section turns by the angle \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) when the band bends. The cross-section moves with the band, so its angular velocity is the time derivative of \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) following a particle that moves with speed \(v\), that is \(w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (chain rule as in lemma 26.1), and the transverse velocity of a particle is \(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). The kinetic energy of rotation per unit length is \(\tfrac12\,\rho I\,(w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{xx}})^2\), and the kinetic energy of the transverse motion is \(\tfrac12\,\rho A\,(w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}})^2\). The angular velocity is the derivative of the transverse velocity with respect to \(x\), so for a mode with wave number \(k\) it is of the order \(k\) times the transverse velocity, and the ratio is of the order \((I/A)\,k^2\) with \(I/A = h^2/12\) for a rectangle of thickness \(h\). For \(h = 0{,}9\) mm this is \(6{,}75\cdot 10^{-8}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 9{,}87\ \text{m}^{-2} = 6{,}7\cdot 10^{-7}\) for the first mode (\(k = \pi/L\)). The estimate is an order of magnitude, not a calculation, and it suffices for accepting the idealization.

Now we derive the equation. The way is that of section 26.1: the momentum of a piece made of the same particles, then the vanishing of the integrand. The band is the same as for the string, and the shear force joins the forces at the ends of the piece.

Theorem 26.36 Equation of motion of the axially moving beam (gibalna enačba gibajočega nosilca)

Let \(w\) be the deflection of an axially moving beam by definition 26.35 without external load, and let the law of momentum hold for every piece of particles: the derivative of the momentum of a piece is the sum of the transverse forces that the two neighbouring parts exert on it. Then for every \(x \in [0, L]\) and every \(t\)

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\big) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} , \tag{26.45}\]

that is

\[\mu\,\big(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big) + \big(\mu v^2 - T\big)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = 0 . \tag{26.46}\]
Proof

We must show that the piece has the momentum \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) with \(g(s, t) = w(s + vt, t)\), that its derivative equals the difference of the forces at the ends of the piece, and that the equation at a point follows from the integral over the piece.

  1. A particle that is at \(x = s + vt\) at time \(t\) has the deflection \(g(s, t) = w(s + vt, t)\). So for every \(t\) the piece has the particles \(s \in [a, b]\), the variable \(s\) is their label and the limits are constant. By lemma 26.1 the velocity of the particle is \(g_{\mathrm{t}} = w_{\mathrm{t}} + v\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) and the acceleration \(g_{\mathrm{tt}} = w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), evaluated at \((s + vt, t)\) (chain rule, lemma 8.29).
  2. The momentum of the piece is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}s\). The limits are constant and \(g_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is continuous, so its derivative in time is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}s\) by lemma 4.19.
  3. The transverse force with which the right part acts on the piece at \(x = b + vt\) is the sum of the component of the tension \(T\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\) (derivation 13.1, the tangent has slope \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\)) and of the shear force \(V = -EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\) (balance of moments of the piece, lemma 13.29, item 1, step 2, with rotary inertia neglected by idealization (ii)). The left part acts at \(x = a + vt\) with the opposite value (law of action and reaction). The force is \(F = T\,w_{\mathrm{x}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\), so the sum of the forces on the piece is \(F(b + vt, t) - F(a + vt, t)\).
  4. The law of momentum from steps 2 and 3 is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b \mu\,g_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}s = F(b + vt, t) - F(a + vt, t)\). By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40, item 1, antiderivative \(F\) in \(x\)) the right-hand side is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{vt}}^{b+vt} F_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), and by the shift \(x = s + vt\) it is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b F_{\mathrm{x}}(s + vt, t)\,\mathrm{d}s\) with \(F_{\mathrm{x}} = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\).
  5. From steps 1 and 4, \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b r(s + vt, t)\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) with \(r = \mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}) - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\), a continuous function. At time \(t\) every interval \([x_1, x_2] \subset [0, L]\) is a piece with \(a = x_1 - vt\) and \(b = x_2 - vt\). So \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} r(x, t)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for every such interval.
  6. Let \(x_1 \in [0, L)\). By step 5 the function \(x \mapsto \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x} r\,\mathrm{d}s\) is identically zero, by the fundamental theorem (item 2) its derivative is \(r(x, t)\), so \(r(x, t) = 0\). For \(x = L\) we take the intervals \([x_1, L]\) and continuity. Thus equation (26.45) is proved, and equation (26.46) follows by rearranging the terms.

Source: WM1990 (5) (PDF p. 2): \(\rho(U_{\mathrm{TT}} + 2VU_{\mathrm{XT}} + V^2 U_{\mathrm{XX}}) - P U_{\mathrm{XX}} + EI\,U_{\mathrm{XXXX}} = F\), the same equation with \(F = 0\) (\(\rho \to \mu\), \(P \to T\)). The source cites Mote 1965 and does not derive it. The proof with a piece of particles is not from the source, the way is as for theorem 26.4.

We test the equation on two limiting cases. For \(EI = 0\) what remains is \(\mu\,(w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}) = T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the equation of the moving string (theorem 26.4). For \(v = 0\) what remains is \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} - T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), a beam with an axial force. For the band of example A the sine is still a solution: \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\cos\omega t\) satisfies the equation exactly when \(\mu\,\omega^2 = T\,(\pi/L)^2 + EI\,(\pi/L)^4\), because \(w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -\omega^2 w\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(\pi/L)^2 w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = (\pi/L)^4 w\). The first term gives \(T\,(\pi/L)^2 = 44\,413\) N/m², the second \(EI\,(\pi/L)^4 = 58{,}0\) N/m², so \(f_1 = 56{,}651\) Hz. The string has \(f_1 = c/(2L) = 56{,}614\) Hz: the bending stiffness raises the frequency by \(0{,}065\) %, which is half the ratio of the second and the first term, \(\tfrac12\cdot 0{,}1306\ \% = 0{,}0653\ \%\).

For \(v \ne 0\) the sine is no longer a solution. The term \(2v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) contains \(-2v\,(\pi/L)\,\omega\cos(\pi x/L)\sin\omega t\), and the cosine occurs in no other term. This is the same reason as for the string (section 26.3): the oscillation is no longer standing. We therefore find the natural oscillations by the Galerkin method with the sines of section 26.5. With \(w = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} q_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\sin(j\pi x/L)\) and \(k_{\mathrm{j}} = j\pi/L\) we get \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) with

\[M_{\mathrm{jj}} = \tfrac12\,\mu L , \qquad K_{\mathrm{jj}} = \tfrac12\,L\,\big(EI\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^4 - (\mu v^2 - T)\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^2\big) , \qquad G_{\mathrm{jk}} = \frac{4\mu v\,j\,k}{j^2 - k^2}\ \ (j + k\ \text{odd}) , \tag{26.47}\]

all other entries are zero. The last value follows from \(G_{\mathrm{jk}} = 2\mu v\,k_{\mathrm{k}} \int_0^L \sin k_{\mathrm{j}} x\,\cos k_{\mathrm{k}} x\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\sin a\cos b = \tfrac12(\sin(a + b) + \sin(a - b))\), where \(\int_0^L \sin(m\pi x/L)\,\mathrm{d}x = 2L/(m\pi)\) for odd \(m\) and \(0\) for even \(m\). The matrix \(\mat G\) is skew (\(G_{\mathrm{kj}} = -G_{\mathrm{jk}}\)). For example A and \(N = 24\) sines we get the first frequency \(f_1\) as follows (the string by the equation \(f_1 = (c/2L)(1 - v^2/c^2)\)):

\(v\) (m/s) 0 20 40 80
\(f_1\) of the beam (Hz) 56,651 54,891 49,613 28,504
\(f_1\) of the string (Hz) 56,614 54,847 49,548 28,352
difference 0,065 % 0,080 % 0,130 % 0,535 %

The difference grows with the speed. The reason is that the motion reduces the tension that is left for bending: \(T - \mu v^2\) is \(2254\) N out of \(4500\) N at \(80\) m/s, while the bending part \(EI\,k_1^2 = 5{,}9\) N stays the same and so has a larger share. How much exactly is told only by the calculation in the table. At \(v = 80\) m/s the difference is still below \(0{,}6\) %. In this range the band is therefore a string and the model of sections 26.1 to 26.5 suffices. When does the bending stiffness overcome the tension? The term \(EI\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^4\) exceeds \(T\,k_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) when \(j^2 > T L^2/(\pi^2 EI) = 766\), that is from \(j = 28\) on. The wavelength is then \(2L/28 = 71\) mm, which is \(79\) times the thickness of the band.

The critical speed remains. There the bending stiffness changes not only the numbers but the content of the theorem.

26.7.2 Critical speed of the beam

Let us see what equation (26.46) says if the band rests in shape and only the material moves. Let \(w\) not depend on time. The terms \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) drop out and what remains is

\[EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + \big(\mu v^2 - T\big)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.48}\]

This is the equation of the column of chapter 8, \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + P\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), with the force

\[P = \mu v^2 - T . \tag{26.49}\]

The reason is Newton's law for a particle. A particle that moves along a curve with curvature \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) at speed \(v\) has the acceleration \(v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (the term \(v^2 w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of lemma 26.1), so the band must act on it with the force \(\mu v^2\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) per unit length. The tension provides \(T\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). For bending there remains \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\), as if the tension were only \(T - \mu v^2\). If this is negative, the band behaves like a column compressed by the force \(\mu v^2 - T\): the acceleration of the particles along the curve eats up the tension and finally exceeds it.

Figure 26.22 shows this for the band of example A. The left graph is the force \(P(v) = \mu v^2 - T\) from \(-T = -4500\) N at \(v = 0\) to \(1900\) N at \(v = 135\) m/s: a parabola that passes from tension (\(P < 0\)) to compression (\(P > 0\)) at the speed of the string \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s. The critical forces of the column are \(\pi^2 EI/L^2 = 5{,}876\) N and \(4\pi^2 EI/L^2 = 23{,}503\) N, which at the scale of \(4500\) N is less than the thickness of a line. So we draw a magnification of the neighbourhood of the point \(P = 0\) and get the right graph: on it the two critical forces are horizontal lines that the parabola crosses at \(113{,}30\) m/s and \(113{,}52\) m/s, which are \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) for simple and for fixed supports.

We name the speed at which this happens and estimate it. For the string we called critical in section 26.4 the speed at which the behaviour changes. For the beam the same holds.

Theorem 26.37 Critical speed of the axially moving beam (kritična hitrost gibajočega nosilca)

Let the axially moving beam be as in definition 26.35 with simple supports (case a) or with fixed supports (case b). Let \(P = \mu v^2 - T\), \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = \pi^2 EI/L^2\) in case a and \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} = 4\pi^2 EI/L^2\) in case b, and

\[v_{\mathrm{c}} = \sqrt{\frac{T + P_{\mathrm{cr}}}{\mu}} . \tag{26.50}\]

For \(\mathcal Q(\eta) = \int_0^L \big(EI\,\eta''^2 - P\,\eta'^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\) it holds:

  1. For every solution \(w\) of equation (26.46), \(\mathcal E^* = \tfrac12\int_0^L \mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x + \tfrac12\,\mathcal Q(w(\cdot, t))\) is constant in time.
  2. For \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\), \(\mathcal Q(\eta) > 0\) for every twice continuously differentiable \(\eta \ne 0\) with the support conditions, equation (26.48) with the same conditions has only the solution \(w = 0\), and with \(\theta = 1 - \max(P, 0)/P_{\mathrm{cr}} > 0\) we have \(\theta\,EI\int_0^L w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x \le 2\,\mathcal E^*\) at every time.
  3. For \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\), equation (26.48) has a nonzero solution: \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\) in case a and \(w = 1 - \cos(2\pi x/L)\) in case b, and \(\mathcal Q(w) = 0\) for it.
Proof

We must show the conservation of the functional in time, the positivity of the form \(\mathcal Q\) below the limit by the theorems on the column, and the solution at the limit. Below, \(w\) has continuous derivatives up to the fourth order and satisfies the support conditions at every time.

  1. We multiply equation (26.46) by \(w_{\mathrm{t}}\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). By lemma 4.19, \(\int \mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\tfrac12\int\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. The term with \(2v\) is \(2\mu v\int w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \mu v\,\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L = 0\), because \(w = 0\) at both supports at every time, so also \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\). The term of the gyroscopic force thus does no work, which is a property of the force (lemma 26.26).
  3. By integration by parts (corollary 3.41), \(\int P\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[P\,w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{t}}\big]_0^L - P\int w_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x = -\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\tfrac12 P\int w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), because \(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) at the supports.
  4. Twice by parts: \(\int EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}}\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,\mathrm{d}x = EI\big[w_{\mathrm{xxx}}\,w_{\mathrm{t}} - w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big]_0^L + EI\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,w_{\mathrm{xxt}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The first term is zero (\(w_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\)). The second is zero for simple supports (\(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\)) and for fixed supports (\(w_{\mathrm{xt}} = 0\), because \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) at every time). What remains is \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\tfrac12\,EI\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  5. The sum of steps 1 to 4 is \(\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm{d}t}\,\big(\tfrac12\int\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + \tfrac12\int (EI\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 - P\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\big) = 0\). This is item 1.
  6. For \(P \le 0\), \(\mathcal Q(\eta) \ge EI\int\eta''^2\), for \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} > P > 0\) by theorem 8.134 (case a) or 8.135 (case b), step 1 of their proofs, \(\mathcal Q(\eta) \ge EI\,(1 - P/P_{\mathrm{cr}})\int\eta''^2\). So \(\mathcal Q(\eta) \ge \theta\,EI\int\eta''^2\). If \(\int\eta''^2 = 0\), then \(\eta''= 0\), \(\eta\) is linear and because of \(\eta(0) = \eta(L) = 0\) equal to zero. Therefore \(\mathcal Q > 0\) for \(\eta \ne 0\). The condition \(P < P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) is \(\mu v^2 < T + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\), that is \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\).
  7. The static solution: we multiply equation (26.48) by \(w\) and integrate by parts twice. The terms at the ends are zero, because \(w = 0\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) or \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), what remains is \(\mathcal Q(w) = 0\), as in the proof of theorem 8.134. For \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\) step 6 gives \(w = 0\). Item 2 follows also from step 5: \(\theta\,EI\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 \le \mathcal Q(w) \le 2\,\mathcal E^*\).
  8. At \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\) we have \(P = P_{\mathrm{cr}}\). For \(w = \sin(\pi x/L)\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -(\pi/L)^2 w\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = (\pi/L)^4 w\), so \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = \big(EI\,(\pi/L)^4 - (\pi^2 EI/L^2)(\pi/L)^2\big)\,w = 0\). The conditions of simple supports hold (\(w = 0\), \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at \(0\) and \(L\)). For \(w = 1 - \cos(2\pi x/L)\), \(w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} = -(2\pi/L)^4\cos(2\pi x/L)\) and \(w_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\pi/L)^2\cos(2\pi x/L)\), so \(EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + P_{\mathrm{cr}}\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = (2\pi/L)^2\cos(2\pi x/L)\,\big(-EI\,(2\pi/L)^2 + 4\pi^2 EI/L^2\big) = 0\), and \(w = w_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) at \(0\) and \(L\). By step 7, therefore, \(\mathcal Q(w) = 0\).

Source: WM1990 (13) (PDF p. 2): \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = \sqrt{\mu^2 + \pi^2}\) for simple and \(\sqrt{\mu^2 + 4\pi^2}\) for fixed supports, in dimensionless notation \(\mu^2 = P L^2/EI\) from WM1990 (6) (our \(T L^2/EI\)). Appendix A (PDF pp. 6 and 7), (A1) and (A2): the static equation and the positive definiteness of \(\langle u, Ku\rangle\). For fixed supports the source gives the static solution only as \(v^2 - \mu^2 = (2n\pi)^2\). In chapter 8 it is shown for fixed ends that the next zero of the determinant is \(kL = 8{,}987\) (\(\tan(kL/2) = kL/2\)): \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) (the first zero) does not change. The functional \(\mathcal E^*\) for the beam is not from the source, the pattern is CHEN2005 (33) (PDF p. 7) for the string.

What we have shown. For \(v < v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the form \(\mathcal Q\) is positive and the functional \(\mathcal E^*\) bounds \(\int w_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), so the shape of the band cannot grow in time beyond the bound set by the initial state. At \(v = v_{\mathrm{c}}\) there exists an equilibrium shape that we may enlarge by an arbitrary factor: the band can stay bent at unchanged tension and speed. The name critical speed has the same reason as the critical force of the column: below it the straight position is energetically stable (definition 8.64), at it the question is decided whether a bent shape stays in equilibrium at all. For \(EI \to 0\), \(P_{\mathrm{cr}} \to 0\) and \(v_{\mathrm{c}} \to \sqrt{T/\mu} = c\): the critical speed of the string of section 26.4 is the limit of the case without bending stiffness.

Now a number. For the band of example A the ratio \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}/T\) is small: \(5{,}876/4500 = 1/766 = 0{,}001306\) in case a. We denote it by \(\varepsilon\), so that \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c\,\sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\). Since \((1 + \varepsilon/2)^2 = 1 + \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2/4\), the difference is \(1 + \varepsilon/2 - \sqrt{1 + \varepsilon} = (\varepsilon^2/4)/\big(1 + \varepsilon/2 + \sqrt{1 + \varepsilon}\big)\) (the difference of the squares divided by the sum). The denominator is larger than \(2\), so the difference is smaller than \(\varepsilon^2/8 = 2{,}1\cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = c\,(1 + \varepsilon/2)\) holds with a relative error below \(2{,}1\cdot 10^{-7}\). Therefore \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 113{,}23\,(1 + 0{,}000653) = 113{,}30\) m/s, which is \(0{,}0653\) % above \(c\). For fixed supports \(\varepsilon = 23{,}503/4500 = 0{,}005223\) and \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = 113{,}52\) m/s, \(0{,}2608\) % above \(c\). The difference between \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) and \(c\) is \(0{,}07\) m/s out of \(113\) m/s for this band, so the critical speed of the string is a good approximation. It is different for a band without tension: for \(T = 0\), \(v_{\mathrm{c}} = (\pi/L)\sqrt{EI/\mu} = 4{,}09\) m/s (simple supports) or \(8{,}18\) m/s (fixed). A string without tension has \(c = 0\), so critical speed zero, while the beam has it at a few metres per second. There the bending stiffness is not a correction but decides.

26.7.3 Test: a window of stability above the critical speed

Theorem 26.37 is one-sided: below \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the band is stable. We try to reverse it. For the column of chapter 8 the opposite holds: above \(P_{\mathrm{cr}}\) the straight position is unstable. So it would be natural for the band to be unstable for every \(v > v_{\mathrm{c}}\). We show that this is not true, and why. The theorem is thereby tested on an example that it does not survive.

We use the dimensionless notation of WM1990: \(L = 1\), \(EI = 1\), \(\mu = 1\) and \(\bar T = T L^2/EI\) (in the source \(\mu^2\), but \(\mu\) is the mass per length for us, so we do not use it) and \(\bar v = v\sqrt{\mu L^2/EI}\) (in the source \(\nu\), which is Poisson's ratio in the book). Let \(\bar T = 100\) and simple supports. By equation (26.47), \(K_{\mathrm{jj}} = \tfrac12\,\big((j\pi)^4 + (100 - \bar v^2)\,(j\pi)^2\big)\), which is negative exactly for \(\bar v^2 > 100 + j^2\pi^2\). The limits are \(\bar v_1 = 10{,}4819\), \(\bar v_2 = 11{,}8101\) and \(\bar v_3 = 13{,}7414\) (SymPy and NumPy, num-07.out). The first is \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) of theorem 26.37.

Figure 26.23 shows what happens to the eigenvalues of the system \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) with \(N = 24\) sines. On the axes are the speed \(\bar v\) from \(10\) to \(13\) and the largest real part of the eigenvalues \(\lambda\). Zero means that all eigenvalues are purely imaginary and the solutions are bounded oscillations, a positive real part means growth like \(e^{\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda\, t}\). The curve is zero up to \(10{,}48\), then rises to \(4{,}77\) at \(11{,}25\) and falls back to zero at \(11{,}81\). Between \(11{,}81\) and \(12{,}18\) it is zero again: all eigenvalues are purely imaginary again. Above \(12{,}177\) the curve rises again and equals \(10{,}3\) at \(13\). The vertical lines mark \(\bar v_1\) and \(\bar v_2\) and the computed end of the window at \(12{,}177\).

The window between \(\bar v_2\) and \(12{,}18\) has an explanation that we prove for the system we use. We look at the first part, above \(\bar v_1\).

Lemma 26.38 Instability for a negative determinant of the stiffness (nestabilnost pri negativni determinanti togosti)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric positive definite \(N \times N\) matrix, \(\mat G\) skew and \(\mat K\) symmetric, all with constant real entries. If \(\det\mat K < 0\), the system \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek 0\) has a solution whose size grows like \(e^{\sigma t}\) with \(\sigma > 0\).

Proof

We must show that the polynomial \(p(\lambda) = \det(\mat M\lambda^2 + \mat G\lambda + \mat K)\) has a root with nonzero real part, and that this root gives a growing solution.

  1. The matrix \(\mat M\lambda^2 - \mat G\lambda + \mat K\) is the transpose of the matrix \(\mat M\lambda^2 + \mat G\lambda + \mat K\) (\(\mat G^\T = -\mat G\)), and the determinant does not change under transposition. So \(p(-\lambda) = p(\lambda)\) and \(p(\lambda) = q(\lambda^2)\) with a polynomial \(q\) of degree \(N\) with leading coefficient \(\det\mat M > 0\) and \(q(0) = p(0) = \det\mat K\).
  2. We write \(q(s) = \det\mat M\,\prod_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{N}(s - s_{\mathrm{k}})\) with complex roots \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\). Then \(\det\mat K = q(0) = \det\mat M\,\prod_{\mathrm{k}}(-s_{\mathrm{k}})\).
  3. If all \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) were real and \(\le 0\), every \(-s_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 0\) and \(\det\mat K \ge 0\). Since \(\det\mat K < 0\), there is an \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\) that is not real and \(\le 0\).
  4. Let \(\lambda\) be a square root of such an \(s_{\mathrm{k}}\). If \(\lambda\) were purely imaginary, \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\), then \(s_{\mathrm{k}} = \lambda^2 = -\omega^2 \le 0\) would be real. This is a contradiction, so \(\lambda\) has a nonzero real part. Since \(-\lambda\) is also a root, we may take \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = \sigma > 0\).
  5. For \(\lambda\) there is \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\) with \((\mat M\lambda^2 + \mat G\lambda + \mat K)\,\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), so \(\vek z(t) = \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\vek\varphi\) is a solution, with \(|\vek z(t)| = \mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}|\vek\varphi|\). Its real and imaginary parts are real solutions that together give \(|\vek z|^2 = |\mathrm{Re}\,\vek z|^2 + |\mathrm{Im}\,\vek z|^2\), so at least one grows like \(\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}\).

Source: The proof is not from the source. The theorem on the eigenvalues of a gyroscopic system with positive definite stiffness (theorem 26.27) is the converse direction, GR §2.11 (PDF pp. 137 to 141).

The lemma says: if \(\mat K\) has an odd number of negative eigenvalues, the system is unstable even if the Coriolis term \(\mat G\) is not zero. Our \(\mat K\) is diagonal, so \(\det\mat K = \prod K_{\mathrm{jj}}\) and the sign is decided by the number of negative entries. Between \(\bar v_1\) and \(\bar v_2\) only \(K_{11}\) is negative (SymPy), so by the lemma the system is unstable for every \(N \ge 1\). This agrees with the figure: at \(\bar v = 10{,}6\) the largest real part is \(2{,}489\), at \(11\) it is \(4{,}508\) and at \(11{,}5\) it is \(4{,}324\) (num-07.out). Above \(\bar v_2\) both \(K_{11}\) and \(K_{22}\) are negative, the determinant is positive again and the lemma says nothing: it proves neither instability nor stability.

The stability in the window is computed, not proved, and we understand it with two sines. Let \(N = 2\) and \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat K = \mathrm{diag}(k_1, k_2)\) with \(k_1, k_2 < 0\), \(\mat G = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & g \\ -g & 0\end{pmatrix}\) (by equation (26.47), \(g = G_{12} = -8\bar v/3\)). The determinant of the lemma is

\[p(\lambda) = (m\lambda^2 + k_1)(m\lambda^2 + k_2) + g^2\lambda^2 = m^2\lambda^4 + \big(m\,(k_1 + k_2) + g^2\big)\lambda^2 + k_1 k_2 .\]

Purely imaginary roots require both roots \(\lambda^2\) to be real and negative. We denote \(b = m(k_1 + k_2) + g^2\). Since \(k_1 k_2 > 0\), the roots have the same sign, their sum is \(-b/m^2\), so both are negative and real exactly when \(b > 0\) and the discriminant \(b^2 - 4m^2 k_1 k_2 \ge 0\), that is \(b \ge 2m\sqrt{k_1 k_2}\). With \(|k_{\mathrm{i}}| = -k_{\mathrm{i}}\) this is \(g^2 - m\,(|k_1| + |k_2|) \ge 2m\sqrt{|k_1|\,|k_2|}\), which is the same as \(g^2 \ge m\,\big(\sqrt{|k_1|} + \sqrt{|k_2|}\big)^2\). At \(\bar v = 12\), \(g = -32\), \(g^2 = 1024\), \(k_1 = -168{,}43\), \(k_2 = -89{,}25\) and \(m = 1/2\), so \(m(\sqrt{|k_1|} + \sqrt{|k_2|})^2 = 251{,}4\). The condition is met with a large margin. The term \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) does no work and cannot add energy, but it couples two modes that would each grow alone into an oscillation. We call it gyroscopic stabilization (giroskopska stabilizacija), because \(\mat G\,\dot{\vek q}\) has the form of a gyroscopic force (section 26.5).

Two sines do not explain the end of the window. For \(N = 2\) the limit of stability moves to \(13{,}85\), for \(N = 4\) it is \(12{,}181\) and for \(N = 24\) it is \(12{,}177\) (num-07.out): modes 3 and 4, which \(G_{\mathrm{jk}}\) couples with modes 1 and 2 (the sum \(j + k\) is odd), move the end of the window. WM1990 gives the window \(11{,}81 < \bar v < 12{,}18\) (PDF p. 6) and \(\bar v_{\mathrm{c}} = 10{,}48\) (figure 4, PDF p. 5), which agrees with our calculation.

What we have got. Theorem 26.37 is correct and says only that below \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the band is stable, not that above it it is unstable. Above \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the band is unstable at least as long as \(\mat K\) has an odd number of negative eigenvalues (lemma 26.38), then the Coriolis term decides. For the column of chapter 8 there is no Coriolis force and theorem 8.119 requires \(\mat G = \mat 0\): here it is not applicable. For the band of example A (\(\bar T = 7559\)) we did not compute windows, the numbers are for \(\bar T = 100\) as in the source. Above \(v_{\mathrm{c}}\) the contribution of the nonlinear terms, which the model does not have, grows with the speed (WM1990 PDF p. 6, Mote 1966, Thurman and Mote 1969): the linear windows are therefore a property of the model, not a prediction.

26.8 Finite elements for the moving string

In section 26.5 we turned the moving string (gibajoča se struna) into a system of ordinary equations with the Galerkin method, where the trial functions were the sines of chapter 13. A sine reaches across the whole string, so every entry of the matrices is an integral over the full length, and at the speed \(v/c = 0{,}9\) two sines gave the second frequency \(5{,}65\) instead of \(1{,}19\). Chapters 7 and 12 showed another way: small pieces that we assemble, where each piece contributes its own matrix, computed once. The question of this section is whether that way also works when the equation is no longer symmetric because of the mixed derivative term \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\). The answer has two parts. The matrix of this term is assembled from elements like the mass and stiffness matrices, and its symmetric part cancels at the interior nodes (figure 26.25), so after the two eyelets hold the ends it is antisymmetric. Therefore the system of elements inherits everything that we proved for the system of sines: the eigenvalues are purely imaginary and the energy is conserved.

Take the steel band of section 26.1: \(\mu = 0{,}3510\) kg/m, tension \(T = 4500\) N, wave speed \(c = 113{,}23\) m/s, span \(L = 1\) m. The dimensions of the band, the tension and the speeds are our own choice, no source in the books gives belt data (section 26.1). Let the band run at \(v = c/2 = 56{,}61\) m/s. By theorem 26.13 the lowest natural frequency is \(f_1 = \frac{c}{2L}\left(1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}\right) = 42{,}46\) Hz. A model of \(n = 4\), \(8\), \(16\) and \(32\) equal elements gives (the numbers are in the table below) \(f_1 = 45{,}32\), \(43{,}16\), \(42{,}64\) and \(42{,}50\) Hz (figure 26.26). All of them are above the true value and approach it. What of this we can prove and what we cannot, the section shows step by step.

The path is as follows, its steps are in figures 26.24, 26.25 and 26.26. First we show that the true solution satisfies a weak equation in which only first derivatives appear (lemma 26.39), because a trial function made of hat functions has kinks at the nodes and no second derivative. Then we compute the three element matrices (lemma 26.40). We assemble them and show that the total gyroscopic matrix is antisymmetric (corollary 26.41). At the end we try an end that no eyelet holds, and show that the energy is then no longer conserved (lemma 26.42).

26.8.1 The weak form

The model is the same as in section 26.1 (the elements are in figure 26.25): a string of mass \(\mu\) per length and tension \(T\) that moves along a fixed track with constant speed \(v\) through two eyelets at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), which are fixed in space and hold the displacement at zero, \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\). The idealizations of section 26.1 apply, the track speed is below critical, \(v < c\) with \(c = \sqrt{T/\mu}\) (definition 13.4). We write \(w\) for the displacement, as in chapter 13, and the letter \(v\) is always the track speed in this chapter, never the displacement of chapter 7. The nodal displacements of an element are written \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) as there. By theorem 26.4 the equation of motion is

\[\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (\mu v^2 - T)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0 . \tag{26.51}\]

A trial function made of hat functions (definition 6.25, one is in figure 26.24) is piecewise linear, has a kink at the nodes, and there the second derivative \(w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) does not exist. We cannot insert it into equation (26.51). As in chapter 6 we multiply the equation by a test function and integrate by parts, so that one derivative passes to the test function.

Lemma 26.39 Weak form of the moving string (šibka oblika gibajoče se strune)

Let \(w\) be a twice continuously differentiable solution of equation (26.51) on \([0, L]\) with \(w(0, t) = w(L, t) = 0\), and let \(\psi\) be a piecewise continuously differentiable function on \([0, L]\) (a test function) with \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\). Then for every time \(t\)

\[\mu\int_0^L \psi\,w_{\mathrm{tt}}\,\mathrm{d}x + 2\mu v\int_0^L \psi\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\,\mathrm{d}x + (T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L \psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 . \tag{26.52}\]
Proof

We must show that equation (26.52) follows from equation (26.51) when we multiply it by \(\psi\) and integrate, and that the last term gets a first derivative instead of a second.

  1. Multiply equation (26.51) at a chosen time by \(\psi(x)\) and integrate over \([0, L]\). The integral is linear (lemma 6.10), so \(\mu\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + 2\mu v\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (\mu v^2 - T)\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\).
  2. The function \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) is continuously differentiable because \(w\) is twice continuously differentiable, and \(\psi\) is piecewise continuously differentiable. By lemma 6.13 with \(N = \psi\) and \(w_{\mathrm{x}}\) in place of \(w\) we have \(\int_0^L \psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \psi(L)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) - \psi(0)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(0, t) - \int_0^L \psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  3. Because \(\psi(0) = \psi(L) = 0\), both boundary terms are zero and \(\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\int\psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\). Insert into step 1: the term \((\mu v^2 - T)\int\psi\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\) becomes \((T - \mu v^2)\int\psi'\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\), which is equation (26.52).

Source: WM1990 (1) (PDF p. 2) for the equation, step 2 is lemma 6.13. We derived the weak form ourselves, WM1990 does not treat elements (PDF p. 6 mentions only global discretizations).

The lemma states only one direction: the true solution satisfies equation (26.52). We do not need the converse. The Galerkin method (definition 6.42) demands that an approximation, not the true solution, satisfies equation (26.52), for every test function from the same family as the trial functions. The term with \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\) is the mass term, the term with \(\psi' w_{\mathrm{x}}\) the stiffness term as in chapter 6, and the term with \(w_{\mathrm{xt}}\) is the one that chapter 7 did not have. Its coefficient \(2\mu v\) is from the lemma on the acceleration of a material particle (lemma 26.1), where the same term arose from the chain rule.

26.8.2 Element matrices

We make the mesh as in chapter 7: \(n\) equal elements of length \(h = L/n\), nodes \(x_{\mathrm{k}} = kh\) for \(k = 0, \dots, n\), on each element the shape functions \(N_1 = (x_{\mathrm{b}} - x)/h\) and \(N_2 = (x - x_{\mathrm{a}})/h\) (definition 7.2). The displacements of nodes \(0\) and \(n\) are zero because of the eyelets, the unknowns are \(d_1(t), \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}-1}(t)\), and the trial function is \(w_{\mathrm{h}}(x, t) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^{n-1} d_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\psi_{\mathrm{j}}(x)\), where \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the hat function of node \(j\).

Each term of equation (26.52) gives one of three integrals over the element. We draw the element as in chapter 7 (figure 26.24). First we take the element of length \(h\) between nodes \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\), in one step the horizontal axis and the two vertical lines that the nodes bound. On it we draw the function \(N_1\), which is \(1\) at the left node and \(0\) at the right, and the function \(N_2\), which is the other way round. Under each of them is a triangle with base \(h\) and height \(1\), its area is \(h/2\). We need the area because the integral of the product \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\,N_{\mathrm{j}}'\) is exactly the area under \(N_{\mathrm{i}}\) times the value of the derivative \(N_{\mathrm{j}}'\), since the derivative is constant on the element: \(N_1' = -1/h\) and \(N_2' = 1/h\).

Lemma 26.40 Element matrices of the moving string (matrike elementa gibajoče se strune)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be an element of length \(h\) with nodes \(1\) and \(2\), \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (d_1, d_2)^\T\) the nodal displacements, \(\mu\), \(T\) and \(v\) constant on the element, and \(N_1\), \(N_2\) the shape functions. The integrals of the terms of equation (26.52) over the element are

\[\mat m_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{\mu h}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mat g_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{T - \mu v^2}{h}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \tag{26.53}\]

where \((\mat m_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = \mu\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x\), \((\mat g_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu v\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \((\mat k_{\mathrm{e}})_{\mathrm{ij}} = (T - \mu v^2)\int N_{\mathrm{i}}' N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x\). Moreover:

  1. The sum \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}} + \mat g_{\mathrm{e}}^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(-2, 2)\) is diagonal, its entry \((1, 1)\) is \(-2\mu v\) and its entry \((2, 2)\) is \(+2\mu v\). It does not depend on \(h\).
  2. For nodal displacements \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) we have \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\,(d_2^2 - d_1^2)\).
Proof

We must show three integrals and two consequences.

  1. By lemma 10.31 with \(\rho A = \mu\) the mass matrix is \(\frac{\mu h}{6}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the integral of the constant matrix \(\mat b_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat b_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac1{h^2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) times a constant coefficient, which is here \(T - \mu v^2\) instead of \(EA\). The proof of lemma 7.5 (steps 2 and 3) uses only that the coefficient is constant on the element, so \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{T - \mu v^2}{h}\left(\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  3. The derivatives are \(N_1' = -1/h\) and \(N_2' = 1/h\) (lemma 1.81), constant on the element. Hence \(\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = N_{\mathrm{j}}'\int N_{\mathrm{i}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The integral \(\int_0^h (1 - s/h)\,\mathrm{d}s = h - h/2 = h/2\) with \(s = x - x_{\mathrm{a}}\), and equally \(\int_0^h s/h\,\mathrm{d}s = h/2\).
  4. So \(\int N_{\mathrm{i}} N_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac h2 N_{\mathrm{j}}'\), which is \(-\tfrac12\) for \(j = 1\) and \(+\tfrac12\) for \(j = 2\), for both rows \(i\). Multiplication by \(2\mu v\) gives \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  5. Item 1: \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}^\T = \mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the sum is \(\mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
  6. Item 2: \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \mu v\,(-d_1^2 + d_1 d_2 - d_1 d_2 + d_2^2) = \mu v\,(d_2^2 - d_1^2)\).

Source: The mass and stiffness matrices as in lemmas 10.31 and 7.5 (COOK (11.3-4) PDF p. 392, COOK (2.2-1) PDF p. 34). The gyroscopic matrix of the element is our own computation (SymPy, outlines/ch-jermeni/num-08.out A), the sources do not give it.

The proof showed why the matrix \(\mat g_{\mathrm{e}}\) differs from \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\): it contains \(N_{\mathrm{j}}'\) and not \(N_{\mathrm{j}}\) or \(N_{\mathrm{i}}'\), so it is not symmetric. Its two rows are equal because the two shape functions have equal areas \(h/2\) under them. Item 1 is what we need: the symmetric part, which is the one that disturbs us, since in the equation \(\mat m\ddot{\vek d} + \mat g\dot{\vek d} + \mat k\vek d = \vek 0\) it would do work or take energy away, is only on the diagonal, namely \(-\mu v\) at the left and \(+\mu v\) at the right node of the element. Item 2 says the same in words: the term \(\vek d^\T\mat g\,\vek d = \mu v\,\big(w(x_{\mathrm{b}})^2 - w(x_{\mathrm{a}})^2\big)\) depends only on the displacements at the edges of the element, nothing comes from the interior. So it equals the integral of a derivative, \(2\mu v\int w\,w_{\mathrm{x}} = \mu v\int (w^2)_{\mathrm{x}}\), which the fundamental theorem computes as a difference of boundary values.

26.8.3 Assembly and antisymmetry

We assemble the elements as theorem 7.13 taught us. Let us see what happens to the diagonal of the gyroscopic matrix (figure 26.25). We draw \(n = 4\) elements with nodes \(0\) to \(4\) along the track. At every node one element reaches in from the right and one from the left. The element on the right of a node has it as its left node and contributes \(-\mu v\) to the diagonal, next to the node stands \(-1\) in units of \(\mu v\). The element on the left has it as its right node and contributes \(+\mu v\). The sum at interior nodes is \(0\), and at the end nodes \(-1\) stays at node \(0\) and \(+1\) at node \(4\). Nodes \(0\) and \(n\) are held by the eyelets, the displacement there is zero and their rows and columns drop out, so the symmetric part drops out of the system of unknowns \(d_1, \dots, d_{\mathrm{n}-1}\) too.

Corollary 26.41 The assembled gyroscopic matrix is antisymmetric (skupna žiroskopska matrika je antisimetrična)

Let the string of section 26.8.1 be divided into \(n\) equal elements with nodes \(0, \dots, n\) and let \(v < c\). Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\), \(\mat K\) be matrices of order \(n - 1\) with entries

\[M_{\mathrm{ij}} = \mu\int_0^L \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad G_{\mathrm{ij}} = 2\mu v\int_0^L \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad K_{\mathrm{ij}} = (T - \mu v^2)\int_0^L \psi_{\mathrm{i}}'\psi_{\mathrm{j}}'\,\mathrm{d}x \tag{26.54}\]

for \(i, j = 1, \dots, n-1\), and let the Galerkin system be \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek d} + \mat G\,\dot{\vek d} + \mat K\,\vek d = \vek 0\) (equation (26.52) with \(\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{i}}\)). Then:

  1. The matrices \(\mat M\), \(\mat G\), \(\mat K\) are the sums over the elements of the element matrices of lemma 26.40, placed as in theorem 7.13.
  2. The matrix \(\tilde{\mat G}\) with all nodes \(0, \dots, n\) has \(\tilde{\mat G} + \tilde{\mat G}^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(-2, 0, \dots, 0, 2)\), which is nonzero only in the first and last entry. The matrix \(\mat G\) is antisymmetric, \(G_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{i}+1} = \mu v\), \(G_{\mathrm{i}+1,\mathrm{i}} = -\mu v\) and all other entries are zero.
  3. The matrices \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric and positive definite.
  4. All eigenvalues of the system are purely imaginary, \(\lambda = \mathrm{i}\omega\) with real \(\omega\), and \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek d} + \tfrac12\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d\) is constant.
Proof

We must show that the assembly happens as for the bar, where the diagonal cancels, and then that the properties of section 26.5 apply.

  1. By lemma 6.10 the integrals in equation (26.54) are sums of integrals over the elements. On an element that is not in the row of the connectivity table of node \(i\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) (theorem 7.13, step 4), on the others \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the shape function of the element (step 5 of the same theorem). The piece of element \(e\) is therefore the entry of the element matrix of lemma 26.40 at the place that the connectivity table gives, which is item 1.
  2. Element \(e\) lies between nodes \(e - 1\) and \(e\). The diagonal entry \(\tilde G_{\mathrm{kk}}\) receives \(-\mu v\) from element \(k + 1\) (node \(k\) is its first) and \(+\mu v\) from element \(k\) (node \(k\) is its second), for \(k = 1, \dots, n-1\), and the sum is \(0\). Node \(0\) has only element \(1\) and gets \(-\mu v\), node \(n\) has only element \(n\) and gets \(+\mu v\). Off the diagonal, element \(e\) contributes its entry \((1, 2)\) at place \((e-1, e)\) with value \(\mu v\) and its entry \((2, 1)\) at place \((e, e-1)\) with value \(-\mu v\), no place gets two contributions, so \(\tilde{\mat G} + \tilde{\mat G}^\T\) is zero off the diagonal. Deleting rows and columns \(0\) and \(n\) removes the only nonzero entries, and \(\mat G\) is antisymmetric with the stated entries.
  3. By item 2 of theorem 7.13, \(\vek d^\T\mat M\vek d = \sum_{\mathrm{e}} \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), every term is by lemma 10.31 nonnegative and positive for \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} \ne \vek 0\). The sum is zero only if every \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \vek 0\), so \(\vek d = \vek 0\). The same theorem gives \(\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d = \frac{T - \mu v^2}{h}\sum_{\mathrm{e}=1}^n (d_{\mathrm{e}} - d_{\mathrm{e}-1})^2\) with \(d_0 = d_{\mathrm{n}} = 0\) (equation (7.14)). For \(v < c\) we have \(T - \mu v^2 = \mu(c^2 - v^2) > 0\), so the sum is zero only if all differences are zero, and so all \(d_{\mathrm{k}}\) equal \(d_0 = 0\).
  4. By items 2 and 3 we have real matrices \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) symmetric and positive definite and \(\mat G\) antisymmetric, which are the assumptions of theorem 26.27, giving purely imaginary eigenvalues, and of lemma 26.26, giving the conservation of \(\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}}\).

Source: Assembly by theorem 7.13, the structure of the system (symmetric \(\mat M\), \(\mat K\), antisymmetric \(\mat G\)) as in GR §2.11 (PDF pp. 137 and 139). Items 1 to 3 are our own proof, the sources do not treat discrete models of moving strings.

The proof showed where the antisymmetry comes from: at every interior node the two neighbours cancel the symmetric part, since the node sees the same entry \(\mu v\) once with a plus and once with a minus sign. The same can be read from the definition: \(G_{\mathrm{ij}} + G_{\mathrm{ji}} = 2\mu v\int (\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}})'\,\mathrm{d}x = 2\mu v\,\big[\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\big]_0^L\), which is zero because all test functions vanish at the ends. For hat functions this means the same as item 2. This computation shows that for the antisymmetry only the eyelets holding the ends matter, not the shape of the elements, so the same holds for other meshes.

We try the corollary on numbers. At \(v/c = 0{,}5\) and \(n = 8\) the smallest eigenvalue of the matrix \(\mat M\) (\(L = c = \mu = 1\)) is \(0{,}0448\) and of the matrix \(\mat K\) it is \(0{,}913\), at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) the matrix \(\mat K\) is still positive definite with smallest value \(0{,}231\) and at \(v/c = 0{,}99\) with \(0{,}0242\). The coefficient \(T - \mu v^2\) falls towards zero as \(v\) approaches \(c\), and \(\mat K\) becomes almost singular. At \(v = c\) we have \(\mat K = \mat 0\), which is the critical speed of section 26.4. The largest absolute real part of the eigenvalues is below \(3 \cdot 10^{-15}\) at all three speeds, so zero up to rounding.

26.8.4 Numbers and convergence

Figure 26.26 shows the error of the frequencies of the element model against the number of elements \(n\). We draw the axes: \(n\) on the horizontal axis with equal spacing per doubling and the frequency error \(\Delta\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{h}} - \omega\) on the vertical axis with decades. For \(v/c = 0{,}5\) the error of the first frequency is \(0{,}1586\), \(0{,}0390\), \(0{,}0097\), \(0{,}0024\) and \(0{,}0006\) at \(n = 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\). The error of the second frequency is \(1{,}288\), \(0{,}317\), \(0{,}078\), \(0{,}019\) and \(0{,}005\). Each time we double the elements the error is divided by \(4{,}06\), \(4{,}02\), \(4{,}00\) and \(4{,}00\) (first frequency), so it goes as \(h^2\), which is the dashed line of slope \(-2\). At \(v/c = 0{,}9\) the error of the second frequency is \(1{,}826\) at \(n = 4\) and still \(0{,}242\) at \(n = 8\). At the doublings from \(n = 4\) to \(n = 64\) it is divided by \(7{,}54\), \(4{,}63\), \(4{,}14\) and \(4{,}03\). The order \(h^2\) is the same, but at the higher speed the factor \(4\) settles only with more elements.

The errors are positive in all computed cases: the frequencies of the model are above the true ones. We observed this and did not prove it. In chapter 10 theorem 10.42 gives an upper bound when the system \(\mat M\ddot{\vek d} + \mat K\vek d = \vek 0\) has no gyroscopic term, but here \(\mat G \ne \mat 0\) and its proof does not apply. We also only measured the order \(h^2\). A proof would need an error estimate for a system with an antisymmetric term, which we did not find in the books that we use.

The table connects the numbers with the band from the start of the section (\(v = c/2 = 56{,}61\) m/s, \(L = 1\) m). The angular frequency \(\omega\) computed with \(L = c = \mu = 1\) is in units of \(c/L\), so the frequency of the band is \(f = \omega\,c/(2\pi L)\) with \(c/(2\pi L) = 18{,}02\) Hz:

\(n\) \(f_1\) (Hz) \(f_2\) (Hz)
4 45,32 108,12
8 43,16 90,64
16 42,64 86,33
32 42,50 85,27
exact 42,46 84,92

We also compare with section 26.5 at \(v/c = 0{,}9\) with the same number of unknowns. Two sines give \(\omega_1 = 0{,}663\) and \(\omega_2 = 5{,}655\), three elements (two unknowns) \(\omega_1 = 0{,}851\) and \(\omega_2 = 5{,}393\), the true values are \(0{,}597\) and \(1{,}194\). With two unknowns both families are poor and the elements are no better. For the sines of the stationary string WM1990 (PDF p. 6) says the same: at high speed they describe the motion poorly. The advantage of the elements is that the error falls with the number of elements as figure 26.26 shows.

26.8.5 An end that nothing holds

The antisymmetry of the matrix \(\mat G\) came from the eyelets. We try what happens without the right eyelet. The lower half of figure 26.25 has the same elements, contributions from the right and from the left and sum, only that node \(n\) is not held and its \(+1\) stays. We try it as a model of the mechanism, not as a description of a real end of a belt. A real free end, where the track leaves the span, is not treated in this chapter and the sources do not derive it. Node \(n\) is now an unknown and the test function \(\psi_{\mathrm{n}}\), which equals \(1\) at \(x = L\), is allowed. In the derivation of the weak form in lemma 26.39 the boundary term \((\mu v^2 - T)\,\psi(L)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t)\) remains. If we set it to zero for every \(\psi(L)\) we demand the boundary condition \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\). At \(x = 0\) the eyelet is still there, \(w(0, t) = 0\).

Lemma 26.42 Energy at an unheld end (energija pri koncu, ki ni držan)

Let the model of section 26.8.1 have an eyelet at \(x = 0\) and the boundary condition \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\) at \(x = L\), let \(v < c\) and let \(w\) be three times continuously differentiable. Let \(\mathcal E^*(t) = \frac12\int_0^L\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}^2 + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x\) be the conserved quantity of section 26.4. Then:

  1. \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal E^*}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2 \le 0\).
  2. In the Galerkin system with elements, where node \(n\) is an unknown, the symmetric part of the matrix \(\mat G\) is \(\mat G + \mat G^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(0, \dots, 0, 2)\), \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek d} = \mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2 \le 0\).
Proof

We must show that the energy is not conserved at an end that nothing holds, and why.

  1. Differentiate in time under the integral (\(w\) is smooth enough): \(\dot{\mathcal E}^* = \int_0^L\big(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{t}}\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}\,w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big)\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. From equation (26.51), \(\mu\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} = -2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Insert: the integrand is \(-2\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} + (T - \mu v^2)\big(w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}}\big)\).
  3. By the product rule, \(2 w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} = (w_{\mathrm{t}}^2)_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{xx}} + w_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{xt}} = (w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{x}}\). The fundamental theorem gives \(\dot{\mathcal E}^* = -\mu v\,\big[w_{\mathrm{t}}^2\big]_0^L + (T - \mu v^2)\big[w_{\mathrm{t}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\big]_0^L\).
  4. At \(x = 0\) we have \(w = 0\) at all times, so \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(0, t) = 0\). At \(x = L\) we have \((T - \mu v^2)\,w_{\mathrm{x}}(L, t) = 0\). What remains is \(-\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2\), which is item 1. With an eyelet at \(L\) we would also have \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t) = 0\) and the quantity would be conserved.
  5. Item 2: the matrix of element \(n\) from lemma 26.40 has its entry \((2, 2)\) equal to \(+\mu v\) at place \((n, n)\), and node \(n\) has no neighbour on the right to cancel it (figure 26.25 below). The other entries cancel as in corollary 26.41. So \(\mat G + \mat G^\T = \mu v\,\mathrm{diag}(0, \dots, 0, 2)\) and \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat G\,\dot{\vek d} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T(\mat G + \mat G^\T)\dot{\vek d} = \mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\).
  6. Multiply the system \(\mat M\ddot{\vek d} + \mat G\dot{\vek d} + \mat K\vek d = \vek 0\) from the left by \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\): \(\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat M\ddot{\vek d} + \dot{\vek d}^\T\mat K\vek d = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathcal E_{\mathrm{h}} = -\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat G\dot{\vek d} = -\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), because \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric.

Source: The derivation is our own. That the energy of the span is not conserved because particles carry energy through the eyelets is in CHEN2005 §2.5 (PDF p. 6) and in equation (32) (PDF p. 7), see lemma 26.23.

The lemma says what would happen: the energy would not be conserved but would fall at the rate \(\mu v\,\dot d_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). The term \(-\mu v\,w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t)^2\) is cancelled only by an eyelet that holds \(w_{\mathrm{t}}(L, t) = 0\). We also compute numbers (\(L = c = \mu = 1\), \(v/c = 0{,}5\)). At \(n = 4, 8, 16\) the matrix \(\mat G + \mat G^\T\) has a single nonzero entry, of value \(1\), which is \(2\mu v\). The largest real part of the eigenvalues is \(-0{,}43\), \(-0{,}42\) and \(-0{,}21\), so all eigenvalues are left of the imaginary axis, which is something quite different from less than \(3 \cdot 10^{-15}\) at the held end. These numbers change with the mesh, so we do not conclude a final decay rate from them. Only that the energy does not grow is proved (item 2 of lemma 26.42). That all eigenvalues lie left of the imaginary axis we merely observed.

26.8.6 What we showed and what we did not

We proved three things. First: the weak form of the moving string has three integrals and the element matrices are these three, among them the gyroscopic matrix \(\mu v\left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\), which does not depend on the length of the element (lemma 26.40). Second: after assembly its symmetric part remains only at the end nodes, the eyelets remove them, so the system of elements is of the same kind as the system of sines and has purely imaginary eigenvalues and a constant energy (corollary 26.41).
